paragraphs.text: INTERPRETATION OF THE PROPHECY OF THE DIVINE EZEKIEL. The eyes of the body were created to judge shapes and colors. When they are healthy they judge correctly and very justly. When they are in a weak condition, they miss what is proper and do great harm to just judgment: either they do not see at all, or they see one thing in place of another and so fail to judge rightly the nature of what they see. The eye of the soul performs this same function for these things too, but it also received another power from its Creator. By this power it distinguishes the qualities not only of shapes and colors, smells and tastes and other such things, but also judges words and reasonings. It separates the impious ones among them from the pious, knows the difference between divine and human things, and, in short, as the wise Solomon says, understands a parable and a dark saying, the words of the wise and riddles. It distinguishes each of these when it is in good condition and freed from unbelief. But when such a mist comes in front of it, it suffers the same thing as the bodily eyes: it sees one thing in place of another, or does not see at all, once the affliction has gained the upper hand. Some people, having fallen into this disease, have tried to accuse divine Scripture, and especially the prophetic oracles, of being veiled in obscurity. The inspired Paul might fittingly say to them: "Even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing"; "for we speak wisdom among the mature." In agreement with this are the words spoken by

our Lord and Savior to the holy apostles: "To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom, but to them it has not been given." And he at once adds the reason: "because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not understand." For they themselves, he says, willingly draw the cloud of ignorance over themselves. As the divine Apostle says, "if they turn to the Lord, the veil is removed." So divine things are not obscure to everyone, but only to those who are willingly blind. These people ought to have considered and recognized that nothing precious lies ready to hand for human beings. The depths of the sea hide the pearl, and likewise the flower of royal purple. The veins of gold and silver do not lie on the surface of the earth but are covered within its bosom. In our houses, too, we keep our more valuable possessions inside in storerooms and put fastenings, bars and seals on the doors. And we usually reveal our more serious plans to our truest friends, not to everyone indiscriminately. Divine things are more venerable than all of these, and better by as much as invisible things are better than visible ones, intelligible things than things of sense, and abiding things than things that flow away. It is fitting, then, that they should be guarded more carefully, and, to use the Lord's words, that the pearls should not be thrown before swine. For what is easily obtained is in fact easily despised, while what is acquired with toil is greatly longed for and very dear. To what has been said we must add one more point. The oracles of the divine prophets contain an accusation of the lawlessness of the Jews, but they hold out a promise of good things to the nations. The prophecy therefore had to be shadowed, so that the Jews, habitually enslaved to envy and bold enough to plot against the good things of others, would not destroy the books that foretold these things. Events testify that this too is a cause of the apparent obscurity. For long ago these things were unclear to the Jews, so that the written record of the blessing concerning the nations might be preserved. But when the prediction was fulfilled and events followed what had been written, then the oracles of the prophets became clear and plain, for those who read the prophetic books take their interpretation from the events. Let no one, therefore, and especially no one nurtured in true religion, be insolent toward the divine Spirit by blaming his words for obscurity. Instead, let whoever wishes to understand the sacred words cry out with the inspired David: "Uncover my eyes, and I shall perceive the wonders of your law." He will surely obtain his request, since he has asked for knowledge for the sake of benefit. For we too, offering this

supplication to the Lord, who "gives wisdom to the blind," as the divine David says, and to "those in darkness and gloom," as the blessed Isaiah says, shall venture upon the interpretation of the inspired Ezekiel. We shall try, as far as we can, to search out the depth of the prophecy, and to set the profit gathered from it before all the pious as a common good. Come, then: before the interpretation, let us go through the subject matter in summary. This prophet began to prophesy in the fifth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah. This captivity was not the first, as some have thought, but the third of Jerusalem, the fourth of Judah, and the sixth of all Israel. First, Tiglath-pileser took the greater part of the ten tribes captive. Second, Shalmaneser enslaved Samaria and the cities around it and went away. Third, Sennacherib besieged the other cities of Judea and deported many captives. But when he attempted, with great impiety, to march against Jerusalem, he received the wages of his blasphemy: he lost his army to a blow sent by God and reached his homeland with only a few men. After him, fourth, came Nebuchadnezzar. In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, Nebuchadnezzar, now king, came into Judea with a great army. He took many talents of gold and silver, many captives from the royal family and some of the sacred vessels, put the king in chains, and departed. After a short time Jehoiakim refused to pay the agreed tribute. So in the eleventh year of Jehoiakim's reign, the eighth of his own rule, Nebuchadnezzar marched against Jerusalem again. He killed Jehoiakim, ordered him to be thrown from the wall, and left him unburied for a very long time. He took all those in authority captive, appointed Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, as king over those who were left (he was the son of Jehoiakim), and went back to Babylon. Three months and a few days later he learned that Jehoiachin had rebelled, and came again. He put him in fetters and led him away captive with no small multitude. As king he appointed Jehoiachin's uncle Mattaniah, also called Zedekiah, who was the brother of the earlier Jehoiakim and a son of Josiah. He took oaths from him that he would keep faith with him and pay the tribute at the proper time. But this king too broke his oaths. He would neither pay the tribute nor keep

faith with him, but fled for help to the Egyptians. So Nebuchadnezzar gathered a great army and came. He took the city together with its inhabitants and burned the palace, the divine temple and every splendid house. All who had escaped death by famine and slaughter in war he led away captive. He also carried off to Babylon all the vessels, not only those made of silver and gold but also the pillars made of bronze, and everything else. The captivity of Jeconiah, then, was not the first, as some have thought, but the third of Jerusalem. This is taught us by the Fourth Book of Kingdoms, by the book of Chronicles, and by the divine prophet Daniel, who begins his prophecy this way: "In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it, and the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, together with part of the vessels of the house of God." And a little later: "And the king told Ashpenaz, his chief eunuch, to bring in some of the sons of the captivity of the sons of Israel and some of the royal seed." The first captivity of Jerusalem, then, took place in the third year of Jehoiakim's reign, which was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar's reign. The same prophet teaches us this when he says: "In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, he dreamed a dream." The second captivity, as I said, took place in the eleventh year of Jehoiakim's reign and the eighth of Nebuchadnezzar's rule. The third took place in the first year of the reign of Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim and the ninth of Nebuchadnezzar's rule. The blessed prophet Jeremiah also teaches us this clearly, and anyone who wishes can easily reckon the dates and learn them clearly from that prophet. Ezekiel, then, began to prophesy in the fifth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah. It was also the fifth year of the reign of Zedekiah, who had been appointed king of the Jews in place of Jeconiah. Daniel had begun to prophesy twelve years earlier. At the same time that these two were prophesying in Babylon, Jeremiah, Zephaniah and Uriah son of Shemaiah were prophesying in Judea. Those three, however, were older not only than Ezekiel but also than Daniel. For the blessed Jeremiah began to prophesy in the thirteenth year of Josiah's reign, and Zephaniah too [is said] to have delivered his prophecy under King Josiah [?]

So when I considered that the loving Lord set a limit of seventy years on the captivity of Judah, and that forty of the seventy years still remained, I realized why the prophet calls this the thirtieth year of the captivity. But when I traced the dates back and searched out the time, I found that the captivity had taken place not thirty years earlier but thirteen. God, however, being good and loving, usually counts the time of chastisement from his own sentence, not from the outcome of events. He did so with the patriarch Abraham as well. He had said, "Your offspring will be sojourners in a land not their own, and they will enslave them and mistreat them for four hundred years." Yet he did not let them spend all that time among the Egyptians, but counts the four hundred years from the sentence. With Noah, too, he had given a term of one hundred and twenty years for repentance, but when he saw lawlessness increasing he did not wait for the end of the term, so as to stop the course of sin. In the same way we shall find the thirty years here, if we take God's sentence as the starting point of the count. God decreed the captivity and servitude of the Jews in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign. Hilkiah the high priest found the law of Moses buried (for lawlessness had so taken hold of the Jews that divine things had been completely forgotten). Then the king read it and saw that what the people had dared to do was directly contrary to the law. Greatly terrified because of this, he urged the high priest to make God favorable. The high priest went to Huldah the prophetess, a pious woman and a guardian of the divine laws. Inspired and filled with the divine Spirit, she said to him: "Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Tell the man who sent you to me: Behold, I am bringing evils upon this place and upon those who live in it, all the words of the book that the king of Judah has read, because they have forsaken me and burned incense to other gods, so as to provoke me with all the works of their hands. My wrath will be kindled against this place and will not be quenched. And to the king of Judah, who sent you to seek the Lord, you shall say this: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Because you heard my words, and your heart repented, and you humbled yourself before me when you heard what I spoke against this place and against those who live [?] [fragments of footnotes: "and they will humble"; "buried"; [?]]

in it, that it would become a desolation, and because you tore your garments and wept before me, I too have heard, says the Lord. Not so: behold, I am gathering you to your fathers, and you will be brought to your tomb in peace, and your eyes will not see all the evils that I am bringing upon this place and upon those who live in it." The book of Chronicles also teaches these things. They were done and spoken in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign, and he reigned thirty-one years. So from the eighteenth to the thirty-first year there are fourteen years. After him Jehoahaz reigned three months, and these must be added to those years, because the prophecy was given in the eighth month of the eighteenth year. Then of Jehoiakim [?] … [?] under whom the first return took place, the seventy-year period is completed. Whoever wishes to count the seventy years of the desolation should begin from the eleventh year of Zedekiah, for that was when the divine temple was burned, and end with the second year of Darius son of Hystaspes, under whom they rebuilt the divine temple with all zeal and the work was brought to completion. The prophet, then, says:

"In the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth of the month, I was in the midst of the captivity by the river Chebar, and the heavens were opened, and I saw a vision of God. (2) On the fifth of the month—this was the fifth year of the captivity of King Jehoiachin." He himself has taught us clearly that it was not simply the fifth year of the captivity, but of the captivity of King Jehoiachin. This, as I said, was Jeconiah, who reigned three months and a few days, for his father Jehoiakim had been slain at Jerusalem in the eleventh year of his reign. He says the heavens were opened, not in reality and fact, but in spiritual contemplation. "And I saw," he says, "a vision of God": not the essence of God, but a "vision," that is, a revelation and, as it were, a representation that human nature can attain. "And I was in the midst of the captivity": the pious man among the impious, the righteous man among

the lawless. So great is the Lord's love for humanity that, for the sake of sinners, he hands over his own servants to grievous misfortunes. (3) "And the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel son of Buzi, the priest, in the land of the Chaldeans, by the river Chebar." He is adorned with two gifts, priesthood and prophecy, and both are gifts of the Spirit. He also names the country and the place where he was granted the divine revelation, and by this he indicates many things. First, that the Divine is uncircumscribed: it does not hold authority in Jerusalem alone or rule over the Jews only, but is the maker and governor of all. This also shows God's ineffable goodness: even when he has handed them over to captivity he does not leave them uncared for, but grants them every kind of providence and the care they need. He grants him the vision beside waters to foreshadow the salvation of all people and to foretell the knowledge of God that would come to the pious through the regeneration of water. In the same way the inspired Daniel saw those divine visions beside waters, and Moses the lawgiver, cast out on the riverbank, found salvation through waters. So again a well and its water brought about a marriage, which happened to the patriarchs before him, not only to Jacob but also to Isaac. But let us return to the interpretation, for at present our discourse is not aimed at these matters. "And the hand of the Lord came upon me." This is what he called the working of the divine Spirit. The inspired Paul too, when inflicting punishment on Elymas for opposing him, said: "Behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind, not seeing the sun for a time." This was the working of the divine Spirit, as Paul himself says: "in the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Spirit of God." "The hand of the Lord came upon me," he says. (4) "And I looked, and behold, a lifting wind was coming from the north, and a great cloud in it, and brightness all around it, and fire flashing like lightning." We must first state the reason for the revelation, and then go on to interpret it in detail. At this time many false prophets were contradicting the prophets, as the blessed Jeremiah teaches us especially. God had commanded him to wear a yoke and to foretell the captivity of the king and of all the people. A certain false prophet, Hananiah, broke the yoke and contradicted what the prophet said. He lied outright, shouting that not only would the city not be laid waste, but those who had already been taken captive would return before long. So God the Lord, still more indignant, commands Jeremiah to put iron bonds

on himself in place of the wooden ones, to foretell the siege and enslavement to those in Judea, and to write to the captives in Babylon telling them to build houses and plant vineyards, since the sentence of seventy years would not fail. It was necessary, then, not only that Jeremiah should say and write these things in Judea, but also that those in captivity should learn them through the prophets who were among them. And so the prophet sees the utter destruction that was to come upon Jerusalem. This is what "a lifting wind was coming from the north" signifies, or, as Symmachus put it, "a storming wind." The violence of the wind signifies the onslaught of the Babylonian. The "very great cloud" signifies the flood of spears, javelins and missiles of every kind. The "flashing fire" signifies not only the terror that would be brought on them but also the destruction of the city by fire. The "brightness all around" signifies the glory of God made manifest through the punishment. For since they had not profited from his benefits, and had refused to recognize the Benefactor through them, they receive knowledge of him through punishment. That is why they cry: "After my captivity I repented." "And in the midst of it, something like the appearance of electrum in the midst of the fire, and brightness in it." Up to this point he has shown us the whole revelation together; from here he moves on to explain it part by part. (5) "And in the midst, something like the likeness of four living creatures." Both man and angel are called a rational living creature, but the one is rational and mortal, the other rational and immortal. Who could interpret this revelation clearly, when the prophet himself struggled to describe it? He did not simply say that he saw four living creatures, nor even a likeness of living creatures, but "something like the likeness of four living creatures." This makes it clear that the inspired prophets did not see the very natures of invisible beings, but certain images and impressions shown to them by the bountiful Giver to meet each need. He then tells us the [?] of the living creatures he saw: "For this," he says, "was their appearance: the likeness of a man was in them. (6) And each one had four faces, and each one had four wings. (7) And their legs were straight, and their feet were winged, and there were sparks like gleaming bronze, and their wings were light. (8) And a man's hand was beneath their wings on their four sides." The form of what he saw, then, was upright

[Editorial note, partly garbled:] in the ed. [?]. The fuller reading is that of A [?]. Alex.: "On their four sides; and the faces and the wings of the four of them were joined one to another; [?] their faces did not," etc.

…he says it was, and that it looked like a man. Each had four faces and four wings, and he said they had as many hands as wings, and that their feet too were full of feathers. By the number of the faces and of the wings of the powers that bear the divine form, he hints at the oversight of God, King of all, which reaches everywhere. Their being winged signifies how swift their nature is. The sparks like gleaming bronze signify their brightness and the purity of their minds. The hands hidden under the wings signify their invisible and varied activity. To these he adds: (9) They did not turn as they went; each went straight ahead. A man walking northward who then wants to cross to the south has to turn around so that his face is toward it [?]. But those whose faces are as many as the four regions of the world have no back. Every face looks out in every direction, and each goes wherever it wishes and has no need to turn. [?] (10) And the likeness of their faces, he says: the face of a man, and the face of a lion on the right for the four, and the face of an eagle for the four, and the face of a calf on the left for the four. These were their faces. But let no one suppose that the invisible powers bear the images of beasts and irrational animals. Through these he hints at other things. Through the lion he hints at kingship, for that animal is royal. Through the calf he hints at priesthood, for one calf was offered for the high priest. Through the eagle he hints at prophecy, for that animal flies high and has very sharp sight. Prophecy is like that: its vision is lofty, and it foresees from far off the things that are to come. Through what has been said, then, he teaches that the whole of human nature, together with its own rulers, is subject to the King of all, and that he has adorned the human race with so many gifts. (11) And their wings, he says, were spread out above for the four; each had two joined to one another, and two covered their body. By this he shows that not everything can be grasped even by the divine powers: some things are plain and others hidden. He also shows that they do not overstep the limits laid down for them. They spread out two wings, delighting in the contemplation granted them, and with two they cover their body, content not to know what is hidden and not striving to learn what it is not lawful…

…and they did not turn. This signifies that the invisible powers obey readily in all things, and that they did not leave the path appointed for them. The divine David teaches this very thing when he says: "Bless the Lord, all his angels, mighty in strength, who do his word, hearkening to the voice of his words." (13, 14) And in the midst of the living creatures there was something like the appearance of burning coals of fire, like the sight of torches whirling about among the living creatures, and the brightness of the fire, and out of the fire went forth lightning. And the living creatures ran and returned, like the appearance of bezek. Symmachus rendered this "like the appearance of a flash of lightning." [?] …and full of dread, and foreshadowing the threat of punishment. The coals of fire, the whirling torches, the lightning sent out from them, the running of the creatures this way and that, and the radiance sent out by their running all point to the evils to come. Blessed David too counts these among punishments. At one point he says, "Hail and coals of fire"; at another, "Coals of fire shall fall upon them"; elsewhere, "He multiplied lightnings and threw them into confusion"; and in another place, "Flash forth your lightning and you will scatter them; send out your arrows and you will throw them into confusion." (15, 16) And I looked, and behold, one wheel on the ground beside each of the four living creatures. And the appearance of the wheels and their workmanship were like the appearance of Tarshish. Symmachus has "like the appearance of hyacinth." "And the four had one likeness, and their appearance and their workmanship were one." Beside each of the living creatures he saw a wheel following it, with the appearance of hyacinth. He said he saw no difference among them: the four were exactly alike. "For their appearance," he says, "and their workmanship were one, as though a wheel were within…"

(17, 18) They went toward their four sides, and they did not turn as they went, nor did their backs. And they had height, and they were fearsome. He speaks of four faces, and through them the word hints at the oversight of God that reaches everywhere. In the same way he explains the appearance of the wheels: "as though," he says, "a wheel were within a wheel." One can picture this by imagining two circles and fitting one into the other

crosswise. A figure like that, resting on the same base, can move toward the four quarters: east and west, I mean, and north and south. This, then, is what the blessed prophet means: "As though a wheel were within a wheel, they went toward their four sides, and they did not turn as they went." Such a figure needs no turning, since from the same base it moves easily toward each of the regions. This too likewise signifies that God is present everywhere, though these things were seen in a cruder and more bodily form because of human weakness. "And I looked at them, and behold, their backs were full of eyes all around, for the four." (19–21) And when the living creatures went, the wheels went beside them; and when the living creatures rose from the earth, the wheels rose. Wherever the cloud was, there the spirit pressed on to go. The living creatures went, and the wheels rose with them, because a spirit of life was in the wheels. When the creatures went, the wheels went; when the creatures stood, the wheels stood; and when the creatures rose from the earth, the wheels rose with them, because a spirit of life was in the wheels. The blessed Paul teaches us this clearly when he lists the orders of the invisible natures and ranks certain Thrones among the other powers. "For in him," he says, "all things were created" (that is, in Christ), "whether visible or invisible, whether Thrones or Authorities, or Angels, or Powers; all things have been created in him and for him." So the Thrones too are a rational and incorporeal company. That is why the prophet says that a spirit of life was in the wheels, and why their movement was spontaneous and willing. No pole or yoke lay on the living creatures. Instead the cloud led the way, and that violent and mighty spirit followed. The divine chariot ran of its own accord: the living creatures went in front, and the wheels moved of themselves and were carried toward the four sides without turning. For their backs, he says, were full of eyes; that is, they were filled with knowledge. The meaning of the name "Cherubim" shows this too, for rendered into Greek the name means "fullness of knowledge." (22–25) And there was a likeness, he says, above the heads of the living creatures, like a firmament, like the appearance of awe-inspiring crystal, spread out over their heads above. And under the firmament their wings were spread out, beating each toward the other [?]…

…from the appearance of the loins and upward. And I saw, from the appearance of the loins and downward, I saw something like the appearance of fire, and its brightness all around. Like the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud on a day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. Everywhere he adds "likeness" and "as." He is teaching us not to stop there, but to know that each of the visions is fitted to the need of the moment. To the patriarch Abraham the Lord of all appeared as a man and showed him nothing fearsome, since he was about to give good promises to him and, through him, to the whole world. The promise of Isaac also contains the birth according to the flesh of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. That is why the blessing of the nations was joined to the promise of Isaac: "For in your offspring," he says, "all the nations of the earth shall be blessed." But when he foretold to Abraham the slavery of his descendants, he did not appear so kindly. Instead he showed a smoking furnace and torches of fire passing between the divided pieces. In the same way, when he wanted to encourage Jacob, who feared Esau, he appeared as a man. To Moses he showed fearful things at first: the fire in the bush, and the bush burning yet not burned up. Afterward, though, he speaks with him gently and shows nothing that could cause dread. And when he wanted to frighten Israel and make his power known, he showed them the whole mountain smoking, crashing thunder, sounding trumpets and thick darkness. In short, he terrified them so much that they begged the prophet not to let God speak with them, but to carry the divine words to them himself. He also showed this difference between visions to the great Elijah: first an earthquake, then fire, then a wind that shattered mountains and crushed rocks, and after these the breath of a gentle breeze, and the Lord in it. For he delights in goodness and wants to order human affairs patiently and gently, but great impiety and lawlessness force him to use those other means as well. That is why it says he was not in those things but in the gentle breeze. Those things answer not to his own will but to human need, while goodness and love for humankind belong to his very nature. So when you hear of different visions of God, do not suppose that the Divine has many forms. It is wholly incorporeal and formless, simple and uncompounded, without shape, invisible and unseen, and bounded by no limit. But he shows the visions, shaping them to fit the need; and [?]

Here, then, he showed those fearful things, but he also showed the benefit that was to come to all people: I mean the incarnate dispensation of our God and Savior. That is why he says the form was human but the natures were two, one of electrum and the other of fire, one bearing and the other borne. For the divine nature had put on the human. So he says that he saw the upper part as the appearance of electrum, and from the loins downward as the appearance of fire. The fire hints at the divine nature ("For your God," he says, "is a consuming fire"), and the electrum at the human. Electrum is like that: its appearance is mixed, as it were, resembling neither gold nor silver but being a kind of blend of the two. The human body is like that too. It is not earth alone, nor water by itself, nor fire, nor air, but is blended from the four elements. Or rather, such is the nature of man: neither a rational soul alone nor a mortal body alone, but both together. That is why the prophet sees, from the loins upward, the appearance of electrum, and yet also the appearance of fire within it all around. For the humanity of God the Word was made radiant, bright and glorious, immortal and incorruptible, by the nature that dwelt in it. So he rightly said: "And I saw something like the appearance of electrum, like the appearance of fire within it all around; from the appearance of the loins and downward, like the appearance of fire." For the divine nature bore the human. "And its brightness all around. Like the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud on a day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around." These too signify the divine gifts. Going out from there like radiance, they do good to the human race, signifying the rain that comes from there and bringing it. Having described everything in this way, the prophet added:

(1) This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord. He did not say, "This is the nature of the Lord," nor "the glory of the Lord," but "the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord." It is as if he were saying: he shaped the sight as he willed, and counted me worthy of the vision. "And I saw, and I fell on my face." And quite rightly. If the seraphim cover their faces as they sing their hymns, what would a man not suffer, clothed in a mortal body [?], when he came to behold the true [?]? But the Master who loves humankind [?] his fear. "For I heard," he says, "one speaking

to me, and he said to me: Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak to you." He calls him "son of man" as if to say: "Do not forget your nature now that you have been counted worthy of a vision beyond your nature, but know yourself. Yet do not stay in this excessive fear, since I am urging you to take courage. Stand and listen to what I say, without being thrown off balance, and show your steadfastness by standing." The good Master did not only say this; he also took away the fear by what he did. (2) "For a spirit came upon me," he says, "and took me up, and lifted me, and set me on my feet, and I heard him speaking to me." That is: a divine power touched me and held me together when fear had undone me, and made me able to stand and hear the words being spoken. (3) And he said to me: "Son of man, I am sending you to the house of Israel, who provoke me, who have provoked me, they and their fathers, and have rebelled against me to this very day." Who could measure the divine love for humankind in words? What mind could reach the ocean of his goodness? After countless acts of impiety and lawlessness he does not give up on their salvation. He accuses both them and their fathers of rebelling, of breaking the covenant they had agreed to, and of persisting in wickedness to this day. Yet he calls them back, and summons to health those who are incurably sick, even though he knows how disobedient they are and how unwilling to listen. That is why he also says:

(4) "And they are hard-faced and stubborn-hearted sons, to whom I am sending you." That is, they are brazen. They do not know how to blush and they are unwilling to change. Advice does not persuade them, and the force of punishment does not change them. "And you shall say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord." "Adonai" itself also means "Lord," but it carries a slightly different emphasis as well. He means, "Thus says the Lord, my Lord." (5) "If perhaps they will hear or be afraid, for it is a provoking house, they will also know that you are a prophet among them." The phrase "if perhaps" does not signify ignorance. He who knows all things before they come to be is ignorant of nothing in the future. That is why blessed David cries out to him: "You knew my sitting down and my rising up," [Dan. 3:89.]

"you understood my thoughts from afar; you searched out my path and my lot, and foresaw all my ways. Behold, Lord, you knew all things, the last and the first." So although he knows exactly how unyielding they are, he says "if perhaps." By this he teaches that the will is free, and that they can be changed if they wish. The same is true of what is said in the Gospel in the person of the father: "I will send my son to the tenants; perhaps they will respect him." There too "perhaps" does not express doubt, for he knew that they would not respect him. But he does what befits his own justice. So that no one should take his foreknowledge to be the cause of how events turn out, he has to use words of doubt. In this way he shows that the will is free, and he keeps a defense for himself on the day of judgment. For this reason, although he foresees their disobedience and refusal to listen, he tries every means to turn them from wickedness. That is why he cries out through the prophet Isaiah, "What more shall I do for this vineyard of mine that I have not done?" and again through Hosea, "What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah?" Even though he knows they are incurably sick, he still applies the remedies. Then on the day of judgment, when the divine benefits are brought forward, the disobedient will receive the sentence passed against them without any reply. This is also why blessed David cries out, "That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged." When our lawlessness is weighed against the divine benefits, it justly subjects us to punishment. The just Judge himself receives the verdict of victory even from those who are punished, since he has shown every kind of love for humankind and left no means of doing good untried. So "if perhaps they will hear or be afraid" does not signify that God is ignorant; it gives them room to repent. God knew Pharaoh's disobedience too. "For I know," he says, "that Pharaoh will not let you go except by a mighty hand and an uplifted arm." Yet he kept on being patient. If the Master inflicted punishments on the basis of his foreknowledge, how would God's justice have been known to those who cannot see the outcome he foreknew? That is why he waits for the outcome and only then brings the punishment. "So you too, O prophet," he says, "carry my words to your countrymen, so that you may bring them benefit, and they may learn that you are a prophet among them, a servant of the divine words." (6) "And you, son of man, do not fear them, nor be dismayed before their face, for

they will rage like goaded cattle, and gather against you on every side, and you live among scorpions. Do not fear their words, and do not be dismayed before their face, for it is a provoking house." The wickedness of those who try to plot against him is reason enough to despise them, for they are lawless and without divine help. So, he says, one must not fear such people, even if they dart at you like scorpions, even if they hurl insolent words, even if they rush at you in a great frenzy and madness. He hinted at this with "they will rage like goaded cattle," a metaphor from cattle: the gadfly drives them while they graze and often forces them to rush over cliffs. It is a kind of fly with a very sharp sting [?] … the cattle [?]. So he used this figure of speech for madness. (7) "And you, son of man, shall speak my words to them, if perhaps they will hear [?]" … contriving [?]. For [?], he says, to be frightened by the threat of punishment, and the threat must be carried out, since they refuse to yield to gentler words. (8) "And you, son of man, listen to the one speaking to you, and do not be provoking like the provoking house. Open your mouth and eat what I give you." He means: Do not oppose what I command you. Do not imitate those who speak against me, but do what you are told.

(9, 10) And I looked, and behold, a hand stretched out toward me, and in it a scroll of a book. And he unrolled it before me, and it had writing on the back and on the front; and there was written on it lamentation, and song, and woe.

(1) And he said to me: "Son of man, eat this scroll, and go and speak to the sons of Israel." He had good reason to say above, "If perhaps they will hear or be afraid." What is handed to the prophet is full of dread: "lamentation, and song, and woe," written over the whole scroll, inside and out. He calls books "scrolls," for that is how people in ancient times kept the record of their writings. The Jews still keep the divine Scriptures in such rolls today. (2, 3) And he opened my mouth and fed me this scroll. And he said to me: "Son of man, your mouth shall eat, and your

belly shall be filled with this scroll that is given to you." And I ate it, and in my mouth it was like sweet honey. "How sweet," says the divine David, "are your sayings to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth." Lamentation over sins is also sweet and very pleasant. "Despondency seized me," he says, "because of the sinners who forsake your law." And: "I saw the senseless and I wasted away, because they did not keep your sayings." His son also urges: "It is better to go to a house of mourning than to go to a house of laughter." So eating the scroll was like honey to the prophet, though the scroll held nothing delightful or pleasing, only lamentation, and song, and woe. But let no one suppose that the scroll was eaten in a physical, bodily way. Just as he saw that vision spiritually, so he also partook of this taste spiritually. (4–6) And he said to me: "Son of man, go, enter the house of Israel, and speak my words to them. For you are not sent to a people of obscure speech or heavy tongue, but to the house of Israel; nor to many peoples of foreign speech and other tongues, or of a [?] tongue, whose words you will not understand." Here he clearly shows the difference between the labors of the apostles and those of the prophets. The prophets were entrusted with the care of a single nation, and they came from that nation themselves, and the same

…whether they will hear.” He has taught clearly that he is not unaware of their disobedience but knows it precisely. At the same time he indicates that it comes from their own choice and not from their nature. “For the house of Israel,” he says, “will not be willing to listen to you, because they do not wish to listen to me.” That is: Do not be grieved at being ignored. It is me they contradict when they resist the words you bring them. The cause of their contradiction is their quarrelsome disposition, the hardness of their heart and the insolence of their mind. But do not be afraid at being sent to such people. 8–9. “For behold, I have made your face strong against their faces, and I will make your contention strong against their contention. And it shall be so continually: I have made your face stronger than rock. Do not fear them, and do not be dismayed before their face, for it is a rebellious house.” Knowing their wickedness [?] of disposition, he says, banish all fear from your mind. I will give you strength to match their contradiction and power equal to the toil. I will make your forehead stronger than any rock, so that whether you are abused, beaten or made to endure any other hardship, you will not flee the ministry of the word or abandon your care for them. 10–11. “And he said to me: Son of man, take into your heart all the words that I have spoken with you, and hear them with your ears. And go, enter into the captivity, to the sons of your people, and you shall say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord, whether they will hear, whether they will desist.” When you speak to them, he says, say nothing of your own. Be the minister of my words and deliver what I command you. It is likely that they will respect your labors and fear my threats. Again, as I said, the doubt does not signify ignorance. It stirs up the impulse of free will. 12. “And the Spirit took me up, and I heard behind me the sound of a great earthquake: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place.” For when I had received these commands, he says, I hastened to fulfill the ministry. I was not even allowed to use my feet: by divine assistance I was carried to those to whom I had been sent. It was necessary that he also perceive the earthquake, so that, pricked by fear, he would fulfill his ministry. He also mentions the hymn he sent up when he perceived the earthquake: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place.” He said this having been taught by God himself…

…for to the blessed Moses [?] to see clearly [?] … 13. “[and I saw the sound of the wings of the living creatures] beating, and the sound of the wheels beside them, and the sound of a great earthquake.” For as these [came] toward me [?], the living creatures moved by using their wings, and the wheels followed. As they moved, a very great quaking was produced, for a great din was carried in from every side. 14. “And the Spirit lifted me up and took me, and I went aloft in the impulse of my spirit.” For the grace of the divine Spirit came to be in me and made me cut through the air between heaven and earth like some winged creature. “And the hand of the Lord was strong upon me.” Again he means the grace of the Spirit. 15. “And I came into the captivity aloft,” that is, not walking but carried through the air. “And I went round among those who lived by the river Chebar, those who were there, and I sat there seven days, living among them.” For when I had reached those to whom I had been sent, he says, I remained silent for seven days, awaiting the divine working. 16–17. “And after the seven days the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel, and you shall hear a word from my mouth and warn them from me.” Take the place of a lookout, he says. People station such a man on a hill and order him to announce in advance the coming raids of the barbarians. So you too, standing as on a watchtower and lookout post of prophecy, proclaim to the people what you foresee, and carry my words across to them. 18. “When I say to the lawless man, ‘You shall surely die,’ and you do not warn him or speak to warn the lawless man, so as to turn him

from his ways, so that [he may live?] [?], that lawless man shall die in his lawlessness, and his blood I will require at your hand [?].” The threat is fearful and full of dread, able to terrify even those who are very hard as stone. [Great?] too is the [loving-kindness?] revealed through the threat. For he threatens to call the righteous man to account unless he makes known to the lawless man the threat of death and teaches him what is the cause [of life?] and what brings death. So greatly does the Maker and Master of all long for the repentance of sinners that if someone gathers every virtue but neglects the souls entrusted to him, he will gain nothing from his own good deeds and will pay the penalty for his neglect of them. But it is likely that one man will offer every kind of treatment and others will remain incurably sick, and so [he adds: 19. “But if you warn the lawless man, and he does not] turn from his way and from his lawlessness, that lawless man shall die in his lawlessness, and you will have delivered your soul.” You will be guiltless, he says, if you do what is fitting and contribute your own part. For even if his sickness remains incurable, he alone will pay the penalty. We should observe that the lawless man who persists in lawlessness [dies] whether or not he has someone to warn him, that is, to teach him. For nature is enough to tell us what ought to be done. Teaching is offered over and above, since divine [providence] devises every means for the salvation of humankind. 20. “[And when the righteous man turns away from] his righteousness and commits a transgression, and I put a torment before his face, [?] he shall die, because you did not warn him; [?] he shall die in his sins, because the righteous deeds he did shall not be remembered, and his blood I will require at your hand.” He did not say simply, “If the righteous man sins,” but “if he turns away from his righteousness and commits a transgression,” that is, if he abandons the straight road he has traveled and turns onto the other one. For the blessed David also committed very great sins, but he did not abandon the road he was traveling. He stumbled and fell, but he got up and kept to the same course. So, he says, suppose the righteous man leaves his own road and embraces the opposite one, and you, [knowing this?], do not at once rebuke the wrong and make no effort to bring him back to the former road. Then he will meet the end that the second road deserves and lose all his former labor. For he has come onto another road,

and the ends are opposite, each suited to its road: the end of the one is life, the end of the other death. So he will necessarily lose the gain of his former labors, falling into the end of the wicked road. But I will require his lost life at your hand and exact from you the penalty for your negligence. 21. “But if you warn the righteous man not to sin, and he does not sin, the righteous man shall surely live, because you warned him, and you will have delivered your own soul.” For you bring about a double life, for yourself and for him. Through your counsel he escapes the pit of [lawlessness] and meets the end that the righteous road deserves. And you will be freed from having to give account and will escape the greatest danger, because you cared for your neighbor’s salvation. These words are enough to rouse us too to zeal and to prepare us to take every care for our brothers, never ceasing to say and do everything for their benefit. Then we may escape the punishment that has been threatened and obtain the salvation that has been promised, in Christ Jesus our Lord, with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages.

“…and there it will be spoken to you.” For quiet suits the contemplation of divine things. When the mind is freed from the distractions that pull at it from outside and is no longer divided this way and that but turns inward on itself, it can understand divine things more precisely. 23–24. “And I arose and went out into the plain, and behold, the glory of the Lord stood there, like the vision and like the glory that I saw by the river Chebar; and I fell on my face. And the Spirit came upon me and set me on my feet.” He enjoys the vision more often so that he may become more zealous in the ministry of the word. We should observe that even VARIANT READINGS.

revelations suited to human nature could not be looked upon even by those who were very pure in mind. So it was with this prophet: although he had already experienced the vision, he falls down as soon as he sees it, and needs the grace that raises him up. “And he spoke to me and said to me: Go in and shut yourself up inside your house.” He commands that the prophecy be given through actions, and that the [siege] of Jerusalem be shown in advance through the things the prophet was ordered to do.

25–26. “And you, son of man, behold, bonds have been laid on you, and they will bind you with them, and you shall not go out from among them. And I will bind your tongue to your throat, and you shall be mute, and you shall not be to them a man who reproves, because it is a rebellious house.” Like a trainer preparing an athlete, the Master anoints the prophet. He foretells the painful things to come and the grim treatment the people will give him, and he urges him to endure, to persevere and to keep silent until he himself permits him to speak. And everywhere he adds “because it is a rebellious house,” teaching him not to fear those who provoke God without fear, for transgressors deserve only contempt. 27. “And when I speak to you, I will open your mouth, and you shall say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Let whoever hears, hear, and whoever disobeys, disobey, because it is a rebellious house.” This too shows clearly that the will chooses for itself. Offer your teaching to all alike, he says. Then, teaching that obedience is voluntary, he adds that whoever wishes should obey, and the disobedient man who thinks otherwise may contradict. Each will receive his wages according to what his will has chosen.

4:1–2. “And you, son of man, take a brick and set it before your face, and draw on it a city, Jerusalem. And put a siege around it, and build bulwarks against it, and throw up a palisade around it, and set camps against it, and post siege engines all around.” He is commanded to draw the siege of Jerusalem. The drawing is made on a brick because the inhabitants were unsound. They had not built their house on the rock, like that wise man, but on the sand. So the rivers came, the rain fell and the winds blew and beat upon their house, and it fell, and great was its fall.

3. “And take an iron pan and set it as an iron wall between you and the city, and set your face against it, and it shall be under siege, and you shall besiege it. This is a sign to the sons of Israel.” The prophet is commanded to take the role of God. That is why he is ordered to place an iron pan between himself and the city drawn on the brick. He is taught that although God is present and watching what is done against Jerusalem, he will not grant them any care. As if shut off by an iron wall, he will seem neither to see what is happening nor to hear those who plead with him. Do these things, he says, giving the prophecy through actions as a sign to those who now disobey and contra[dict]…

4–5. “And you shall lie on your left side and lay the iniquities of the house of Israel on it, according to the number of the hundred and fifty days that you lie on it, and you shall bear their iniquities. And I have given you their two iniquities as a number of days, a hundred and ninety days, and you shall bear the iniquities of the house of Israel and bring them to completion.” After Solomon, in the time of Rehoboam, the twelve tribes were divided. The ten were called sometimes Ephraim and sometimes Israel, while Judah and Benjamin were called Judah. Nevertheless they were one people, tracing their descent from Israel and from Abraham. So, treating them as one people, he joined again what he had spoken of separately. He assigned the hundred and fifty days to Israel and the forty to Judah, and then joined them again into the hundred and ninety days, as belonging to one body and one kinship. And after joining them he divided them once more, and

6. “And you shall lie a second time, on your right side, and bear the iniquities of the house of Judah forty days; I have appointed them to you a day for a year.” The lawlessness of the people called Israel was greater. They had departed from God entirely and worshiped now the heifers, now idols of every kind. That is why he assigns a hundred and fifty days to them and forty to Judah, each day counted as a year. The forty days of Judah signify the forty years remaining of the seventy. For God had declared through the prophet Jeremiah that they would spend seventy years in Babylon. But thirty years had already passed, since the divine Ezekiel began his prophecy in the thirtieth year of the captivity. And from the fifth year of Jeconiah’s captivity to the first year of the reign of Cyrus the Persian

the remaining forty years are completed. This can be gathered not only from the chronicles but also from the divine Scriptures. For the blessed prophet Jeremiah and the book of Chronicles teach that in the thirty-seventh year of the captivity of Jehoiakim, also called Jeconiah, Evil-merodach lifted up his head and brought him out of the prison house in the year he became king. After him Belshazzar reigned over the Babylonians, though not for long, for he acted impiously and was killed. He ruled about three years, since Daniel saw one of his visions in the third year of Belshazzar’s reign. After him Darius son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, received the kingdom, and he too ruled only a short time. The blessed Daniel teaches us this when he says: “In the first year of Darius son of Ahasuerus, in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, understood from the books the number of the years, according to the word of the Lord that came to Jeremiah the prophet, for the completing of the desolation of Jerusalem: seventy years.” So the forty days assigned to Judah signify the number of the remaining forty years. The hundred and fifty assigned to Israel signify a hundred and fifty years, after which the city was built and filled with inhabitants, walled and given back its fortifications, and the other cities of Israel and Judah regained their strength and received many inhabitants. This happened in the twentieth year of the reign of Artaxerxes son of Xerxes. In his time Nehemiah, who had been his cupbearer, asked a favor of the king, came to Judea with great eagerness and did all the things mentioned above. The book of Ezra teaches this clearly. If anyone wishes to learn the number of years precisely, let him begin his count from the fifth year of Jeconiah’s captivity, for that is where we began counting the forty. You will find forty years up to the first year of Cyrus the Persian. Then come the remaining twenty-nine years of Cyrus, then seven of Cambyses, then thirty-five of Darius son of Hystaspes, and after these twenty of Xerxes and nineteen of Artaxerxes, for in his twentieth year Artaxerxes ordered the walls of the city to be rebuilt. And let no one say that the rebuilding of Jerusalem did not matter at all to Israel, which had long ago been divided from the tribe of Judah. After the [return] the division did not continue. All who obtained the return lived on in concord, with Jerusalem as their mother city. 7. “And you shall set your face toward the siege of Jerusalem,” he says, “and you shall make your arm strong, and you shall prophesy against it.” Setting the face signifies indignation, and strengthening the arm the [punishment?] to be brought upon them…

8. “And behold, I have put bonds upon you, and you shall not turn from one side to the other until the days of your siege are completed.” For they must learn through what you do that they will not be called back before the appointed time. So you must spend the appointed time on each side without moving, so that they learn the sentence passed against them. 9–10. “And you, son of man, take wheat and barley and beans and lentils and millet and spelt, and put them into one earthen vessel, and make them into loaves for yourself, according to the number of days that you lie on your side. For a hundred and ninety days you shall eat them. And the food you eat shall be by weight, twenty shekels a day; you shall eat it at set times.” The prophet is given toilsome commands. He takes on in himself the figure of those being punished, and through what he was ordered to do he teaches the people about the famine that would come upon Jerusalem. That is why he is ordered to make his bread not from wheat alone but also from millet, spelt and beans. Such food is a sign of want, and the weight in turn signifies scarcity. You shall eat twenty shekels once a day, he says. These make three ounces and a little more, according to those who have studied these weights and measures precisely. 11. “And you shall drink water by measure, the sixth part of a hin; you shall drink it at set times.” This too indicates how severe the want caused by the siege would be. The hin was one of their measures, and according to the Syrian its sixth part held half a sextarius. The prophet was ordered to drink this measure in order to foreshow the scarcity of necessities that the siege would bring upon them. 12. “And you shall eat them as barley cakes baked in the ashes; you shall bake them on cakes of human dung before their eyes.” Make bread from these various grains, he says, in the way people usually make barley loaves, and let human dung be the fuel for the baking fire. This shows the defilements they would suffer among the nations. So he adds: 13. “Thus shall the sons of Israel eat their bread unclean among the nations to which I will scatter them.” For when they were captives mingling with foreign nations, they could not avoid living outside the law, and the mingling gave them many occasions for transgression. 14. “And I said: By no means, Lord God of Israel! Behold, my soul has not been defiled with uncleanness

“…and I have not eaten anything that died of itself or was torn by beasts from my birth until now, nor has any stale or unclean meat entered my mouth.” The prophet was forced to lay bare his lawful way of life, and he begged the loving Master to cancel what had been commanded by giving another order. He won him over at once, for the Lord is good and readily yields to those who plead with him. That is exactly what happened then: he told him to use cow dung for baking the bread. To this he adds (4:16–17): “Son of man, behold, I am breaking the staff of bread in Jerusalem, and they shall eat bread by weight and in want, and drink water by measure and in ruin, so that they may lack bread and water; and a man and his brother shall be brought to ruin, and they shall waste away in their iniquities.” That baking signifies two things. The weighing signifies the famine in Jerusalem, and the unclean way the bread was prepared signifies their life among the lawless nations. But the punishment is just. “For they shall waste away,” he says, “in their iniquities”; that is, they will pay the penalty for the sins they went on committing.

But the [?] punishment [?]. “For they shall waste away,” he says, “in their iniquities”; that is, they will pay the penalty [?] for the sins they went on committing. [?] CHAPTER 5. [?] (5:1) “And you, son of man, take a sharp sword, sharper than a barber’s razor. Get it for yourself and bring it over your head and over your beard. Then take scales for weighing, and divide the hairs.” [?] The sword hints at the power to punish. The removal of the hair from the head and the beard signifies the loss of their beauty. The scales [?] signify [?] the justice of the sentence, for nothing goes unweighed [?] in his unsearchable

judgments. [?] (5:2) “A fourth part you shall burn with fire in the middle of the city when the days of your siege are completed. Take a fourth and burn it in the middle of it. Cut a fourth to pieces with the sword all around it. Scatter a fourth to the wind, and I will draw out a sword after them.” He interprets this himself a little later. There he calls the fire famine and death, and this is why he ordered two of the fourths to be given over to the fire: both famine and death consume people as fire does. The sword signifies the enemies’ attack and the slaughter they will carry out. The scattering signifies the captivity and the dispersion that was to come. He added about these: “And I will draw out a sword after them.” For indeed, after they were taken captive, they suffered countless kinds of death.

(5:3–4) “And you shall take from there a few in number,” he says, “and wrap them in your cloak. From these you shall take some again, throw them into the middle of the fire, and burn them up in the fire. From it a fire will go out to the whole house of Israel.” By this he means those who were left behind, whom Nebuzaradan the chief of the guard left with Gedaliah. They too were destroyed in various ways. Some were killed by one another, and others ran away to Egypt and did not give up their impiety. The prophecy of Jeremiah teaches us this clearly. The words “From it a fire will go out to the whole house of Israel” hint at the rage of the Babylonian at that time and at the destruction brought upon them in Egypt. They also foretell the factions that arose after the return, in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, which plunged them into those countless calamities. Above all they foretell their madness against Christ the Master, and the total destruction that followed the cross, and their dispersion through the whole world. When you have done these things, he says, tell them also the reasons for the punishment. (5:5–6) “Thus says the Lord God: This is Jerusalem. I have set her in the middle of the nations, with the countries all around her. And you shall say: She has turned my ordinances into lawlessness more than the [nations?] [?] around her. For they have rejected my ordinances and have not walked in my statutes.” The God of the universe chose the nation of the Jews because he wished to do good to all people through them. That is why he gave them a law that set them apart from everyone else, so that this too would make them stand out. He also gave them the middle of the world as their place to live. To the east and north they had Asia, to the west Europe, joined to them by the sea, and to the south Libya. These are the three parts into which the sons of Noah divided the world. “I have set Jerusalem, then,” says God, “in the middle of the nations, so that they might draw benefit from her and learn from her every kind of piety and good order. But she has done the exact opposite. Not only did she fail to share with them the good order I had given her; she even took on their impiety.” (5:7–8) “Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because your form is taken from the nations around you, you have not walked in my statutes or carried out my ordinances; you have not even acted according to the ordinances of the nations around you. Therefore thus says

the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I will execute judgment in your midst in the sight of the nations.” Since you have stamped yourselves with the character of the nations, he says, and mixed yourselves up in their practices, and spat on my ordinances and statutes, and gone to such lengths of lawlessness that you outdid in impiety the very nations from whom you learned it, I will judge you openly. The nations will watch the court and hear the case, so that, since they gained nothing from your good order, they may at least draw some benefit from your punishment. (5:9) “And I will do in you what I have not done, and the like of which I will never do again, because of all your abominations.” Then he explains what he is threatening. (5:10) “Therefore fathers shall eat their children in your midst, and children shall eat their fathers.” This happened both in the Babylonian siege and in the Roman siege, when the extremity of the famine drove them to that unholy act. “And I will execute judgments in you.” That is, I will judge you justly. “And I will scatter all your survivors to every wind.” These words need no interpretation, since the events cry them aloud. (5:11) “Therefore, as I live, says the Lord God, because you have defiled my holy things with all your detestable things and with all your abominations, I will surely reject you.” By “holy things” he means not only the statutes but also the temple that was set apart for him, which they profaned by setting up idols in it. He calls the idols “detestable things” and “abominations”: abominations because they are full of abomination, and detestable things because they are filled with everything loathsome. Rebekah’s words are of the same kind: “I am sick of my life because of the daughters of the Canaanites. If Jacob my son takes a wife from among them, why should I live?” That is, I loathe the daughters of the Canaanites intensely. Again, God says through David: “Therefore I was sick of that generation, and I said, They always go astray in their heart”; that is, I loathed them. And again the same prophet says of the lawless man: “But evil he did not detest”; that is, he did not loathe wickedness. “My eye will not spare, and I will have no pity.” So excessive is their lawlessness that the Merciful One cannot bring himself to show mercy, and the Lover of humankind does not spare those being punished. Then he recounts what has already been interpreted: how he will give one fourth over to famine and another share to death, then another to slaughter in war, and the remaining fourth to captivity, with punishment following even these. And he adds:

(5:13) “And my wrath and my anger against them will be spent, and I will be comforted. And they shall know that I the Lord have spoken in my zeal, when I have spent my wrath against them.” The Divine is free of passion and wholly without anger. He uses human words here and gives these names to his acts of punishment. “My wrath against them will be spent” means it will come to an end. Once they learn by experience that I am God and Master, and that I brought the punishment because I loathed their lawlessness, I will be comforted, for that is why I brought the punishments. (5:14) “And I will make you a desert and a reproach to those around you.” This alone is enough to cause bitter grief: that the people who live nearby, who have always been at war with them, should laugh at them and gloat over their desolation. “And your daughters around you, in the sight of everyone who passes by.” By “daughters” he means the cities and villages under her. (5:15) “And you shall be [an object of groaning?], and made an example by chastisement and destruction, and your daughters around you among the nations around you.” I will make you conspicuous in your misfortunes, he says, so that all who hear of your destruction and of the destruction of your [?] cities and villages will groan and lament. “When I execute judgments in you in wrath and in anger, in the vengeance of anger and with rebukes.” Then, to show that what he has said is not false, (5:16) “I the Lord,” he says, “have spoken.” Naming who is speaking is enough to show that it is true. “When I send out against them my arrows of famine, they shall come to an end. I will send them to destroy you, I will bring famine upon you, and I will break your staff of bread. (5:17) And I will send against you the sword and evil beasts, and I will punish you; death and blood shall pass through you, and I will bring the sword upon you from every side. I the Lord have spoken.” He says the same things many times because he wants to frighten his hearers. He hopes that fear of suffering will turn them to piety, so that he will not have to carry out his threat. By “evil beasts” he means the extremely savage Chaldeans, who came at them like flesh-eating beasts, slaughtering some and taking others alive as prisoners of war.
(6:1–2) “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them,

and say.” The mountains are not rational or even alive; they have no senses at all. But he speaks to lifeless things in order to rebuke rational ones. In the same way, in the time of Jeroboam, the man of God addressed his words to the altar. (6:3–4) “Mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord God. Thus says the Lord God to the mountains and the hills, to the glens and the ravines: Behold, I am bringing a sword upon you, and your high places shall be destroyed. Your altars shall be made desolate, your sacred precincts shall be smashed, and I will throw down your slain before your idols.” They had raised altars to the idols in all these places, so he has to foretell the coming attack of the enemies, the slaughter that will take place everywhere, and the sacking of the idol precincts. (6:5–6) “And I will lay the corpses of the sons of Israel before their idols, and I will scatter your bones around your altars, in all your dwelling places.” He has turned his speech from lifeless things to rational beings, and he threatens to fill the idols’ precincts with corpses and the demons’ altars with human bones. Through the punishment he teaches that they gained nothing from serving the demons and got no help from them in the calamities that came upon them. “And the cities shall be laid waste and the high places made desolate, so that your altars may be destroyed and left in ruin [?] and smashed.” Symmachus rendered “left in ruin” as “laid waste.” “And your idols shall cease, your sacred precincts shall be removed, and your works shall be wiped out.” He has shown the reasons for the punishment. The loving Master punishes as a physician does, to stop the course of their impiety. I do all these things, he says, and I will bring desolation, in order to quench their madness for idols and [?]

(6:7) “And your slain shall fall in your midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord.” So punishment teaches the knowledge of God. That is why blessed David said: “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your ordinances.” (6:8) “And I will leave some of you who escape the sword among the nations, when you are scattered in the lands.” Since he said, “You shall know that I am the Lord,” he must show who will benefit. For those

scattered by the captivity will reap benefit from the punishment. So he adds: (6:9) “And those of you who escape will remember me [among the nations] where they were taken captive.” Useful, then, [?] is the discipline that God brings. [?] For it is the mother of repentance. [?] “For I have sworn by their heart that goes whoring, that has turned away from me, and by their eyes that go whoring after [?] … of their practices, that they shall weep before their own faces for the evils they committed in all their abominations.” [?] (6:10) “And they shall know that I the Lord have not spoken in vain about doing all these evils”

[?] they loved the worship of idols, which is what he has called fornication here. And they will learn by experience itself that I wrapped them in these punishments neither unjustly nor to no purpose: their impiety shows that the punishments are just, and their repentance shows that they are beneficial. (6:11) “Thus says the Lord God: Clap your hands and stamp your foot and say, Well done, well done! over all the abominations of the evils of the house of Israel. By sword, by famine and by death they shall fall.” When I give judgment and pass sentence of every kind of punishment, he says, clap your hands and marvel at the justice of the verdict. Then he foretells the same things again: that they will be given over to famine, death, slaughter by the enemy and captivity, and that they will be slaughtered around the [idolatrous?] altars and in the groves they honored. “And under the leafy oak,” he says, “they offered a pleasing aroma to all their idols.” He also points out the [?] of the desolation.
(6:14) “For I will make the land,” he says, “a destruction [?] [from the wilderness?] [?] in all their dwelling places, and they shall know that I am the Lord.”

[?] the unbroken series of grievous predictions, enough to soften even the very stubborn, he foretells the painful events in another way. (7:1–2) “For the word of the Lord came to me,” he says, [“saying:] And you, son of man, thus says [the Lord God] [?]”

“[?] of Israel.” This means: Your affairs have come to an end. Do not imagine that you will escape the evils that have been threatened if you do not repent, for destruction will sweep over you completely. “And I will send my wrath upon you and judge you according to your ways.” Now is the time to say with blessed Paul: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God”; for “he will repay each one according to his works.” That is what he said here too: “And I will judge you according to your ways. And I will lay upon you all your abominations.” That is: You will reap what you have sown, and you will receive what your deeds deserve. (7:4) “My eye will not spare you, nor will I [have pity].” When we fall into lawlessness without measure and sink into an incurable disease, we shut ourselves off from God’s mercy. “For I will bring your way upon you, and your abominations shall be in your midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord.” For those being punished, the greatest consolation is to know the God who punishes them. (7:5–7) “Thus says the Lord God: One evil, behold, an evil is coming. The end has come, the end has come; it has risen up against you. Behold, the end has come. The entanglement has come upon you who dwell in the land.” God’s love for humankind is beyond words. He threatens punishment so that he will not have to bring it. When we do not fear the threats, we receive them as experience. This is what happened to these people: they heard that the end had come, but they did not fear the end. By “one evil” he means the total destruction that was brought upon them, and by “entanglement” the bonds of sin. For “each one,” it says, “is bound tight by the cords of his own sins.” And Isaiah says: “Woe to those who drag their sins along as with a long rope, and their iniquities as with the strap of a heifer’s yoke.” “The time has come,” he says, “the day is near, not with tumults or with birth pangs. (7:8) Now I will soon pour out my wrath upon you.” There will be no delay in the punishment, he says; its time is here and has arrived. Then he again recounts how they will pay the penalty for their own wrongdoing. A little further on he says: “The rod has blossomed, insolence has sprung up, and it will break the support of the lawless.” By “rod” he means the punishment, watered by their lawlessness until it blossomed. By “insolence” he means their impiety toward God, which they kept practicing for a very long time, despising God’s patience. But now, he says, it “has sprung up, and it will break the support of the lawless.” So he adds: (7:12) “Let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn, for wrath is upon all its multitude.

And the buyer will no longer return to the seller.” That is, wanting to cancel the contract. For all of them will fall into the same evils, wailing and groaning alike. Yet, he says, “their life is still among the living, for the vision concerning all its multitude will not be turned back.” With so many evils hanging over them, he says, they do not give up on life, and the [?] vision does not seem trustworthy to any of them. But they ought to have known, he says, that “a man will not prevail by the eye of his life.” That is, things do not always turn out as people hope. Often someone who was confident [?] that he would live has met the opposite.

(7:14) “Blow the trumpet and judge everything, but there is no one going out to war, for my wrath is upon all its multitude.” Since you think, he says, that my predictions are false, use your trumpets and imagine that you are stronger than everyone. But you will gain nothing from it. You will have no one able to fight, for he brings every kind of punishment upon all alike. (7:15) “The war and the sword are outside, and the famine and the death are inside. Whoever is in the field will die by the sword, and famine and death will finish off those in the city.” How then, he says, will you be able to fight, surrounded by so many great evils? (7:16) “And those of them who escape,” he says, “will escape and be on the mountains like moaning doves.” Lamenting and wailing, they will be like moaning doves, for the voice of doves sounds like groaning. “I will kill them all,” he says, “each one in his iniquities.” I will not bring the punishment unjustly, but will exact from each the penalty he deserves. (7:17) “All hands will grow weak, and all thighs will be wet with water.” Both are signs of cowardice. (7:18) “And they will gird themselves with sackcloth, and terror will cover them; shame will be on every face, and baldness on every head.” When they see the cloud of evils coming upon them, he says, with no help appearing from anywhere, then they will give up. They will throw away their weapons and put on the dress of mourning. That is why he mentioned sackcloth and shaven heads, for this is what mourners customarily did in those days.

14. "And their silver will be thrown out in the streets, and their gold will be disregarded." Then he also explains why their wealth will be disregarded: "For their silver and their gold will not be able to rescue them on the day of the Lord's wrath." Seeing that owning silver and gold does them no good, they will leave it lying where it was thrown, and will no longer guard it as they once did. "Their souls will not be satisfied, and their bellies will not be filled, because it became the torment of their iniquities." What benefit will gold or silver bring them when famine wages war and the lack of necessities presses on them? Because of it their bellies [are empty] of food and their souls [crave] bread, while the torment and the reckoning for their iniquities [grows]. Then he again sets out the causes of [?].

[They turned the beauty of their] ornament into pride, and from it they made images of their abominations and loathsome things." They made gold, silver and precious stones the material of their arrogance and also of [?]. From them they fashioned costly ornaments for themselves, and they spent most of them on [the making] of idols. "Therefore," he says, "I have given these things to them for uncleanness. (21–22) And I will deliver them into the hands of [strangers] to plunder them, and to the pests of the earth as spoil, and they will profane them." He called the Babylonians "the pests of the earth" because they were most savage and most lawless, and had been raised in every kind of impiety. "To these," he says, "I will hand over the gold and silver idols you fashioned and the costly ornaments you made for yourselves. And they will profane them"; that is, they will put your precious idols to some other use. "And they will [?] my place of oversight, and they will enter it unguarded and profane it. (23) And they will make confusion." By "place of oversight" he means the temple dedicated to him, from which he was thought to oversee Israel and grant it his providence. "I will hand over to the Babylonians," he says, "not only their idols, but also the temple set apart for me, from which I [watched over] you." "And they will enter it unguarded"; that is, they will not be purified or cleansed according to the law, nor will they first receive circumcision. Instead they will come in their bloodstained gear, clad in full armour, slaughtering inside and daring to violate even the innermost sanctuary. He indicated this when he said, "And they will profane them, and make confusion." Then he also gives the cause:
