"... the land is full of peoples, and the city is full of lawlessness." The multitude of their transgressions, he says, can be compared to the multitude of people throughout the inhabited world. 24. "And I will bring the wicked of the nations, and they will take possession of their houses, and I will turn back the insolence of their strength, and their holy things will be defiled." He did not say "my holy things" but "their holy things." That is: "[The things] dedicated to me, which I did not need but accepted because of their devotion, I will now let be defiled and trampled because of their transgression." 25. "Atonement will come, and it will seek peace, and there will be none." At the height of their troubles, he says, they will beg to obtain favour and release, and they will not obtain it. [?] 26. "Woe will come upon woe, and report upon report." Evil will follow evil for them, and one bad report will follow another. "And a vision will be sought from a prophet, and the law will perish from the priest, and counsel from the elders." These things still hold among them even now, to this day. Among them no priesthood functions according to the laws, and the grace of prophecy [?]

27. "The king will mourn, and the ruler will clothe himself with desolation, and the hands of the people of the land will be paralysed." Jeremiah teaches this more clearly when he narrates what happened to Zedekiah and his flight. "According to their ways I will deal with them, and by their own judgments I will [?] them, and they will know that I am the Lord." [Thus], he says, I will exact from them the penalty for the wrongs they committed, demanding an account. It is fitting for all of us to gather benefit from each of these sayings. We must not provoke punishment against ourselves by wickedness, but heal the wounds of sin with the remedies of repentance, so that the vessel may not [?] be sunk [?] according to the just judgments of God. To him be glory to the ages of ages.

1. "And it came to pass in the sixth year, in the fifth month, on the fifth day of the month, that I was sitting in my house, and the elders of Judah were sitting before me." The prophet clearly fell into captivity along with Jeconiah, and so he marks the time from that event everywhere. He continued to act as a kind of tutor to those in captivity, keeping them in order and guiding them according to the divine will. He showed this by saying, "The elders of Judah were sitting before me." Then he adds, "And the hand of the Lord Adonai came upon me." He calls the working of the divine Spirit "the hand of the Lord." 2. "And I looked, and behold, the likeness of a man: from his loins downward there was fire, and from his loins upward something like the appearance of brightness, like the appearance of amber." [This is the one] he saw upon the cherubim; [now he sees him] without the cherubim. He appears to him sometimes in a fearsome way and sometimes gently, arranging everything according to need. His is the saying, "I multiplied visions, and by the hands of the prophets I was represented in likenesses." [It was not] in my essence that I was seen. That is why the prophet too says that he saw a "likeness." 3. "And he stretched out," he says, "the likeness of a hand and took me by the crown of my head. The Spirit lifted me up between earth and heaven and brought me to Jerusalem in a vision of God, to the entrance of the inner gate that faces north, where the pillar of the image of [?] of the purchaser stood." It should be noted that the prophet said he saw these things "in a vision of God." So there was no bodily transfer, and he did not see with the eyes of the flesh. He saw this whole vision while sitting in his house among the elders of Judah. He makes this clear after [the end] of the vision: "For I came up," he says, "from my vision," that is, "I came back to myself." Since he foretells grievous punishments, he must also teach their causes. So he sees in the divine temple the pillar of the image of jealousy. This was an idol set up there unlawfully. And "jealousy" [?]

is what he calls it, by a metaphor taken from adulterous wives who drive their husbands to jealousy. God himself said this through the great Moses: "They provoked me to jealousy with what is no god." To explain it, he added, "They provoked me to anger with their idols." 4–5. "And behold, the glory of the Lord God of Israel was there, as in the vision I had seen in the plain. And he said to me, 'Son of man, lift up your eyes toward the north.' So I lifted up my eyes toward the north, toward the gate facing east, by the altar, where the [image] of jealousy was, at the entrance." As we said before, the prophet is being taught that the punishment of the Jews is just. For this reason the just Judge shows him everything they dare to do. 6. "And he said to me, 'Son of man, have you seen what these people are doing, the great lawless deeds that the house of Israel is committing here, so as to keep away from my holy things?'" Do you see, he says, how they bring punishment upon themselves by their own wickedness? By acting impiously and despising my worship they will end up far from my holy places, as David prophesied: "Those who distance themselves from you will perish." 7–9. "And he brought me to the entrance of the court, and I looked, and behold, there was a hole in the wall. And he said to me, 'Son of man, dig into the wall.' So I dug, and behold, there was a door in the wall. And he said to me, 'Go in and see the wicked lawless deeds these people are committing here.'" Having shown him the impiety they dare to commit openly, the Master also shows him what [they do] in secret.

10–11. "So I went in," he says, "and looked, and behold, every likeness of creeping things and of beasts, vain abominations, and all the idols of the house of Israel, portrayed on the wall all the way around. And seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel, with Jaazaniah son of Shaphan standing in their midst, each had his censer in his hand, and the smoke of the incense was rising." Besides their impiety, their folly is extreme. What could be more senseless than to worship images of venomous reptiles and irrational beasts? We have been [told] to kill the reptiles as harmful and treacherous, while the Master assigned the beasts to serve and attend us. "For," he says, [?]

"... and green plants for the service of human beings." Let us consider, then, how irrational it is to worship images of servants and slaves. So the Master, rightly indignant, [says] to the prophet [?]

"... in his secret chamber, because they said, 'The Lord does not see; he has abandoned the land.'" Forgetting God is the cause of impiety. They persuaded themselves that God sees none of the things they do, and so they went on to that lawlessness. Blessed David, however, teaches us both to think and to say the opposite: "I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken." 13–14. "And he said to me, 'You will see still greater lawless deeds that these people are committing.' And he brought me to the entrance of the gate of the Lord's house that faces north, and behold, women were sitting there, mourning for Tammuz." Here he accuses them [not] only of impiety, but also of licentiousness. For in the Greek language Tammuz is Adonis. The lament, then, belongs to the rites of Aphrodite, for a licentious demon who because of his licentiousness received the [?]

15–16. "And he said to me, 'Son of man, you will see still greater practices than these.' And he brought me into the inner court of the Lord's house. At the entrance of the Lord's temple, between the porches and the altar, there were about twenty-five men, with their backs to the Lord's temple and their faces toward the east, and they were worshipping the sun toward the east." This too is an enormous act of impiety. To turn their backs on the Master and worship the sun, their fellow servant: what height of madness does that fall short of? He called the vestibule of the divine temple the "ailam," for the bronze altar stood in front of it. He said that it was standing between the ailam and the altar that they dared that impiety. After the things he has shown, the Master fittingly speaks to his own servant, as if offering a defence of the punishment of the Jews. He says to him: 17. "Have you seen, son of man? Is it a small thing for the house of Judah to commit the lawless deeds they have committed here? For they have filled the land with lawlessness, and they have turned to provoke me to anger. And behold, they stretch out the branch, as if mocking me." "For I chose them," he says,

"wishing through them to turn the others away from impiety as well. Yet not only did they share no benefit with others, they even dared more impious deeds, so that now the whole land has become full of lawlessness. They stretched out the branches of impiety, acting against my purpose." Therefore he says: 18. "And I will deal with them in wrath. My eye will not spare, and I will have no mercy. They will cry into my ears with a loud voice, and I will not listen to them." "Just as they stretched out the branches not of piety but of impiety, and increased the harm done to their neighbours, so I will unsparingly apply the surgeon's knife to them. I will not bear with their entreaties or listen to their cries." Sparing such people is not mercy. A physician must attend not to the tears and words of the one being cut, but to the rules of his art.

CHAPTER 9. 1. "And he cried into my ears with a loud voice, saying, 'The punishment of the city has drawn near'; and each one held his instruments of destruction in his hand." Then he explains what the instruments were. 2. "And behold, six men came from the high gate that faces north, each with an axe in his hand." The idol had been set up on the north side, and the women were mourning Tammuz there, so the punishment necessarily enters from there too. We should recall what was said above, that he declared a fourth part of the city would be handed over to death. See, then, the punishing powers ready for the appointed chastisement. One angel struck down the many myriads of the Assyrians, and one was ordered to kill the firstborn of the Egyptians. Here, however, six were entrusted with the punishment of the Jews, because of the extremity of their impiety. "And one man in their midst," he says, "was clothed in a long robe, with a sapphire belt on his loins." The seventh is dressed as a priest. He was not one of those who punish, but one of those who redeem the people worthy of salvation. And since [the law] decreed that the seventh day should be honoured, he naturally presents the seventh as the most honoured. "And they went in and stood beside the bronze altar." This stood in the court in front of the temple's [?]

3. "And the glory of the God of Israel, which was upon the cherubim, went up from them to the open court of the house." Since he is about to pronounce the sentence against the city, he does so outside the holy places. For those [?] of salvation, not of punishment [?]

"And he called the man clothed in the long robe, who had the belt on his loins. (4) And the Lord said to him, 'Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and put the mark on the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the lawless deeds committed in their midst.'" It is good to exhort and advise sinners. But when they argue back and will not be persuaded, lamentation becomes necessary and useful. That is why blessed Paul said, "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?" And again: "I fear that when I come to you my God may humble me, and I may mourn over many who sinned before and have not repented." These men too were godly, lamenting and groaning over the people's lawlessness. So they are marked, so that they will not share in the punishment. Having given him these instructions, he says, he then commands the rest: 5–6. "Go through the city after him and strike. Do not let your eyes spare, and have no mercy. Kill old men and young men, virgins, little children and women, to utter destruction. But do not come near anyone who bears the mark. And begin with my holy ones." Again I say, in the words of blessed Paul, "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God." And I add the words of the inspired David: "Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times," for "in the evil day the Lord will deliver them." We find both these things in what has just been said. Some are cut down without mercy, whole families together, and the punishment reaches every age. Others are justly saved and remain free from sharing their fate. He orders the punishing powers to begin with his holy ones. He does not call them truly holy; he uses the name because they were thought to be holy, as men set apart for divine service. This was not said about the holy places, as some have supposed, but about the people set apart for the service of God. What follows in the prophecy makes this clear, for he immediately adds: "And they began with the elders who were inside the house." He orders them to be killed inside, for it is just that those who transgress there should pay the penalty there. 7. For he says to them, "Defile the house, and fill the [ways] with corpses. Go out and strike." Since they themselves

had defiled the house, the just Judge orders that this be done by the slaughter of the lawless. "And they went out and struck down the city. (8) And while they were striking, I was left alone. I fell on my face and cried out, saying, 'Alas, Lord Adonai! Will you wipe out the remnant of Israel by pouring out your wrath on Jerusalem?'" [The prophets] love humankind and are readily moved to mercy. Blessed Paul was like this too, praying to be accursed from Christ for the sake of the Jews. But the Master comforts his most devoted servant and teaches him that the punishment is just. 9. "For the iniquity of the house of Israel [and Judah]," he says, "has become exceedingly, exceedingly great." By repeating the word he indicated how extreme it was. "For the land is filled with many peoples, and the city is filled with injustice and uncleanness, because they said, 'The Lord has abandoned the land; the Lord does not see.'" "They dare these things," he says, "because they have persuaded themselves that I do not watch over them or see what is done."

1. "And I looked, and behold, above the firmament over the heads of the cherubim there was something like sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne upon it." Here at last he plainly calls the living creatures he saw "cherubim." As I said, the name means "fullness of knowledge." 2. "And he said to the man clothed in the robe, 'Go in among the wheels beneath the cherubim.'" Note that he ordered none of the six to approach the cherubim, but only the one clothed in the robe. Evidently they were not worthy to draw near to the divine powers, the cherubim. "And fill your hands with coals of fire from among the cherubim, and scatter them over the city." What he sees is full of dread: coals of fire being scattered, that is, punishing powers going all around the city. 4. "And the glory of the Lord rose from the cherubim to the open court of the house." Since he had ordered the coals to be taken and scattered over the city, he seems in a way to withdraw and make room for the one commanded to carry out the order. That man would surely have been afraid to approach the divine glory that rode upon the cherubim. And a very loud sound [came] from the cherubim's moving wings, so that one would have thought it was thunder, a divine voice. Where the text says "like the voice of God Shaddai," Symmachus and Theodotion translated "thunder of God the All-Sufficient." That is, you might compare the sound to the [thunder] of the all-sufficient and mighty God [?]

"…voice": that is, by the thunder produced through divine power. "And he came," it says, "and stood beside the wheels." (7) "And the cherub," it says, "stretched out his hand from among the cherubim into the midst of the fire that was among the cherubim, and took some, and put it into the hands of the one clothed in the holy robe; and he took it and went out." Here too we can learn the difference between the invisible ranks. Some were ordered not even to come near the cherubim. This one does come near, but does not dare to [?] the cherubim; instead the cherubim themselves hand him the coals. (8) "And you would see," it says, "that the cherubim had the likeness of human hands beneath their wings." The hands signify activity. Then he describes the wheels again [?]. He had already said everything about them before, and now says only that he saw the form of their colour changed. There, according to Symmachus, he said he had seen something like the appearance of hyacinth; but here, according to the Seventy, he saw something like the appearance of a carbuncle. From this we can learn that he did not see the very nature of the [invisible powers], but certain likenesses and images, and that is why he sees them changed. He saw the same change in the cherubim. There he said that the first face resembled a man, the second a lion, the third a calf, and the fourth an eagle. Here, however, the order is reversed: he says he saw first the cherub's face, which is that of a calf, second that of the man, then that of the lion, and then that of the eagle. So the nature of the [invisible] powers is not like this. Rather, God arranges such forms according to need. And I think that because he saw this vision in the temple, he saw the calf's face placed first, since the calf is a type of the priesthood. (12) "And their backs, and their hands, and their wings, and the wheels were full of eyes." This teaches [?] their knowledge, which their very name also [signifies]. (13) "And to these," it says, "[a name] was given in my hearing" [?]. That is, they were commanded to revolve and be set in motion. (15) "And the cherubim rose up." Then he teaches that this is the living creature he saw by the river. At that time he enjoyed the [vision] but did not know its name; now he has learned this too. (16) "And when the cherubim went, the wheels went, and they too were beside them; and when the cherubim lifted their wings to rise from the earth, their wheels did not turn, and they too [?] from…" [Apparatus: B reads "we have learned"; "likeness"; [?]. In B it is placed after "vision".]

"…beside them. (17) And when they stood, these stood, and when they rose, these rose with them, because the spirit of life was in them." The wheels, it says, followed the cherubim in everything. When the cherubim moved, the wheels moved with them; when the cherubim flew, the wheels followed; when the cherubim stood, the wheels stood. They were not dragged along by some force, but did each of these things of their own accord, for they too shared in life spiritually. (18, 19) "And the glory of the Lord went out from the threshold of the house and mounted upon the cherubim. And the cherubim lifted their wings and rose from the earth before me as they went out, and they stood at the entrance of the gate of the house of the Lord that faces east, and the glory of the God of Israel was over them, above." When he ordered the coals to be taken, the glory seemed in some way to withdraw, so that the man given the order might have the courage to come near. Once that was done, it seems to return and to ride upon the cherubim. The cherubim, he says, rose aloft and were carried more easily through the air, using the motion of their wings instead of feet, and the wheels followed without separating from them even a little. What rode upon them was the glory of God, not God himself, for he has no bounds, is present everywhere, and fills all things. It was his glory, which appears for the purposes of his dispensation. (20) "This," it says, "is the living creature that I saw beneath the God of Israel by the river Chebar; and I knew that they were cherubim." That is: I had already enjoyed the vision before, but now I have learned the name. From this too we can clearly learn that he did not see the very essence of the invisible natures, but certain likenesses and images. In the first vision he said that each cherub had four wings, but here [?]. Their nature would not have undergone a change; rather, the vision was shaped to suit the need. The prophet had received more knowledge from the divine conversation, and wings indicate sharpness of knowledge. So, to signify the knowledge that had been added to him, God shows him the cherubim's wings doubled. Indeed, their very name, in the Greek language, signifies abundance of knowledge.

(11:1–3) "And the Spirit took me up," it says, "and brought me to the gate of the house of the Lord that faces east. And behold, at the entrance of the gate were about twenty-five men, and I saw among them Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah, the leaders of the people. And the Lord said to me: Son of man, these are the men who devise vain things and give wicked counsel in this city, who say: Have not the houses been newly

built? This city is the cauldron, and we are the meat." He accuses both the leaders and those under them. They were plotting against God, contradicting the prophets, and refusing to believe that they would be handed over to the enemy. Instead they claimed they would go on living in the city and meet the end of their lives there. "For the houses," they say, "are newly built; we will live in them and reach the end of our lives in them." That is why God, in his anger, foretells through the prophet the coming attack of the enemy.

(5) "The Spirit of the Lord fell upon me," it says, "and said to me: Thus says the Lord." That is: filled with the power of the Spirit of God, I was commanded to say these things in the person of God. "This is what you have said, house of Israel, and I know the thoughts of your spirit. (6–8) You have multiplied the dead in this city and filled its streets with the wounded. Therefore thus says the Lord: Your dead, whom you have struck down in its midst, they are the meat, and the city is the cauldron; but you I will bring out of its midst. You fear the sword, and the sword I will bring upon you, says the Lord Adonai." He means: You declared the city a cauldron, having filled it with countless dead. For this reason you will not obtain what you hope for, nor will you come to a painless end of life. Instead you will soon be handed over to the enemies you fear and become the spoil of their sword. (9) "And I will bring you out of its midst, and hand you over into the hands of foreigners, and execute judgments among you." He means: I will punish you justly. Since you killed your own kinsmen, you will justly be handed over to foreigners and enemies. (10) "At the borders of Israel I will judge you, and you will know that I am the Lord." He means: You will pay the penalty for your impieties outside the city, and you will learn by experience that I am the Master. (11–12) "This city will not be a cauldron for you, and you will not be the meat in its midst; at the borders of Israel I will judge you. And you will know that I am the Lord." He means: You will not die in the city, nor will you be granted burial in it as you hope; you will be killed far from it. And he teaches the reasons: "Because you did not walk in my statutes," he says, "and did not carry out my judgments; indeed, you did not even act according to the judgments of the nations around you." It is the height of lawlessness and the clearest proof of impiety not only to transgress the divine law, but to act more impiously than the nations who live in impiety.

(13) "And while I was prophesying, Pelatiah son of Benaiah died; and I fell on my face and cried out with a loud voice and said: Alas, alas, Lord Adonai, are you making an end of the remnant of Israel?" The prophet sees the work of those who had been ordered to strike down the city without mercy, and he is afraid that the city will be utterly destroyed and everyone killed. In his distress he had forgotten that many had received the signs of salvation, and so he begs the Master who loves humankind to temper justice with mercy. He is taught, however, that these men will be handed over to the enemy because of their great wickedness, while those already led away as captives will find comfort even in a foreign land and will be granted a return. (15) "For, son of man," it says, "your brothers, and the men of your captivity, and the whole house of Israel have been brought to an end." Meaning: some [?] who have been taken captive and have paid the penalty for what they dared, I will keep for myself as a people. "To them the inhabitants of Jerusalem said: Keep far away from the Lord; the land has been given to us as an inheritance." Those still living in Jerusalem mocked them and dared to say: "The Master has driven you far from himself, but he has given us the promised land as our lot." "Therefore," he says, "everything will turn out the opposite: you I will hand over to slaughter, but for them I will provide." (16) "Therefore say: Thus says the Lord Adonai: I will drive them out among the nations and scatter them over all the earth, and I will be for them a little sanctuary in the countries to which they go." He means: For a time I will [?] them, but even in exile I will give them comfort through the expectation that their misfortunes will change and through the hope of good things. He indicated this by saying, "I will be for them a little sanctuary." And before long I will restore them and bring them back to the land of their fathers. (17–18) "For I will gather them," he says, "from the nations, and receive them from the countries where I scattered them, and I will give them the land of Israel; and they will enter it and remove from it all its abominations and all its iniquities." The history of Ezra teaches this, and so does the book of the Maccabees. After the return from Babylon they abandoned the worship of idols and went on diligently serving the God of the universe. (19) "And I will give them," he says, "another heart, and I will give them a new spirit." By these words he did not indicate the abolition of free will, but

the help that he would give them, and his support in doing good. He called the soul's impulse toward the good a "new spirit": since it had [inclined] toward the opposite, he called its change for the better a new spirit. When he said "another heart," he did not mean a change of nature, but the will's inclination toward the better; in the same way, by the "new spirit" he showed the very same thing. What follows also bears this out: "For I will pull out," he says, "the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh." No one in his right mind would suppose that the heart of stone is made of stone by nature. It is the heart that is disobedient and hard and unwilling to yield to God; and the heart of flesh, in turn, is the one that is compliant and obedient. (20) "So that they may walk in my commandments and keep my statutes and do them; and they will be my people, and I will be their God." He means: Since from now on their way of life will follow my laws, I will be called their God, and they will be called my people. Having said this about those who had already been taken captive, he turns the discourse back to those who were then living in Jerusalem. (21) "But as for them," he says, "their heart went after the heart of their abominations and their iniquities; I have brought their ways down upon their heads, says the Lord Adonai." He means: These people were not brought to their senses by the misfortunes of the others but keep clinging to impiety, so I will bring upon them the punishment their crimes deserve.

(22–23) "And the cherubim lifted their wings, and the wheels were beside them, and the glory of the God of Israel was upon them, above them. And the glory of the Lord went up from the midst of the city and stood on the mountain that was opposite the city." When these things had been said, he says, the cherubim left the city, carrying the glory of God, which rode upon them, and it stood on the mountain opposite Jerusalem. This is the mountain called the Mount of Olives, from which our Saviour's ascension in the flesh also took place. It was fitting, then, that at that time too he should appear in human form and show the two natures in one person, hinting at the divine nature through the fire and indicating the human nature through the amber, and that, having pronounced sentence against Jerusalem, he should go to this mountain and from there make his ascent into heaven. For after the cross and his death he again pronounced sentence against Jerusalem, that not one stone would be left upon another that would not be thrown down, and then [went] to that mountain
[Apparatus:] ¹⁰ "through … the human": B reads "and the human through the amber." ¹¹ "heaven": B adds the article before it.

with his disciples, and was taken up into heaven, carried by spiritual and invisible powers. So the things shown to the prophet were a type of what was to come. Having seen these things, he says: (24) "The Spirit took me up and brought me to the land of the Chaldeans in a vision, in the Spirit of God." He means: I was not really carried off bodily, now to Judea, now to the land of the Chaldeans, but "in a vision," that is, in a sight. "In the Spirit of God" means: my mind was enlightened by the power of God, and I received prophetic eyes, and so I saw each of these things. To make this clearer, he added: "And I came up out of the vision that I had seen. (25) And I spoke to the captives all the words of the Lord that he had shown me." He means: I came back to myself when the spiritual vision had ended. I no longer saw those things, but only the elders who were present with me, and I told them everything I had seen and heard. Now is the time to quote that saying of the Gospel: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." What has been said teaches us this well enough: although many were sitting in the same place, the prophet alone enjoyed that spiritual vision. Let us too strive and pray to attain this purity. Then, freed from every defilement, we may carry the remembrance of God in our souls continually in this present life, and be counted worthy to see him with confidence [?] … Amen. [?] glory for ever and ever. Amen.

(12:1–2) "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, you are living in the midst of a rebellious house, who have eyes to see and do not see, and have ears to hear and do not hear, for it is a rebellious house." The word has shown that the soul can incline either way: "For they have eyes to see," it says, "and do not see, and they have ears to

hear and do not hear." And to teach that they did not suffer these afflictions by nature, he added: "For it is a rebellious house." Symmachus translated "rebellious" as "contentious," that is, quarrelsome, disobedient and unwilling to listen. The Master told the prophet this in advance because he was about to command him to prophesy through actions. It was as if he were excusing himself, explaining that the people's hardness and disobedience forced him to give such orders. (3) "And you, son of man, prepare for yourself baggage for captivity, and go into captivity by day before their eyes; you shall go as a captive from your place to another place before them, so that they may see, for it is a rebellious house." And to make what he said clearer, he adds: (4–6) "And you shall bring out your baggage, like baggage for captivity, by day before their eyes, and you shall go out in the evening before them, as a captive goes out. Dig through the wall for yourself and go out through it before them. You shall be carried on men's shoulders and go out in secret; you shall cover your face, and you shall not see the land; for I have made you a portent to the house of Israel." He means: Imitate someone under siege. When the city is being taken he is forced to flee, so he digs through a wall, devises a way out, and covers his face so that those who see him will not recognize him. Through you doing these things I want to foretell the coming captivity to those who live in Jerusalem. The divine Jeremiah teaches us each of these things more clearly. He tells how Zedekiah, when the city was taken, fled by night with his household and bodyguards, having contrived a way out through the palace garden. Then the prophet tells us that he carried out each of these instructions, since he was fulfilling divine commands. When I had done these things, he says, (8–11) "the word of the Lord came to me in the morning, saying: Son of man, did not the house of Israel, that rebellious house, say to you, 'What are you doing?' Say to them: Thus says the Lord Adonai to the ruler and leader in Jerusalem, and to the whole house of Israel who are among them. Say: I am performing a portent; as I have done, so shall it be done to them; they shall go into exile and captivity." He means: When these disobedient and stubborn people ask you why you are doing these things, tell them plainly: "I am a portent and a sign for you. I prophesy through actions and sketch out in my own person the things

that will happen [?] to the king of Jerusalem and to all the rulers." (12) "For their ruler too will be carried on men's shoulders in their midst and will go out in secret through the wall, and he will dig through it so that he can go out by it. He will cover his face so that no eye may see him, and he himself will not see the land." Yet even though he flees like this and contrives everything to escape notice, he will be captured by the enemy. (13) "And I will spread my net over him," he says, "and he will be caught in my snare, and I will bring him to Babylon, to the land of the Chaldeans; yet he will not see it, and there he will die." By all these words he taught that he would use the enemy as his instruments to exact the penalty for impiety from the king, the rulers and all the people under them. He called the enemy his net, and the siege his snare. Both 2 Kings and the blessed Jeremiah teach this clearly. Nebuchadnezzar sent a detachment of cavalry to the wilderness near Jericho, seized Zedekiah and those who had fled with him, and brought them to Riblah. There he first killed Zedekiah's sons and made him watch the slaughter of his children; then he gouged out his eyes, put him in bronze fetters, and led him away to Babylon, where he forced him to live in a mill-house. That is why the prophecy says: "He will be brought to Babylon, yet he will not [see] it."

(14–15) "And all who are around him," he says, "his helpers, and all who support him, I will scatter to every wind, and I will unleash the sword after them. And they will know that I am the Lord, when I disperse them among the nations and scatter them through the countries." He means: Those who escape the slaughter of war I will have led away as captives, and I will make them exiles scattered abroad, so that these events may teach them that the idols are mute and utterly powerless, but I am Lord and Master. (16) "And I will leave a small number of them from the sword, from famine and from death, so that they may recount all their iniquities among the nations to which they have gone; and they will know that I am the Lord." He means: These very people, who will be what is left after famine, death and the slaughter of war, will become accusers of their own impiety and lawlessness. They will teach the nations among whom they live as exiles that they are paying the penalty for the sins they committed against [?].

12:17–18. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, you shall eat your bread with pain, and drink your water with torment and affliction. This again is a sign of the famine that would come during the siege. 12:19–20. And you shall say to the people of the land: Thus says Adonai the Lord to those who live in Jerusalem, in the land of Israel: They shall eat their bread in want, and drink their water in desolation, so that the land may be laid waste with all that fills it, because of the impiety of all who live in it. Their inhabited cities shall be laid waste, the land shall become a desolation, and you shall know that I am the Lord. For since you enjoyed the good things I gave and lived in luxury on the fruits of the earth, yet [?] the Giver and were ungrateful to your benefactor, you will learn my lordship when you are deprived of those good things and your cities are left desolate. The prophet foretold these things to those in Jerusalem while he himself was in captivity. God wished both to console those already taken captive, since they were not the only ones to suffer such things but would have the others as companions, and to persuade those still living in Jerusalem to stop their wickedness out of fear of the evils prophesied. Besides this, those living in Jerusalem contradicted the words of the divine Jeremiah, and those living in Chaldea likewise contradicted the words of the inspired Ezekiel. So the two prophets had to confirm each other's words by prophesying in agreement, and their agreement shows the words to be divine. If they had lived near each other, there might have been some room to suspect their agreement. But since many days' journey separated them and they still foretold the same things, what they said is shown beyond doubt to be divine. This is why Jeremiah writes to those in Chaldea and Ezekiel to those in Judea, for the God of the universe devises every means of helping both. 12:21–22. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, what is this proverb of yours about the land of Israel, which says, “The days are long, and every vision has come to nothing”? Why is it, he says, that those living in Judea usually say to the prophets: “You foretell things that will happen after a great many years, you mix falsehood into your words, and nothing you predict is true”? 12:23. Therefore say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: I will put an end to this proverb, and the house of Israel shall no longer repeat it. For you shall say to them: The days have drawn near, and the time of every vision. For since they call my long-suffering

a lie, let them be assured that the prophecy will be fulfilled immediately, and the punishment foretold will soon appear at their very doors. 12:24. For there shall no longer be any false vision, nor anyone in the midst of the sons of Israel who divines to please them. For I will put an end, he says, to your false prophets, who try to foretell the opposite of what my prophets say and falsely announce to you that good things are coming. 12:25. For I will speak my words and I will do them, and they shall no longer be delayed; for in your days, O provoking house of Israel, I will speak a word and do it, says Adonai the Lord. Do not think, he says, that my prophets talk to no purpose. I speak through them, and quicker than a word I will bring [?] to its fulfillment, making you eyewitnesses of the truth of what they say. He signified the same things again in other words. Some accused the prophets of saying nothing about the present and of falsely predicting things that would happen long afterward. To these he threatened that what was prophesied would swiftly come true: 12:28. For none of my words that I speak, he says, shall be delayed any longer, for I will speak a word and do it, says Adonai the Lord.

13:2. For, Son of man, he says, prophesy against the prophets of Israel who prophesy. And so that the shared name might not do people harm (for both the true and the false were called prophets), he rightly added: “And you shall say to the prophets who prophesy from their own heart.” That is, to those wholly without the working of the Spirit, who speak falsehoods from their own reasonings. And you shall prophesy, he says, and say to them: Hear the word of the Lord. (13:3.) Thus says Adonai the Lord: Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart, who follow their own spirit and see nothing at all. Lamentation, he says, will overtake those who are not moved by the divine Spirit but follow their own impulse. For by “their spirit” he meant the choice of their soul. 13:4–5. Your prophets, O Israel, are like foxes in the deserts. They have not stood on firm ground, and they have not gathered a flock for the house of Israel. Those who say, “in the day of the Lord,” did not rise up as in war. Symmachus rendered this more clearly: “Like foxes among

ruins are your prophets, O Israel. You did not go up into the breaches, nor did you build a fence around the sons of Israel so that they might stand as in war on the day of the Lord.” For your prophets, O Israel, he says, are like foxes that live among ruins. Foxes do not block up the openings in the ruins; anyone who wishes may go in and out through them. In the same way these prophets saw the people's slackness, yet did not wall off their paths to wickedness or fence them round with pious words, so that on the day of wrath they might overcome their enemies. Instead they exploited the people's weakness for their own gain. 13:6–7. They see false things, he says, and divine vain things, those who say, “The Lord says,” though the Lord has not sent them; and they began to establish a word. Have you not seen a false vision and spoken vain divinations, and said, “The Lord says,” when I have not spoken? You have abused my name, he says, by offering false divinations to the people, for I inspired none of these things in you. 13:8–9. Therefore say: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Because your words are false and your divinations vain, therefore, behold, I am against you, says Adonai the Lord. I will stretch out my hand against the prophets who see false things and utter vain things. They shall have no place in the counsel of my people, nor shall they be written in the register of the house of Israel, nor shall they enter the land of Israel; and they shall know that I am Adonai the Lord. I will discipline my own people, he says, but these men will be handed over to utter destruction. No record of them will be kept, and they will not be numbered with my people. And the reason

13:10. Because, he says, they led my people astray, saying, “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace. I foretold war, slaughter and captivity to the people, wishing to bring them to their senses by threatening them with evils. But these men, working against me, promised them peace. [?] a wall, and they plaster it. Will it fall? (13:11.) Say to those who plaster it: It will fall. For the people, he says, is building a rotten wall through its wickedness and impiety. These men apply their favourable predictions and good promises to the wall like a coat of plaster, when they ought to tear down the unsafe structure and see that it is built solid. And by plastering the wall they thought they were making it secure. Tell them, then, that it will fall and be broken apart.

13:11–12. For there will be a flooding rain, he says, and I will hurl stones as from catapults into its fastenings, and it will fall; a sweeping wind will come, and it will be torn apart. And behold, the wall has fallen. He spoke of everything figuratively, as though of a wall, but through it all he pointed to the enemy's attack. By the fastenings of the wall he meant the king and the rulers, who held the people together as tie-beams hold a building. And by the flooding rain, the stones as from catapults and the sweeping wind he meant the Chaldeans. When the wall has fallen, then, he says, “Will they not say to you: Where is the plaster you plastered it with?” When events teach them that your predictions were false, and they see war, slaughter and captivity instead of the peace they hoped for, will they not say to you: Where are your [?] good words and your promises of peace? Having said the same things again at greater length, he threatened a deluge of war-missiles, showers of stones like snow, the destruction of the badly built wall down to its foundations, and the exposure of the lies of those who had foretold good things. Then he makes his meaning clearer. For I said to you, he says: The wall is no more, nor are those who plaster it, (13:16) the prophets of Israel who prophesy about Jerusalem and see peace for it when there is no peace, says Adonai the Lord. Everything will vanish, he says: the plaster, the wall, and the prophets who applied the plaster. For siege and captivity, instead of the promised peace, will overtake Jerusalem. After saying these things about the false prophets, he turns to the false prophetesses. The destroyer of human nature found these women too to be his instruments, and through them he worked his falsehood. He set the false prophets against the prophets, and against the women deemed worthy of prophetic grace he set [?] women who had received the working of falsehood. So he foretells to these women too what will befall them. 13:17–18. And you, son of man, set your face against the daughters of your people who prophesy from their own heart, and prophesy against them, and say: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Woe to the women who sew pillows for every elbow and make coverings for the heads of people of every age, in order to pervert souls. They have perverted the souls of my people and kept souls for themselves. Symmachus rendered this more clearly, saying: “Woe to the women who sew

elbow-cushions for every elbow and make neck-pillows for the heads of people of every age, in order to hunt souls.” Through these he figuratively hinted at softer and more pleasing words. Neck-pillows and elbow-cushions give a kind of rest and comfort to the limbs they are placed under. Pleasing words, even when false, tickle the ears for a while but bring every kind of perversion to souls. In the same way the false prophetesses, by prophesying what seemed pleasant, brought harm to the people's souls and money to themselves. This is what he hinted at when he said, “They have perverted the souls of my people and kept souls for themselves.” For by perverting the people and drawing them away from God, they got them to attach themselves to the prophetesses instead. Then he shows how paltry their gain was. 13:19. And they profaned me before my people for a handful of barley and for scraps of bread. What could be cheaper than these? And what could be worse than the ruin they bring on? “To kill souls,” he says, “that should not die, and to keep alive souls that should not live, by uttering vain utterances to a people that listens to you.” For the sake of small gain you praised some people among the people without cause, and said that others deserved punishment, wickedly exploiting the people's fickleness and credulity. For they believed what you said, so they unjustly spared some and needlessly slaughtered others. Having thus exposed their impiety, he threatens punishment. 13:20–21. Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I am against your pillows, on which [?] you gather souls, and I will tear them from your arms. I will set free the souls that you have led astray, scattering their souls abroad. I will tear your coverings and deliver my people from your hand, and they shall no longer be in your hands to be gathered up; and you shall know that I am the Lord. I will refute your words, he says, and show them to be false. Instead of those pleasing promises, which are like soft neck-pillows and elbow-cushions, I will bring painful things on the people who believed you, and I will scatter them, teaching them your falsehood by experience. Yet I will set them free from your lies, persuading them through what they suffer no longer to heed your words, but to acknowledge me as Lord and Master.

13:22–23. Because you unjustly perverted the heart of the righteous, though I did not pervert him, and strengthened the hands of the lawless altogether, so that he should not turn from his evil way and live, therefore you shall no longer see false things or divine divinations; and

I will deliver my people from your hand, and you shall know that I am the Lord. For you troubled and tossed the righteous (for so Aquila rendered it), he says, by foretelling grievous things to them, and you made the lawless bolder by predicting good things for them, and in both you acted against my purpose. For this reason I will hand you over to utter destruction, put an end to your false divination, and free my people from the ruin you bring. Having foretold these things about them, he moves on to another subject.

CHAPTER 14. 14:1–3. And some men of the elders of Israel came to me, he says, and sat before me. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, these men have set their thoughts upon their hearts and placed the punishment of their iniquities before their faces. Shall I really answer them? Aquila rendered this more clearly: “These men have taken their idols into their hearts and set the stumbling block of their lawlessness before their faces.” For they carry out what they have wickedly planned, he says, and shamelessly despise the punishment threatened against the unjust. Yet they have come to you wanting to ask something and expecting to be given an answer. 14:4–5. Therefore speak to them and say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Any man of the house of Israel who sets his thoughts upon his heart, places the punishment of his iniquity before his face, and comes to the prophet, I the Lord will answer him in the things in which his mind is entangled, so that he may lead the house of Israel astray according to their hearts, which are estranged from me in their designs. Those who were slaves to impiety consulted prophets and false prophets alike. They did not ask in order to carry out at all costs what God commanded, but because they wanted to learn whether the predictions agreed with their own reasonings. For this reason the God of the universe says through the prophet: Every man of the house of Israel contradicts the divine teachings, obeys only his own reasonings, and despises the punishment threatened against the lawless. Even if such a man goes to a false prophet, wanting to fulfil his own desires and testing whether the predictions agree with his own reasonings, I will answer him, he says. Since his mind is not upright, I will allow

the false prophet to confirm his reasonings, for he deserves ruin and destruction. This is why he says, “so that he may lead the house of Israel astray according to their hearts, which are estranged from me in their designs.” For since they put themselves far from my care and delight in the deceit of the false prophets, I will let them reap the fruits of their own labours. One can find this happening in the case of Ahab as well. Zedekiah the false prophet made himself iron horns and said to Ahab: “With these you shall gore Syria.” Jehoshaphat would not accept what the false prophets said but looked for a prophet of God, and so Micaiah was sent for. But because he prophesied the opposite of Zedekiah, he did not persuade Ahab. For Ahab did not consult the prophet because he wanted to do what God foretold; he wanted by every means to confirm his own purpose. So, with God's permission, the false prophets foretold falsehoods, and Ahab believed them, went out, and paid the penalty for his

14:6. Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Turn back, and turn away from your practices and from all your impieties, and turn your faces. He offers counsel that leads to salvation and shows what they will gain from it. 14:7. For any man of the house of Israel, or of the proselytes who live as proselytes in the house of Israel, who estranges himself from me, sets his designs upon his mind, places the punishment of his iniquity before his face, and comes to the prophet to inquire of him concerning me, I the Lord will answer him in the things in which he is entangled. Here again he said these things more clearly. Someone may make himself a stranger to my care and take wicked reasoning as his guide. He may know the punishment threatened against the wicked, yet despise it and go to one of the false prophets, as though he wanted to learn from me what he should do. I myself will give the answer, he says, and allow the so-called prophet to answer in keeping with that man's reasonings. Then he threatens the fitting punishment: 14:8. And I will set my face against that man and make him a wilderness and a desolation, and cut him off from the midst of my people; and you shall know that I am the Lord. And to show that he is not saying these things about the divine prophets, but about those who bear the name without the reality, he added:

14:9–10. And if the prophet is led astray and speaks a word, I the Lord have led that prophet astray, and I will stretch out my hand against him and destroy him from the midst of my people Israel. And they shall bear their iniquity. But it is not fitting for a just judge both to lead the prophet astray and then to punish him for being led astray. So he does not mean that he leads the prophet astray by actively causing it, but by permitting it. That is: Though I could expose his falsehood at once, I bear with him, I am patient, and I allow him to practise deceit; for he practises it by choice and not by compulsion. This is why he threatens the same punishment to the one who asks wickedly and to the one who answers wickedly. “For as the iniquity of the one who inquires is,” he says, “so too shall the iniquity of the prophet be, (14:11) so that the house of Israel may no longer go astray from me or be defiled any more by all their transgressions; and they shall be my people, and I will be their God, says Adonai the Lord.” I will not bring this punishment on them for nothing, he says. By their destruction I will be doing good to my people and freeing them from their impiety. For I wish to have them as my people, and I want to be their God, taking every care of them.

14:12–14. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, suppose a land sins against me by committing a transgression, and I stretch out my hand against it, break its staff of bread, send famine upon it, and cut off from it both people and animals. Even if these three men, Noah, Job and Daniel, were in it, they would save only themselves by their righteousness, says Adonai the Lord. If I decide to punish a nation that has sinned, he says, and hand it over to famine, and those being punished refuse to repent, they will obtain no pardon, not even if Noah, Job and Daniel were found among them. Those men will reap the fruits of their own righteousness and enjoy salvation, but they will not free the others from the punishment brought upon them. He mentioned these men because what happened in their times closely matches what he has said. Noah lived in an impious generation and could not save from the total destruction of the flood those who refused to repent. Daniel likewise lived at the time of the captivity, and because of the others' great impiety he did not free them from the evils brought upon them. Yet he himself, though taken captive in war, prevailed over the enemy and made subjects of those who had enslaved him. Nor did Job's children benefit from their father's righteousness; he alone, proving stronger

[?] …was shown [?] from the plots of the one who waged war. Again, through several further examples, he says this: “For even if I bring death upon that land, or an uprising of wild beasts, or an attack of enemies, and these three men are found in its midst, they will not be able to save even their own sons or daughters, but they alone will obtain salvation.” It is clear that those who are bereft of repentance reap no benefit from the righteous. That salvation follows repentance, divine Scripture is witness, since it teaches this everywhere. For the Ninevites had neither Noah, nor Job, nor Daniel, but Jonah, who did not intercede for them but wished to be proved truthful; yet they found salvation through repentance. The prophetic word therefore teaches that those who live with lawlessness, refusing to repent and priding themselves on living among the righteous, will have no pardon. Besides this, the God of all wishes to show that what he has not done for any other nation, he has done for Israel. 21, 22. “For thus,” he says, “says the Lord Adonai: Even if I send my four evil vengeances (by ‘evil’ he means ‘severe’), sword, famine, evil beasts and death, upon Jerusalem, to destroy from it both man and beast, yet behold, there will be left in it those who escape from it, who will bring sons and daughters out of it; behold, they will come out to you, and you will see their ways.” By “death” he means sudden demise, by “sword” slaughter, by “famine” obviously want, by “evil beasts” those who cruelly enslave, and by “evil vengeances” those that are severe and bitter. “When I have brought these punishments upon Israel,” he says, “I leave sons and daughters escaping from them, so that all may learn their great impiety and their wicked practices, and may know the justice of the punishment. And you, their kinsmen, will not accuse the punishment of cruelty once you have seen their wickedness.” Making this clear, he added: “And you will repent over the evils which I brought upon Jerusalem, over all the evils which I brought upon it. (23) And they will comfort you, because you will see their ways and their thoughts, and you will know that I have not done in vain all that I did in it, says the Lord Adonai.” “For this reason,” he says, “I will not hand them all over to total destruction, but will leave some of them saved, so that through them all may learn the justice of the punishment brought upon them.”
CHAPTER 15. 1–2. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, what would the wood of the vine be, out of all the wood of the

branches that are among the trees of the forest? (3) Will they take wood from it to make it into anything? Will they take a peg from it to hang any vessel on? (4) Besides, it is given to the fire to be consumed; the fire consumes its yearly pruning, and it fails completely. Through the prophets he always called Israel a vine. Through David he says, “You brought a vine out of Egypt”; Isaiah says, “My beloved had a vineyard”; and Jeremiah, “How have you turned to bitterness for me, O true vine?” So here, figuratively, he uses the branches of the vine to show how useless Israel is. “For just as the wood of the vine,” he says, “is less fit for work than any other wood (no one can make even the cheapest peg from it; it is only food for the fire, and its yearly pruning is handed over to the fire), so this people is fit for nothing else but destruction and punishment.” “The fire consumes its yearly pruning,” he says, “and it fails completely. Will it be made into something useful? (5) Not even while it is still whole will it be fit for work. How much less, when the fire has consumed it completely, will it still be fit for work?” For if it is fit for no work before it is handed over to the fire, it will hardly be useful after it has become fuel for the fire. Having stated the parable in this way, he adds its interpretation. 6, 7. “Therefore say: Thus says the Lord Adonai: As the wood of the vine among the trees of the forest, which I have given to the fire to be consumed, so have I given up the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And I will set my face against them.” He has said this by metaphor, drawing on people who show an angry and grim face. “They will come out of the fire,” he says, “and fire will devour them.” For once released from famine, they will be handed over to slaughter and captivity. “And they will know that I am the Lord, when I set my face against them. (8) And I will make the land a desolation, because they have fallen into transgression, says the Lord Adonai.” For I will hand them over to captivity and slaughter, and I will make desolate the land they used to farm, since there will be no one to farm it. They will suffer these things as the penalty for their offences. Since, then, whatever was written beforehand was written for our benefit, so that through the endurance and encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope, let us not become wood, hay

and straw, which are food for the fire, but [?] gold and precious stones, material for the royal diadem, so that we may reign with Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen. Amen. CHAPTER 16. 1, 2. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: [?] Son of man, testify [?] to Jerusalem [?] her sins. Good is the rebuke of sins [?], since it is given for our benefit. For it instils awareness in those who are sick with insensibility, and brings [?] knowledge of their own offences. It is wretched and very grievous to be sick, but it is much worse not even to know of the sickness. That is why physicians often teach patients in this condition, who are unwilling to accept that they are suffering, how serious their disease is, so that once they are aware of it they may give up [?] harmful substances and follow the rules of the medical art. The God of all does the same with those who are sick and without feeling. To the sinner he says through David, “I will rebuke you, and set your sins before your face”; and to Jerusalem through Jeremiah, “Know that you have acted impiously against the Lord your God”; and again, “Look at your ways in the burial ground, and know what you have done”; and countless other such passages can be found. Here too, then, he commands the prophet Ezekiel to do this: “Testify,” he says, “to Jerusalem her lawless deeds.” “Show the wounds,” he says, “point out her sores, so that she may not think the punishment harsh, but may learn that the cut is a physician’s cut and be grateful [?] to the physician.” Then he himself recounts her offences one by one. [?] (3) “…your origin is from the land of Canaan; your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite.” The Jews prided themselves on their kinship with Abraham. That is why, in the holy Gospels, they said to the Lord, “We are the seed of Abraham

and have never been slaves to anyone.” The blessed John the Baptist also demolishes this arrogance, saying: “Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bear fruits worthy of repentance, and do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father’; for truly I tell you, God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones.” Just as this inspired man likened them to venomous beasts, because they were beastly and lived with wickedness, so here too the Lord God through the prophet calls their root Canaanite, their father an Amorite and their mother a Hittite, and in short their origin foreign. They had emulated the impiety of these peoples, so they rightly received kinship with them, being counted as one race with them because of the way they lived. This was quite enough to strike them hard, not only because of the lawlessness of these very nations at that time, but also because of their base origin from of old. For Canaan was laid under curses and condemned to slavery by his forefather Noah. “You are his descendant,” he says, “and have no kinship with Abraham and Shem. You denied their piety, and so you have lost even your kinship with them and been stripped entirely of that noble birth.” Having struck them in this way with the base birth of Canaan, he recounts in detail both their lawlessness and his own kindness. 4. “Your navel,” he says, “was not cut.” That is: you still draw Egyptian nourishment. By her birth he means the exodus from Egypt. Physicians say that the navel is to the embryo in the womb a kind of root, through which it is nourished and grows. Since, then, midwives usually cut off the part of the navel that sticks out from the baby, he speaks figuratively, by metaphor: “Your navel was not cut”; meaning, “Even today you draw the nourishment of impiety from your mother’s womb,” that is, from Egypt. “And you were not washed in water for salvation.” This too is perhaps [?] said by metaphor from babies, who after birth are washed, cleansed and freed of the mother’s blood. “You, then,” he says, “were not freed of these things, but even today you bear the marks of your mother’s womb.” “Nor were you rubbed with salt, nor wrapped in swaddling clothes.” “You did not receive,” he says, “the salt of teaching, nor the swaddling clothes that were offered to you through the law.” These are put on babies

so that if any limb has been twisted out of straight during labour, it may be set right and take its proper shape. 5. “Nor did my eye spare you, to do for you even one of all these things, to have compassion on you; and you were cast out on the face of the plain, for the crookedness of your soul, on the day you were born.” “For immediately,” he says, “as soon as you were born and freed from Egypt and had been taught by me the equity of the law, you turned aside, always loving what is crooked and perverse.” Here he has called equity a “plain.” “In Egypt,” he says, “I gave you no law, nor the salt of the commandments, nor the cutting of the navel, nor the setting of your limbs by swaddling clothes; but after your deliverance from there, I judged you worthy of every kind of care.” Therefore he adds: 6, 7. “And I passed by you, and saw you weltering in your blood, and I said to you, ‘Live in your blood,’ and I said to you, ‘With your blood is life; multiply innocently,’ as I have made you like the sprouting of the field.” “For when I saw you defiled with the blood of idolatry and embracing the blood of sacrifices, I allowed you to sacrifice, not to idols, but to me.” He indicated this by saying, “With your blood is life; multiply innocently”; that is, sacrificing not unlawfully but lawfully, not to demons but to God; and for this you will be adorned with every kind of fruit. “And you multiplied and grew great, and entered into cities of cities.” “The deed followed my blessing,” he says. “For I said, ‘I have made you like the sprouting of the field’; and you received the blessing and gained both numbers and greatness. You became notable and renowned, and held the greatest of cities in subjection.” Having thus shown briefly her origin and her advance, he again explains her growth in detail. “Your breasts,” he says, “were raised, and your hair grew.” All these things he says figuratively, by metaphor from children, showing through them a more mature condition. By “breasts” he means the discernment of reason (for the breasts cover the heart), and by “hair” the adornment [?] that comes from [?]. “But you were,” he says, “naked and in shame.” For you had not yet received the law’s

[?] 22. “And you slaughtered your children,” he says, “and gave them up to them as offerings to avert evil. This was beyond all your harlotry and your abominations.” For truly the most loathsome and abominable thing of all is the unjust slaughter of children, which these madmen carried out to avert evil, contriving for themselves, as they foolishly supposed, deliverance from misfortunes. “And you did not remember the day of your infancy, when you were naked and in shame, and weltering in your blood, and

8. “And I passed by you and saw you, and behold, your time was a time for lodgers; and I spread my wings over you and covered your shame, and I swore to you and entered into a covenant with you, says the Lord Adonai.” “For when I saw that you were now fit to receive fellowship with me through the law, I stretched out the teaching of the saving commandments over you like wings, and covered the nakedness of your lawlessness; and the marriage was accompanied by a dowry contract.” “For I entered,” he says, “into a covenant with you.” “And since an oath also had to be written into the contract, I did not refuse to do this either. Though I was trustworthy enough when I promised by word alone, I added an oath to my word.” Anyone who wishes to read the writings of the law can easily learn this, for in the song of blessed Moses he will find the God of all himself saying: “I will lift up my hand to heaven, and swear by my right hand, and say: I live forever.” “And you became mine,” he says. That is: you were joined to me, and the marriage was completed. 9, 10. “And I washed you with water, and washed away your blood, and anointed you with oil. And I clothed you in embroidered garments, and shod you with hyacinth, and girded you with fine linen, and put a hairnet about you.” He went through his acts of kindness one by one. “First,” he says, “I washed you with the water of teaching, and I also provided purifications and sprinklings.” Then: “I anointed you with oil.” Here he goes on to list the elements of the priesthood. For the priests were anointed with the holy oil, and they also put on the vestments of fine linen and hyacinth. He also hints at the wealth, both bodily and spiritual, that came to the people through his care. “And I put a hairnet about you.” This is a net made of hair and placed on women’s heads. Figuratively, then, he indicated the beauty bestowed on them through every kind of care. He also hints, I think, at the tabernacle made of skins and hair, in which the sacrifices for sin and those for consecration were offered, and divine revelations came from the mercy seat when God spoke with the high priest. 11, 12. “And I adorned you with ornaments, and put bracelets on your hands and a necklace on your neck. And I put a ring in your nose, and earrings in your ears, and a crown of glory on your head.” Each of these should be understood figuratively. “Bracelets put on the hands” stand for practical virtue;

the necklace placed around the neck, for the yoke of the law; the ring put in the nose, for the overthrow of vice through the commandments, applied like a bridle. This metaphor is drawn from bulls, which take an iron ring in their nostrils and are led this way and that by it. That he likened their insolence to cattle is attested by the prophet Hosea, who says in the person of God: “Like a heifer stung by the gadfly, Ephraim has run wild.” By the earrings put on the ears he means good teaching, which adorns the hearing through ready obedience; by the crown placed on the head, the good repute that comes from piety, good order and every good thing. 13. “And you were adorned with gold and silver, and your garments were of fine linen, hairnet and embroidery.” Each of these too can be understood in this way. But to what has been said we must add that these words hint not only at spiritual things but also signify bodily prosperity. For as soon as they left Egypt they borrowed silver and gold vessels from the Egyptians and despoiled the Egyptians, claiming a just wage for their forced labour. They also plundered all the wealth of the nations living in Palestine. So besides spiritual things he also signifies bodily abundance. Therefore he adds: “You ate fine flour, and honey, and oil.” “You enjoyed,” he says, “all the good things of the earth.” “And you became exceedingly, exceedingly beautiful.” By fulfilling the law you had the beauty that comes from good order. “And you prospered into a kingdom.” “You grew so great,” he says, “that you became fearsome to all your neighbours and enjoyed royal honour.” For he hinted at this through the words

14. “And your name went out among the nations because of your beauty.” For you became notable and famous everywhere. Then he also gives the reason for this: “Because it was perfect in the splendour which I set upon you, says the Lord Adonai.” “For I was the cause of this splendour of yours, since I adorned you with my own commandments and laws.” 15. “And you trusted in your beauty.” This is the beginning of evils: to abandon hope in God and pride oneself on one’s own achievements. “And you played the harlot on the strength of your name, and poured out your harlotry on every passer-by; it became his, and it will not be.” “When you had become most renowned,” he says, “and grew proud because of it, you departed from me and ran aground in the utmost licentiousness, taking not one lover, nor two, but everyone who [wished] to pass by you

…whoever wished; and you consorted with each one, accepting intercourse unlawfully. This is what he indicated by saying, "It was his, and it shall not be"; that is, you joined yourself to others, though you were in no way suited to them, for you had dedicated yourself to me from the beginning. Here he calls idolatry fornication, and by "every passer-by" he means the various schemes of the demons. 16. "And you took some of your garments and made for yourself stitched idols, and you committed fornication with them; and you shall not enter, nor shall it be [?]." Your idolatrous practices, he says, are new and strange. You did not merely copy the vices of others. You devised others of your own, making images of idols out of garments and proclaiming them gods, even though I had forbidden you such things through the law. 17. "And you took the vessels of your boasting, made from my silver and my gold, which I had given you, and you made for yourself male images, and committed fornication with them." You took the silver and the gold from me, he says, and you make gods out of my gifts, and you have preferred them to my service. He called them "male images" because he figuratively calls idolatry fornication. 18–19. "And you took," he says, "your embroidered clothing and put it on them, and you set my oil and my incense before them. And the bread I gave you—I fed you fine flour and honey and oil—you set before them as a fragrant odor." The good things you received from me, he says, you offered to those adulterous demons, using some to adorn and embellish them and others to perform sacrifices and libations to them. "And so it was, says the Lord Adonai. (20) And you took your sons and your daughters whom you had borne, and sacrificed them to them to be consumed." Then comes the reproof, in irony: "As though your fornication were a small thing!" From this it is plain and very clear that here he calls the worship of idols fornication…

…21–22. "And you slaughtered," he says, "your children, and gave them over to them by offering them as sacrifices to avert evil. This was beyond all your fornication and your abominations." For truly the most loathsome and polluted thing of all is the unjust slaughter of children, which those madmen carried out to avert evil, contriving for themselves, as they foolishly supposed, a deliverance from their ills. "And you did not remember the day of your infancy, when you were naked and shamed, and weltering in your blood, and

you lived." You did not call to mind, he says, the former things: that [I took?] you when you were naked and [bereft] of all care, [?] stained with blood, [?] and I made you enjoy both life and [every] kind of care. 23. "And after all your wickedness it came about—woe, woe to you, says the Lord Adonai." As the fruit of this ungrateful mind you reap lament and wailing. Then he sets out her impiety more fully. 24–25. "And you built yourself a brothel, and made yourself a [?] in every street. And at the head of every road you built your brothels, and you defiled your beauty, and spread your legs for every passer-by." One can learn these things more clearly from the history of Judges and from the book of Kingdoms. Everywhere, in houses and in marketplaces, they set up shrines to idols. They filled even the rooftops with this impiety, and in the very temple of God they built altars to the accursed demons and set up images and [?]. This is what the Master charges here too, calling the [?] precincts a "brothel." To expose the excess of this fornication, he shows her lying open to all who wished to consort with her. She filled the roads, the streets and the marketplaces with idols, defiled the beauty of piety, and admitted every passer-by into such licentiousness, worshipping now the gods of the Egyptians, now those of the Assyrians and Chaldeans. To teach this he added: "And you multiplied your fornication. (26) And you committed fornication with the sons of Egypt, your neighbors, the great of flesh, and many times you committed fornication to provoke me to anger." Figuratively again he called "great of flesh" those who were excessively devoted to the worship of idols. For these people worshipped goats, oxen and sheep, dogs and apes, crocodiles, ibises and hawks. 27. "And behold, I will stretch out my hand against you, and I will take away your ordinances, and I will hand you over to the will of those who hate you, the daughters of the foreigners who [turned you aside] from the way in which you acted impiously." I will move my hand to discipline you, he says, and I will strip you of the splendor of the law. I will make you an object of gloating for your enemies and make the neighboring cities laugh at you, for they did not rival the excess of your impiety. 28–29. "And you committed fornication," he says, "with the sons of Assyria, and not even so [were you satisfied]

and you committed fornication, and were not filled. And you multiplied your fornications toward the land of Canaan and toward the Chaldeans, and not even with these were you satisfied." Each nation, he says, served its own idols. But you worshipped the gods of all of them and embraced the worship of idols from everywhere, and even today you have not had your fill of impiety. 30. "With what shall I cleanse your heart, says the Lord Adonai, since you have done all these things, the works of a brazen harlot?" What punishment worthy of your impiety, he says, shall I bring upon you? What remedy shall I use to cleanse your foul-smelling sores? For you have dared the deeds of a woman who has scraped all modesty from her brow and pursues licentiousness shamelessly and openly. "And you committed fornication threefold with your daughters." Your lawlessness, he says, is three times that of the cities subject to you. She who ought to have been the teacher of piety has become the pattern of all impiety.

31. "When you built," he says, "your brothel at the head of every road, and made your [?] in every street, you were not like a harlot gathering wages." No lack of necessities drove you to this licentiousness. You enjoyed every good thing and luxuriated in my gifts, and what I gave you, you offered to them. So you are like a woman married to a husband who gives her bloom away to adulterers, carrying off her husband's goods and lavishing them on her lovers. 32. "For the adulterous woman," he says, "who goes to strangers while under her husband, is like you: she takes wages from her husband and pays wages besides to all who commit fornication with her." And he goes through the same point more fully, to expose its absurdity clearly. 33. "For wages are given to all harlots," he says, "but you gave wages besides to your lovers, and loaded them with gifts so that they would come to you from all around in your fornication." For no one has ever received any good from the avenging demons. Those who choose to serve them offer them what God provides, and so draw their domination upon themselves. This is what he hinted at in saying, "And you loaded them with gifts so that they would come to you from all around in your fornication." By what you offered, he says, you urged them to approach you, to run to you, and to be with you continually. VARIANT READINGS. [?] "With what shall I cleanse your heart": the received reading in the Septuagint is [?] … your daughters. "And … your daughters": absent in the Hebrew.
