"In … road" … "strangers" [?]. 10 [?] "who commit fornication." 11 "For": B reads "he says."

34. "And there was perversity in you beyond other women in your fornication, and after you none will commit such fornication. For in your paying wages besides, while no wages are given to you, perversity has come about in you." You are like licentious women, he says, who are available to all, in your intercourse with many lovers. But by handing out a wage instead of receiving one, you go on doing the opposite of what they do. So in this kind of licentiousness you have surpassed both the women before you and those after you. Having thus laid bare her lawlessness, he gives her a name drawn from her deeds, and in giving it he says:

35–36. "Therefore, harlot, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord Adonai: Because you poured out your bronze, your shame will be uncovered in your fornication with your lovers, and in all the devices of your lawless deeds, and in the blood of your children whom you gave to them." Coin that is counterfeit, with other metals mixed into it, is called "brassy." Since, then, he says, you mixed no small amount of lawlessness into my laws, but poured in so much bronze that the nature of the gold no longer appears and your whole coin looks like bronze, I will from now on strip you of my providence and fill you with shame. I will exact the penalty for every kind of lawlessness, and especially for the unjust slaughter of your children, which you offered to the bloodthirsty demons. 37. "Therefore, behold, I am gathering against you all your lovers with whom you mingled, and all whom you loved, together with all whom you hated, and I will gather them against you from all around." By your very lovers, he says, I will punish you. You copied the impiety of the Chaldeans and Assyrians, the Canaanites and Egyptians, and I will use them as my instruments against you, bringing on you the punishments you deserve. Alongside your lovers I will also gather those you hated, so that both alike may behold your great lawlessness. "For I will uncover your wickedness to them," he says, "and they shall see all your shame." 38. "And I will punish you with the punishment of adulteresses and of women who shed blood, and I will set you in the blood of wrath and jealousy." You will pay the penalty of murderous and adulterous women: whose lawlessness you imitated, their punishment you will receive. 39. "And I will hand you over into their hands, and they will raze your brothel"—that is, the precincts of the demons. "And they will pull down your base." By this he hinted at the divine temple, for its base, foundation and footing was the worship performed in it. "And they will strip you of your garments

and take the vessels of your boasting, and leave you naked and shamed." By these words he indicated the sacking and the enslavement. 40–41. "And they will bring crowds against you, and stone you with stones, and slaughter you with their swords; and they will burn your houses with fire, and execute vengeance on you before many women." These things refer to the time of the captivity. But he describes them figuratively, as of an adulterous woman who is stoned, slaughtered and burned. That is why, keeping to the figure, he added, "And they will execute vengeance on you before many women." He does not mean actual women by "women"; figuratively he gives this name to the cities, since he brings Jerusalem, a city, into court as a woman. Then the

…I will bring the punishment upon you. 43. "Because you did not remember the day of your infancy, and grieved me in all these things, behold, I too have brought your ways upon your head, says the Lord Adonai." You yourself, he says, drew this flood of evils upon yourself, because you would not consider what you had become and from what, and how, when you were lowly, small and utterly obscure, I made you renowned and most illustrious. "And even so I did not deal with you according to all your impiety in all your lawless deeds." You are suffering nothing worthy of your sins, he says, for the punishment is small compared with the impiety. 44. "These are all the things they have spoken against you in a proverb, saying: As the mother, so the daughter." The proverb that is going around fits you, he says: the daughter is like her mother. Earlier he named her mother as the Hittite. 45. "You are the daughter of your mother, who rejected her husband and her children; and the sister of your sisters, who rejected their husband and their children." By this he shows that God is not the God of the Jews only, but of the nations too, for long ago he was called their God as well. VARIANT READINGS. [?] Above, [?] "will depart"; "my jealousy … day," as above; "of the," etc. So [?].

…before they took on the defilement of idolatry. That is why he said that they too rejected their husband and their children: they denied God and sacrificed their children to the demons. Then he makes his meaning clearer: "Your mother was a Hittite, and your father an Amorite. (46) Your elder sister is Samaria, she and her daughters, who dwells on your left; and your younger sister, who dwells on your right, is Sodom and her daughters." He calls Samaria the elder sister not by age but as the teacher of impiety, since by age Sodom is older. It was Samaria's practices that Jerusalem copied first, and then little by little she extended her lawlessness until she could be likened even to Sodom. He calls Sodom the younger sister because Jerusalem embraced kinship with her later, for he calls fellowship in impiety kinship. "On the right" and "on the left" he says because of where the places lie. For someone in Jerusalem facing east, Sodom lies on the right, since it is more to the south, and Samaria on the left, since it lies more to the north. By the daughters of each he means the cities and villages subject to them. Wishing to show the excess of her impiety, he added:

47. "And you did not merely walk in their ways or act according to their lawless deeds; within a little while you surpassed them in all your ways." You enlarged their wicked practices with inventions of your own, he says, and you are in danger of carrying off the prize for impiety. 48. "As I live, says the Lord Adonai, Sodom your sister, she and her daughters, did not do as you have done, you and your daughters." Then he shows the difference. 49–50. "This, however, was the iniquity of Sodom: in pride and in fullness of bread and in plenty they lived in luxury, she and her daughters. This was in her and in her daughters, and they did not take the hand of the poor and needy, and they boasted. And they committed lawless deeds before me, and I removed them, as I saw." Gorged on an abundance of good things, he says, they ran aground on pride and arrogance, and those who enjoyed every luxury looked down on those in want. From there they fell into the depths of licentiousness and suffered penalties worthy of their impieties. 51. "And Samaria did not commit half your sins; you multiplied your lawless deeds beyond theirs, and you have justified your sisters by your sins and by all

the lawless deeds you have committed." He makes this comparison not only by the kind of sin but also by the measure of care each had received. Samaria sinned and dared countless lawless deeds, yet she was far from the divine temple and had at least some small excuse: she lived under another king and could not perform the lawful rites in the divine temple. And Sodom had neither prophet nor lawgiver, and enjoyed only the teaching of the natural law. But you had the law, priests, prophets, the divine temple and the worship prescribed by law, and still you practiced their impiety. So you make them appear worthy of pardon. 52. "And you, bear your surpassing torment, by which you corrupted your sisters with your sins, in which you acted more lawlessly than they, and you justified them above yourself." He did not simply say "you justified," but "above yourself." You imitated their lawlessness with the help of the law and the prophets, and so you have no defense; they, because of the excess of your impiety, can hope to obtain pardon. Receive, then, the punishment for your practices, by which you did harm to them as well. "And you, be ashamed and receive your dishonor, for you have justified your sisters." When someone held in honor does not understand it, he comes to recognize his former honor once he is clothed with dishonor. So Jerusalem, which did not recognize the honor God had given her, came to know her own God through the siege and the captivity. That is why, taught by blessed David, she cries out: "The shame of my face has covered me, at the voice of the one who reproaches and slanders, before the face of the enemy and the persecutor." 53. "And I will turn away," he says, "their turning away: the turning away of Sodom and her daughters, and I will turn away the turning away of Samaria and her daughters." One must know the idioms of Scripture, for otherwise it is impossible to discern its aim. Among many others it has this idiom: it speaks of things that have happened as though they were still to come, and of things to come as though they had happened. So here too he speaks of things already done as future. Sodom turned away from me, and the cities under her, and likewise Samaria with her subjects; but I too turned away and exacted the penalty for their sins. "And I will likewise turn away your turning away in their midst, (54) so that you may bear your torment and be dishonored for all that you did in provoking me to anger."

You too will suffer the same as they did, he says, and pay the penalty for your offenses against me. 55. "And your sister Sodom and her daughters will be restored as they were from the beginning; and you and your daughters will be restored as you were from the beginning." Here he means restoration not to something better but to something worse; once again the [?] idiom of Scripture applies to Sodom. What he says is this: Sodom was splendid and densely inhabited, yet I returned it to its ancient form and made it wholly uninhabited, as it was before it was settled. In the same way I will strip you of all your [prosperity?] and make you return to your former state. 56–57. "And was not Sodom your sister a byword in your mouth in the days of your pride, before your wickedness was uncovered, just as now you are a reproach among the daughters of Syria and all around you, and among the daughters of the foreigners who surround you on every side?" If you had not learned of Sodom's punishment, he says, and if their utter destruction had not been on your lips, as your siege now is in the cities of Syria and Palestine, what worse evil could you have done? Their example did you no good at all. You knew both what they had dared and the evils that came upon them, yet you persisted in lawlessness all the same. Therefore: 58. "Your impieties and your lawless deeds, you bear them, says the Lord. 59. Thus says the Lord Adonai: I will do to you as you have done, since you dishonored the curse by transgressing my covenant." The law had a curse that attended those who transgress it. It commanded the tribes [?] standing on Mount Ebal to recite this curse, and all the people to answer "Amen," as if signing it and assenting to the curse of the law. Since, then, he says, you did not fear even the curse, but transgressed my covenant without fear, reap the sheaves of what you have sown. Then he also promises the good things that will follow the punishment. 60. "And I will remember my covenant with you in the days of your infancy, and I will establish for you my everlasting covenant." You trampled on your agreements with me, he says. Even so, this will not persuade me to abandon you altogether. When I have brought you to your senses by discipline and taught you gratitude, I will remember the agreements I made with you long ago, while you were still an infant. By this he means the time they spent in the wilderness. "And I will establish my covenant, an everlasting covenant": not the covenant of the law but that of grace; not the one through

…of Moses, but the one given through the apostles. For the one is temporary, the other eternal. He also promised through Jeremiah the prophet to do this. “For I will make,” he says, “a new covenant with the house of Israel and Judah, not like the covenant I made with their fathers on the day I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; for they did not remain in my covenant, and I rejected them. But I will make a new covenant with them: I will put my laws into their minds, and I will write them on their hearts.” Here too he promises this…

61. “And you will remember your ways,” he says, “and you will be put to shame when you receive your sisters, your elder ones together with your younger ones.” Your punishment will make you aware of your own ways. Seeing the dishonour that surrounds you, you will recognize your own Master. And you will see these sisters of yours enjoying this covenant together with you, or rather you will see yourself gaining it along with them. “For I will give them to you to build you up, and not from your covenant.” For it is not they who will benefit through you; you will reap the benefit from them. And this fellowship will not come from the covenant you now live under, but from the eternal covenant that will be given later. By Sodom and Samaria he hints at the piety that will come about in the same way among all the nations and among the Jews, and at the faith in one God that the New Covenant will bring about…

62. “And I will establish my covenant with you, and you will know that I am the Lord.” For the gospel was first preached to the Jews, and then to all the nations; but it will be preached again through the great Elijah before the end of the world. “I, then,” he says, “will do everything to bring about your benefit. From these things you will learn what you have done to me, and what good things I have provided for you.” That is why he added: 63. “So that you may remember and be ashamed, and may no longer open your mouth because of your disgrace, when I make atonement for you for all that you have done, says the Lord Adonai.” The three young men in the furnace also used these words. For they made the people's transgressions their own and said in prayer: “And now we cannot open our mouth; we have become a shame and a reproach to your servants and to those who worship you.” The inspired Daniel likewise cried out in prayer during the captivity:

“To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness, and to us shame of face, as on this day, to our kings, to our rulers, and to our fathers.” And they fittingly showed the cause by adding: “Because we have sinned against you.” So this prophecy too has been fulfilled, for the one who inspires the prophets does not lie. We too, then, must examine our own affairs and scrutinize closely how we have lived, setting God's benefits beside our offences. We must use these words in prayer. Our shame for the sins we have already committed should make us flee the conduct that produces shame, and we must fill the soul with light by remembering God. For in this way we will be able to keep far from the snares of sin, to wait constantly on God, and to enjoy his grace, in Christ Jesus our Lord, with whom glory is fitting to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages.

CHAPTER 15. 1–3. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, tell a tale and speak a parable to the house of Israel. And you shall say: Thus says the Lord Adonai. He orders the prophet to deliver the prophecy in riddles. In this way the hearers, not understanding what is said, would become more eager to search out its meaning and would receive the interpretation from the prophet by asking [?]. “The great eagle, great-winged, long in extension, full of talons.” By these words he hinted at Nebuchadnezzar. He called him “great” because he had become very famous; “great-winged” because he had extended his rule very far; “long in extension” because he was proud and boastful;
and he called him “full of talons” [?] because he had a large army, both cavalry and infantry, both light-armed and heavy-armed. For soldiers are a king's talons,

and he called him “full of talons” [?] because he had a large army, both cavalry and infantry, both light-armed and heavy-armed. For soldiers are a king's talons. They occupy the extremity of the body, since they are subject to their commanders, and they are sharp and strong for

striking and tearing, like a wild beast, those who try to resist. “Who has the command,” he says, “to enter Lebanon.” Here he taught clearly that Nebuchadnezzar did not come to Jerusalem of his own accord; the God of the universe invisibly moved him and led him there. For he called Jerusalem “Lebanon,” not only because it was renowned, but also because at that time it was flourishing, with a multitude of inhabitants, with priests serving according to the law, and with prophets foretelling divine things. “And he entered,” he says, “and took the choice parts of the cedar. (4) He broke off the top of its tender growth.” By these words he hinted at Jeconiah. He said “the choice parts of the cedar” because of his kingship. He said “the top of its tender growth” not only because of his high rank but also because of his youth; for while still young he both received the kingdom and endured captivity. The word “broke off” is also apt, since he had called the king an eagle armed with very many talons. “And he brought them,” he says, “into a city of Canaan; in a walled city he set them.” By these words he signified Babylon. He named it “a city of Canaan” because its ways were akin to those of Canaan. 5. “And he took some of the seed of the land and put it in a sown field, so that it might take root like plants; beside much water he set it to be watched over.” By this he indicated Zedekiah. For after appointing him king in place of Jeconiah, Nebuchadnezzar departed. And he no longer calls Jerusalem Lebanon, but “a sown field,” because it had become humbler…

7, 8. “And there was another great eagle, great-winged and with many talons. And behold, this vine was twining itself toward him, and its roots were turned toward him, and it sent out its branches to him, so that he might water it together with its clod, away from the stock where it had been planted. In a good field, by much water, it will drink [?], so as to put out shoots and bear fruit, and to become a great vine.” He calls the kings eagles because of their rule. For the eagle is a royal creature, and has been allotted rule over the birds. By these words he hinted at the king of the Egyptians. This was Hophra, whom Jeremiah the prophet also mentions. For Zedekiah made a treaty with him, breaking the oaths and the agreements he had made with Nebuchadnezzar. The phrase “It sent out its branches to him” signifies the money that Zedekiah sent to the king of the Egyptians. “And he sent,” he says, “so that he might water it together with its clod.” That is, so that the Egyptian might fight to defend both the king and his subjects. For he called the people the “clod,” keeping to the metaphor, since he had named the king a vine. A vine is planted in the earth, sends its roots into the earth, and draws moisture from it [?]. So Zedekiah, he says, sent money to the king of the Egyptians, so that through his help both Zedekiah and the people might enjoy protection, “so as to put out shoots and bear fruit.” And “remaining a vine” means not losing the rank it had received. 9. Therefore say: Thus says the Lord Adonai: Will it prosper? Will not the roots of its tender growth and its fruit rot, and all its early sprouts wither? It will be disappointed in its hope, he says, and will not obtain what it expects. For the Egyptian's watering will bring it no benefit at all. Instead, it will rot its roots and wither the shoots that grow from them. And this is what actually happened. For Zedekiah, trusting in the Egyptian's help, broke his agreements with Nebuchadnezzar. Nebuchadnezzar then marched against him, took him captive, enslaved the people, and burned the city. “And not with a great arm, nor with many people, so as to pull it up from its roots.” For the Egyptian, he says, will not send him a large army. And even this army will not only fail to help him but will pull him up by the roots. 10. “And behold, it will drink [?]; will it prosper?” For a while, he says, it will [?] the help, but it will not enjoy it to the end. “As soon as the scorching wind touches it, will it not wither with drought? Together with the clod in which it sprang up, it will wither.” For immediately, he says,

when the Babylonian king arrives, both the king and all his subjects will be enslaved. For here again he called the people the clod, and the army of the Babylonian a scorching wind. Just as he called the king a vine and the people the clod (for the king had been planted in the people), so he figuratively called the Egyptian's help a watering, and the Babylonian's attack a scorching wind.

11, 12. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, say to the rebellious house: Do you not know what these things mean? Say to them: Behold, the king of Babylon comes against Jerusalem, and he will take its king and its princes and bring them to himself in Babylon. “Behold, he comes” means “behold, he came.” For so far he is recounting things that have already happened, and he has been describing these events concerning Jeconiah. In his usual manner [?], he speaks of past events as though they were happening [?]. What follows shows that he said these things about Jeconiah, who, according to the prophet's own teaching, was already in the sixth year of his captivity. 13, 14. “And he will take,” he says, “one of the royal seed, and make a covenant with him, and put him under a curse. And he will take the leaders of the land, so that it might be a weak kingdom that would not raise itself up at all, but would keep his covenant and stand by it…” [?] …had happened six years before. So “he will take, and make a covenant, and put him under” means “he took, and made a covenant, and put him under.” For when he made the agreement with Zedekiah, he demanded the most dreadful oaths from him not to break its terms. But Zedekiah soon trampled on the oaths. And in appointing him king, he says, Nebuchadnezzar will take captive all who abound in wealth. We are taught this by Second Kings and Second Chronicles, and likewise by the blessed Jeremiah the prophet. The Babylonian, he says, contrives all this in order to make the kingdom weak, so that it will always obey him and have no pretext for revolt. 15. “And he will revolt from him by sending men to Egypt, so that they might give him horses and many people.” What he said above obscurely and in parables, he has here taught clearly. Then he adds a question: “Will he prosper? Will the one who acts against these terms be kept safe? Will one who breaks a covenant escape?” I make you the judges, he says, of whether it is just for one who has broken oaths and agreements to escape punishment and find safety. But since you give no answer, I pronounce the verdict.

16, 17. As I live, says the Lord Adonai, [?] in the place of the king who made him king, whose curse he dishonoured and whose covenant with him he broke, in the midst of Babylon he will die. And not with great power, nor with a great crowd… The king of the Babylonians, he says, who does not know me, made him swear by me. But this man, though he lived under my laws, broke the oaths. Therefore he will be handed over to the king who appointed him, and in Babylon he will meet the end of his life. “And Pharaoh will make war with siege mounds and with the building of siege towers, to cut off many lives.” The blessed Jeremiah the prophet also teaches us this. For while the Chaldeans were besieging Jerusalem, the king of the Egyptians came to help the Jews, and the Chaldeans, fearing his attack, withdrew. But the God of the universe warns Zedekiah through Jeremiah the prophet not to trust in the Egyptian's help. “For very soon,” he says, “the king of Babylon will come and take the city.” Here too God [?] these things through Ezekiel. 18. “And he dishonoured the oath by breaking the covenant. And behold, he gave his hand, and did all these things to him [?]; will he be kept safe?” He will gain no benefit, he says, from his alliance with the Egyptian, but will pay the penalty for breaking the covenant. 19–21. Therefore say, Thus says the Lord Adonai: My oath, which he dishonoured, and my covenant, which he broke, I will bring down on his head. And I will spread my net over him, and he will be caught in its snare. And I will bring him to Babylon, and there I will judge him for the wrong he did against me in all his desertions. And all his chosen men, with all his battle lines, will fall by the sword, and all who remain of them I will scatter to every wind. And you will know that I, the Lord, have spoken. Trusting in the help of the Egyptians, he says, he trampled on my oaths. But I will use the army of the Chaldeans like a net, take him alive, and send him off to Babylon. I will hand over his picked men and the best of his army to slaughter. Those who escape death in the war I will hand over as captives of the spear. And you will learn from experience itself that my words are not false. For this is what he signified…

(22, 23.) Thus says the Lord Adonai: I will take some of the choice parts of the lofty cedar, from its top. I will set it from the head of its shoots; from the heart of its crown I will break it off, and I will plant it on a high mountain. And I will hang him on a lofty mountain of Israel, and I will plant him, and he will put out a shoot and bear fruit, and will become a great cedar. And every bird will rest beneath him, and every winged creature will rest under his shade, and his branches will be restored. Truly Israel is a rebellious house: they have eyes and do not see, and ears and do not hear. If this is not so, let them show us who it is that was taken from the choice parts of the lofty cedar, from the heart of its crown. Who was first planted on a high mountain, then hung on a lofty mountain of Israel? Who, after being hung, put out a shoot, bore fruit, and became a great cedar, so that every bird and every winged creature rests under his shade? It is not four-footed beasts or creeping things, but every bird and winged creature. If they should say this was spoken of Zerubbabel, let them show on what mountain Zerubbabel was hung, or that all the birds and winged creatures rested under his shade. For Zerubbabel ruled only over the people who came back with him from the captivity. The other nations not only did not obey him but even made war on him continually. That is why the building of the divine temple was not quickly completed. If what is said here does not fit Zerubbabel at all, still less could it fit anyone else. And if they should try to drag the prophecy over to the Maccabees, their nonsense [?] will be easily refuted. For the Maccabees were not of the royal tribe but of the priestly one, whereas here he calls the royal family the cedar. He spoke the same way about Jeconiah: “The great eagle, the great-winged, broke off the tender shoots of the cedar and carried them away to Babylon,” meaning the royal family. So if what is said fits neither Zerubbabel nor the Maccabees, it is clear that these things were foretold about our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. He traced his descent according to the flesh from David, and his forefathers came not from some side-shoots of the royal house but from the very line of the kings. The blessed Matthew teaches us this precisely. He says that Solomon was the son of David and Rehoboam the son of Solomon, then goes through all the generations in order down to the deportation to Babylon, and adds: “And after the deportation to Babylon Jeconiah fathered Shealtiel.” This is the very Jeconiah who had been taken captive. “And Shealtiel fathered Zerubbabel.” And this is the one who after

the return led the people. From these the Master, Christ, traces his descent according to the flesh. That is why he says: “I will take some of the choice parts of the lofty cedar, from its top,” that is, from the royal root itself. And again, signifying the same thing: “And I will set it from the head of its shoots; from the heart of its crown I will break it off.” The Babylonian broke off the captives, but the Master himself broke off the flesh he assumed, as we said before; for he built the human temple for himself. “And I will plant it on a high mountain”: I, not the Babylonian. By a high mountain he means the conspicuous glory of the Church. Isaiah and Micah prophesied in the same way: “And in the last days,” he says, “the mountain of the Lord will be manifest, and the house of God on the tops of the mountains,” and so on. Having thus shown how renowned he would be through his miracles and through the preaching, he also foretells the passion: “And I will hang him on a mountain of Israel.” For it was by God's permission that the passion was carried out. The Lord himself made this clear in speaking with Pilate. When Pilate boasted that he had authority both to punish him and to release him, the Lord said: “You would have no authority unless it had been given to you from above.” So he spoke of the permission as an act. “And I will hang him on a lofty mountain of Israel.” Golgotha, where the saving cross was set up, is high. Then he foretells the resurrection after the passion and the sprouting of the preaching: “And I will plant him, and he will put out a shoot and bear fruit.” The world harvests and feeds on this fruit, and so hopes for eternal life. “And every bird will rest beneath him.” Then, more clearly: “And every winged creature will rest under his shade.” Nothing muddy, nothing creeping or grovelling on the ground, but whatever has wings, travels through the air, and is drawn toward the things above. Such are those nourished by the faith: they send their minds upward, picture the things of heaven, and sit under the shade of the greatest cedar. He called him a cedar with respect to his humanity, since he had also named the Davidic kingship a cedar. The cedar does not decay, just as the Master, even in his humanity, was without sin. “And his branches,” he says, “will be restored.” He added this because of the desolation Jerusalem was then to suffer. It is as if he said: Do not look to the desolation the city will suffer after the captivity. For this eternal King will set out from there and reign, and will take branches from it. By these he means the band of apostles. So the kingship, he says, will be restored to the tribe of David, according to the covenant God made with David. Then:
24. And all the trees of the field will know that I am the Lord, who brings low the high tree and raises up the low tree, and dries up [?] the tree…

[?]… “making the green tree dry and making the dry tree flourish. I the Lord have spoken, and I will do it.” All people, he says, will know that it is easy for me to bring low what is lofty, to raise up what is lowly, to dry up what is moist, and to make what is dry flourish. For after the city has been laid waste, they will see a shoot spring from it, as Isaiah prophesied: “For a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall come up from the root.” When they see this one proclaimed king of the whole world, all will know that I am the Lord, who foretell things and make the deed follow the word.

CHAPTER 18. Verses 1–4. “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, what do you mean by this parable in the land of Israel, when you say, ‘The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth were set on edge’? As I live, says Adonai the Lord, this parable shall no longer be used in Israel. For all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son. All souls are mine, and the soul that sins shall die.” Some think that the prophecy passes on to another subject here. But one can see that what is said fits with what came before. He had mentioned the lawlessness of Zedekiah, and then foretold that rule over the world would come from the royal line. So he has to teach the people not to use the proverb that accuses God of injustice: that when the fathers ate sour grapes the children's teeth were set on edge, or, as Symmachus renders it, “ached.” “For see,” he says, “although the kings of that time are lawless, the offspring descended from them will rule the world. I will not consent to make the children pay for the offenses of their fathers. I am Master of both the one and the other, and I take the same care of all. For all souls are mine, and it is the soul that sins that will pay the penalty.” Then he teaches us what the forms of righteousness are, and how it is possible both to enjoy life and to escape punishment. Verse 5. “But the man who is righteous, who does judgment and righteousness.” That is, the one who holds the scales of justice level. Verse 6. “He shall not eat on the mountains.” This means, he says, the one who keeps far from the worship of idols, since their shrines were set up on the mountains. “And he shall not lift up his eyes to the desires of the house of Israel.” In place of: if he does not

follow the evil notions of Israel. With these words too he points to both impiety and lawlessness. “And he shall not defile his neighbor's wife, and shall not approach a woman in her impurity.” It is fitting, he says, that he should neither violate another man's marriage bed nor approach a woman who has a flow of blood, for this too was forbidden.

Verse 7. “And he shall not oppress anyone, and shall return the debtor's pledge, and shall not seize plunder.” He should be seen to be free, he says, of every kind of greed. Then comes a higher degree of virtue: “He shall give his bread to the hungry and cover the naked with a garment.” For it is not enough not to rob; one must also take the needy as sharers in what one has. Verse 8. “He shall not lend his money at interest, and shall not take increase.” For these too are forms of greed. “He shall turn his hand away from injustice.” In brief, he forbade lawlessness. “And he shall execute judgment between a man and his neighbor.” That is, if he proves to be a just judge, who does not cast his vote out of favor or hostility. Then, in brief: Verse 9. “And he has walked in my ordinances and has kept my statutes so as to do them. This man is righteous; he shall surely live, says Adonai the Lord.” The one who has done everything mentioned, he says, and is free from everything forbidden, will be honored with the name of righteous and will harvest the fruits of life. Verse 10. “And if he begets a son who is a pest, who sheds blood and commits sins.” Then, in brief: “He does not walk in the way of his righteous father.” Rather, he did each of the things already forbidden and traveled the opposite road. This man, he says, has done lawlessness. Verse 13. “He shall not live. He has done all these lawless deeds; he shall surely be put to death; his blood shall be upon him.” The lawless man, he says, will gain nothing from his father's virtue, since he chose a life opposite to his. He will reap the fruits of what he himself has sown. Verse 14. “But if,” he says, “he begets a son, and the son sees all the sins his father committed, and is afraid, and does not act like them.” Then he goes on to say that this son freed himself from the worship of idols and took no part in the lawlessness of the house of Israel. He did not scheme against other men's marriages, and he hated every form of greed. He gave the needy what help he could, driving away hunger from some and clothing others and freeing them from nakedness. And he kept all the commandments together.

Verse 17. “This man,” he says, “shall not die for the iniquities of his father, but shall surely live.” For it is not just that he should pay the penalty for the other's lawlessness. Verses 18–19. “But his father,” he says, “since he oppressed and seized plunder and did what was wrong in the midst of the people, also died in his iniquity. And you said, ‘Why has the son not borne the iniquity of his father?’” You, he says, judge unjustly. You want the son of the lawless man to suffer punishment for his father, and you ask one another, “Why ever did he not pay for his father's transgressions?” But I say to you: “Because the son has done judgment and righteousness and mercy, and has kept all my statutes and done them, he shall surely live.” He did not travel the same road as his father but preferred my way to his father's, and so he found an end worthy of the road. Verse 20. “But the soul that sins shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of his father, nor shall the father bear the iniquity of his son.” He indicated the same things again, more clearly and briefly: “The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the lawlessness of the lawless shall be upon him.” He often says the same things because he wants his hearers to remember them firmly. Verses 21–22. “And if the lawless man turns from all the iniquities he has committed, and keeps all my commandments, and does judgment and righteousness and mercy, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of the transgressions he has committed shall be remembered against him; he shall live in the righteousness he has done.” So far am I, he says, from exacting a penalty from one person for another, that I will receive even the transgressor of the law himself, though he has committed countless transgressions, if he changes, repents and chooses the road of righteousness, and I will count him worthy of life. Then he makes his own goodness plain. Verse 23. “Do I at all desire the death of the lawless man, says Adonai the Lord, rather than that he should turn from his evil way and live?” It is not the death of the lawless that I long for, he says, but their repentance. For I did not create human nature in order to punish it, but in order to give it a share in life. And the facts bear witness to the words. If he wished to punish, he would not have inspired prophets, sent apostles, given written laws, promised good things and threatened Gehenna. He would have let people be carried along wherever they wished. As it is, he keeps doing all these things in order to free them from the terrors he has threatened. That these are not words only, but that the facts [?] …

what has happened and is happening also bear witness, divine Scripture testifies. For Hezekiah was the son of an impious father, Ahaz. Yet not only did he not pay the penalty for his father, but he became most illustrious through his own piety. The utterly wretched Manasseh, on the other hand, traveled a road diametrically opposed to his father's and gained nothing from his father's piety; but when he repented he obtained salvation. His son Amon imitated his father's wickedness but not his repentance, and he ended his life badly. Amon's son Josiah abhorred his father's impiety and adorned his soul with every form of virtue. He has been numbered in the roll of the saints, having suffered no harm from his father's lawlessness. Josiah's sons did not imitate him but lived in every kind of impiety, and they paid the penalty for their own offenses, gaining no benefit from their father's devotion [?]. So the history of the holy Scriptures itself shows that the Master's words are true. Come, then, let us return to the sequence of the interpretation. Verse 24. “And when the righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits injustice, doing all the injustices that the lawless man did, he shall not live. None of the righteous deeds he has done shall be remembered. He shall die in the transgression he has committed and in the sins he has sinned.” Just as, he says, I will accept the repentance of any lawless person who abhors his former life and chooses the opposite one, and count him worthy of life, so also if any righteous person entirely abandons the road of righteousness and turns to the other road, he will lose all his former course and find an end suited to the road he took. For he will die in his sins. We should note that he did not simply say “if he sins,” but “if he turns from his righteousness and commits injustice, doing all the injustices that the lawless man did.” For some of the pious also stumble, but they get up again and travel the same road, and by repenting they obtain salvation. But if they depart from that road entirely, they reap the fruits of the opposite road. Verse 25. “And you said,” he says, “‘The way of the Lord is not right.’ Hear now, house of Israel: is my way not right? Is it not your way that is not right?” You see this just verdict of mine, he says, and you dare to accuse me of injustice? Yet you ought to bring the accusation against yourselves, because you see such justice in the judge and still choose injustice. Then he briefly goes over the same points again: the righteous man who turns to the opposite road will be handed over to the death of sin, and

the sinner, if he repents and chooses to travel the road of every virtue, will reap life from his repentance. Verse 29. “Yet seeing this,” he says, “the house of Israel says, ‘The way of the Lord is not upright.’ Is the way of the Lord not upright, house of Israel? Is it not your way that is not upright?” The facts themselves, he says, cry out that my judgments are upright and just, while your choices are full of lawlessness. Verse 30. “Therefore I will judge each of you according to his way, house of Israel, says Adonai the Lord.” Having uttered this threat and pronounced the just verdict, he turns his words to exhortation. Verse 31. “Turn, and turn back from all your impieties, and injustice shall not become a punishment for you. Cast away from yourselves all the impieties you have committed against me, and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why will you die, house of Israel?” Abandon, he says, the road [?] of impiety, take up a different mind and turn [?] to my laws, so that you do not reap death from your wickedness. By “a new heart and a new spirit” he means the turning of the soul toward better things. Then he also shows his own goodness. Verse 32. “For I do not desire the death [?] … but that he should turn from his way and his soul should live, says Adonai the Lord. Turn, then, and you will live.” Since you know, he says, that I long not for the destruction [?] but for the repentance of the sinner, repent and receive the fruits of life. This [?] befits you as well, for God is “not the God of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles,” “Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him.” Let us therefore abandon the road of wickedness, whose end is destruction and [?], and [?] the divine path that leads up to [?] and provides [?]. May we obtain it in Christ Jesus our Lord, with whom be glory to the Father [?] with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
CHAPTER 19. Verses 1–2. “And you, take up a lament for the ruler of Israel, and say: Why was your mother a lioness?”

Foretell, he says, what will happen to the king of Israel, and lament him for it. By the king of Israel he does not mean the one who reigned in Samaria, for that kingdom had been abolished long before, but the one in Jerusalem. For the king of Judah reigned over everyone who was left at that time. The fourth book of Kingdoms and the second book of Chronicles teach us this. He called Jerusalem the king's mother, since the kings came from there. He calls her a lioness not only because the city was royal but also because of its bold character. “She lay down among lions.” She imitated, he says, the ways of the surrounding kings. “Among lions she multiplied her cubs.” He is referring to what happened after Josiah, for within a short time four kings led Jerusalem: Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jeconiah and Zedekiah. Verses 3–4. “And one of her cubs sprang away. He became a lion, and learned to seize prey; he devoured men. And the nations heard of him, and he was caught in their pit, and they brought him in a muzzle to the land of Egypt.” He means Jehoahaz. He succeeded his father Josiah, and he was impious toward God and lawless toward his subjects. But Pharaoh Neco, king of the Egyptians, took him captive and brought him in fetters into Egypt, and there he paid the penalty for his lawlessness. He indicated this when he said, “He was caught in their pit.” Then he adds: Verses 5–7. “And she saw that he had been thrust away from her, and her hope had perished, and she took another of her cubs and made him a lion. And he moved about among lions; he became a lion, and learned to seize prey, and [devoured] men. And he roamed in his boldness, and laid waste their cities, and ruined the land and all that was in it with the sound of his roaring.” By these words he refers to Jeconiah, the son of Jehoiakim. He is speaking of those who were taken captive and ended their lives in a foreign land, which is why he leaves Jehoiakim unmentioned for the present: Jehoiakim was slain in Jerusalem. So he briefly recounted the lawlessness of Jeconiah, who reigned for three months and a few days and filled the city with unjust murders. That he is hinting not at Jehoiakim but at Jeconiah is confirmed by what follows. For he says: Verses 8–9. “And nations from the surrounding lands set upon him, and spread their nets over him, and he was caught in their pit. And they put him in a muzzle and in a cage,

and brought him to the king of Babylon, and put him in prison, so that his voice would no longer be heard on the mountains of Israel.” Jehoiakim was not led away captive but was killed in Jerusalem, while Jeconiah suffered everything foretold here. Since he was speaking of a lion, he fittingly called the army's attack “nets,” and the bonds put on him a “muzzle” and a “cage.” Because he had called him a lion figuratively, he consistently names what happened to him figuratively too, for nets and a cage are suited to a lion. Having told these things in this way, he moves on again to another kind of parable, and says:

Verses 10–11. “Your mother was a vine, like a pomegranate blossom planted by water. Her fruit and her shoots came from abundant water. And she became a rod of strength over a tribe of rulers, and she was lifted up in her greatness among the stems, and she saw her greatness in the multitude of her branches.” Your mother, he says, is like a vine, and like a pomegranate tree planted on the bank of a stream, flourishing because of the water it draws from there, adorned with blossoms and laden with much fruit. We should note that he did not call the fruit good. By the water he meant the manifold gifts of God, and by “a rod of strength” he meant the kingdom itself, for the rod is an instrument of discipline. He added “over a tribe of rulers” because the kingdom did not rule all Israel, only the ruling tribe of Judah. The words “she saw her greatness in the multitude of her branches” point to the arrogance that came to her from her prosperity. So he goes on: Verse 12. “And she was broken off in wrath and cast down on the ground, and a scorching wind dried up her choicest branches. Her rods of strength were punished and laid waste. Fire dried her up; fire consumed her.” All of this is figurative and parabolic, as of a vine and a pomegranate tree. He called the enemies' assault a “scorching wind,” and the punishment that overtook them from the divine wrath “fire.” He said that the rods of strength were dried up because the kingdom was extinguished. Then he teaches what would happen after Zedekiah was taken captive.

Verse 13. “And now they have planted her in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty land.” After the city and the divine temple were burned, and all those in authority had been either killed or led away captive, Nebuzaradan set

Gedaliah as governor over the poor who were left there. The city was completely deserted, or rather the whole of Judea was, since the walls had been torn down, the houses burned, and most of the inhabitants given over to slaughter and captivity. That is why he says, “And they have planted her in the wilderness.” But even so, he says, she will not endure; even what remains will be destroyed.

Verse 14. “For fire,” he says, “will go out from the rods of her chosen ones and devour her.” For Ishmael, who was of royal descent, envied Gedaliah. Under a show of friendship toward him, he secretly plotted against him and killed him, together with most of those who were with him. Then, fearing the consequences of what he had done, he fled. All the rest, afraid of the wrath of the Chaldeans, went to Egypt with Jeremiah the prophet. He indicated this when he said, “And fire will go out from the rods of her chosen ones and devour her. And there shall be in her no rod of strength, no tribe, no scepter to rule. It is a parable of lamentation, and it will become a lament.” Clearly he is speaking of the time before the return. For then she was lamented by her own people, and she became a byword of lament among foreigners. People are accustomed to say of those who fall into the greatest calamities, “May I not suffer what So-and-so has suffered.” This, then, is what he called a “parable of lament.” He added that there is in her no rod of strength, no tribe, no scepter. For before the return she had no ruler and no body of people able to form a tribe; after the return she regained her former splendor. Having foretold these things in this way, he places a short narrative in the middle of the prophecy, and immediately joins the prophecy to the narrative.

CHAPTER 20. Verses 1–4. “And it came to pass in the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month, that some of the elders of the house of Israel came to inquire of the Lord, and sat before me. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, speak to the elders of Israel and say to them, Thus says Adonai the Lord: Have you come to inquire of me? As I live, I will [not] answer you [?] … says the Lord. Will you judge them with judgment? [?] … Son of man, will you judge them?” Very [?] …

…in heaven, will enter the kingdom of God.” These men too lived in wickedness and refused to be healed by the remedies of repentance, yet they tried to question the Master. They did not mean to carry out his commands whatever they might be. They wanted to learn whether the divine oracles agreed with their own reasonings. Zedekiah often did the same. He made Jeremiah swear to tell him plainly what God had decided, and when he had learned what was commanded, he did the opposite. Those who went down into Egypt after the captivity dared the very same thing. For this reason the God of all is unwilling to answer them, for, as the holy Gospels teach, he himself knows what is in a man. So he also tells the prophet to disregard them and to offer no supplication on their behalf. That is what he meant by saying, “Will you avenge them with vengeance, son of man, will you avenge them?” In other words: do not concern yourself with them as though you were their guardian, and do not accept their inquiry. 5–6. “Testify to them,” he says, “about the iniquities of their fathers. And you shall say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: From the day I chose the house of Israel and made myself known to the seed of the house of Jacob, and made myself known to them in the land of Egypt, and took hold of their hand, saying, I am the Lord your God, on that day I took hold of them with my hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt into the land I had prepared for them, a land flowing with milk and honey. It is a honeycomb beyond all the earth.” He means: O prophet, show these men who have come to you my benefits, and list the transgressions of their fathers. Tell how I appeared in Egypt to their fathers while they were still ungodly and serving the idols of the Egyptians, and taught them that I am both God and Master. I spoke these words because I wished to free them from slavery, to fulfil my promises, and to give them the promised land, the mother of countless good things, which bears every kind of fruit for those who live in it. One would not be wrong to declare it better than all the earth and to call it the work of bees. That is what he showed by saying, “It is a honeycomb beyond all the earth,” for this is his name for honeycombs filled with honey. 7. “And I said to them,” he says, “Let each of you cast away the abominations of his eyes, and do not defile yourselves with the practices of Egypt. I am the Lord your God.” He means: I urged them to flee from any share in the ungodliness of the Egyptians and to recognize my lordship, which I had taught them through signs and wonders

but they would by no means pay attention to my counsels. To show this he added: 8. “But they rebelled against me and were unwilling to listen to me. They did not each cast away the abominations of his eyes, and they did not forsake the practices of Egypt.” Then he shows that his wrath was just: “And I said I would pour out my fury upon them, to spend my anger against them in the midst of Egypt.” Next he shows the loving-kindness and long-suffering with which he governs human nature. 9. “But I acted so that my name should not be profaned at all before the nations among whom they were, in whose sight I made myself known to them, to bring them out of the land of Egypt.” He means: I wished to punish them at once for their disobedience. But since they were called my people, I did not exact the penalty from them in front of their enemies, so that my name might not be profaned at all before the nations they lived among. I did not want their punishment to become a pretext for blasphemy against me, since I also wished to change the minds of those nations through my kindness toward this people. The book of Exodus teaches us this more clearly. The blessed Moses tells how the whole people [?] him while he carried the divine words to Pharaoh. He means: Using this long-suffering, then, 10–12. “I brought this one out of the land of Egypt. And I brought them out of the land of Egypt and led them into the wilderness. And I gave them my ordinances and made known to them my statutes, which if a man does, he shall live by them. And I gave them my Sabbaths to be a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them.” He means: Having freed them from that bitter slavery, I trained them in the wilderness with good and beneficial laws, as if in a wrestling school, and through keeping these laws I provided life for them, since the laws were able to give life. He calls them ordinances and statutes. The ordinances are not one thing and the statutes another. The same laws are called by different names. They are ordinances because they were written by God the Master and commanded to be kept. They are statutes because they were justly written and contain justice, and also because they are able to justify the person who fulfils them. It is important to note that he set the Sabbaths apart from these ordinances and statutes, which can give life to those who keep them. For after saying, “I gave them my ordinances
[?] … Sabbaths … that … them … ordinances, etc. … there them … [?]

and made known to them my statutes,” and after showing what was gained from them, “which if a man does, he shall live by them,” he then added, “And I have given them my Sabbaths.” He did not say, “so that by keeping them they may live by them,” but “that it may be a sign between me and them, and that they may know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them.” He means: I legislated the Sabbath rest for them, not because it could give life, but so that the distinctiveness of their way of life would separate them from the practices of the nations and remind them of my benefits. By resting from bodily concerns, attending on God, and hearing the divine oracles, they gained something. From the divine oracles they learned that God is both Creator and Benefactor. So it is not the rest by itself that gives life, but attendance on God. “And I said,” he says, “to the house of Israel in the wilderness: Walk in my ordinances.” 13. “But the house of Israel provoked me in the wilderness. They did not walk in my ordinances, and they rejected my statutes, which if a man does, he shall live by them, and they greatly profaned my Sabbaths.” Here again he mentioned the Sabbaths separately and did not join them to the other statutes. They do not give life as the others do. Instead they hold a certain distinctive mark of a way of life. The law of nature taught other people too, “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not murder, you shall not steal,” and the commands that go with these. But nature does not teach the keeping of the Sabbath. That comes from the enactment of the law. So although they shared other things with other peoples, the keeping of the Sabbath made them appear to have a way of life of their own. None of the other nations kept this rest. Not even circumcision set them apart from others as the Sabbath did. All the Idumeans, who trace their descent from Esau, practised circumcision, and so did the Ishmaelites. The Egyptians also learned it from the Jews and were eager to keep it. God made this clear through the prophet Jeremiah when he said, “And I will punish all who are circumcised in their foreskin, Egypt and Edom,” and so on. But only the Jewish nation kept the Sabbath. That is why God said, “I gave them my Sabbaths to be a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them.” So after describing their disobedience in Egypt and his own long-suffering, he again recalled the laws and exhortations given in the wilderness, and their contradiction and transgression. Then he shows both his just wrath and his ineffable goodness.

14. “And I said I would pour out my fury on them in the wilderness, to consume them. But I acted so that my name would not be profaned at all before the nations from among whom I had brought them out before their eyes.” The divine Moses also teaches this when he reports that God said, “Now let me alone, and in my anger I will destroy them, and I will make you into a great nation.” Then he describes his own supplication, and at the end adds: “If you strike them, Egypt will hear and say: Because the Lord was unable to bring them into the land he promised to their fathers, he destroyed them in the wilderness.” He hinted at this here too by saying, “And I acted so that my name would not be profaned at all before the nations from among whom I had brought them out before their eyes.” Then he explains more fully that he wished to subject them all to total destruction in the wilderness, since they had trampled on the statutes that give life and profaned the Sabbaths. And after again mentioning the Sabbaths separately, he adds: 17. “Yet my eye spared them, so that I did not wipe them out, and I did not make an end of them in the wilderness.” He handed those lawless men over to various punishments, but he preserved their children, even though the children would turn out no better, and brought them into the land promised to their forefathers. 18–20. “And I said,” he says, “to their children in the wilderness: Do not walk in the customs of your fathers, do not keep their statutes, and do not mix yourselves in their practices. I am the Lord your God. Walk in my ordinances, keep my statutes, and do them. And hallow my Sabbaths, and they shall be a sign between me and you, that you may know that I am the Lord your God.” He means: I also exhorted their children in the wilderness once they were separated from their fathers' teaching. I counselled them to be rid of their ancestral habits, to recognize my lordship, to follow my ordinances, to fulfil the statutes I had given, to show the distinctiveness of their way of life by keeping the Sabbaths, and to be guided toward the Lawgiver through [?]. But these too, he says, went on despising these laws. To show this he added: 21. “And their children also provoked me. They did not walk in my ordinances, and did not keep my statutes to do them, which a man shall do and live by them, and they profaned my Sabbaths.”

Then he adds that he wished once again to exact from these too the penalty for their ungodliness, handing some over to captivity and others to slaughter. That is what he meant by saying: 23. “And I lifted up my hand against them in the wilderness, to scatter them among the nations and disperse them through the countries.” He means: so that no harm should come from this among the Egyptians and the Canaanites, I did not do this, but… 25. “And I gave them ordinances that were not good, and statutes by which they shall not live.” Some have taken this to refer to the worship of idols, understanding “I gave” as “I permitted.” They plainly have not grasped the meaning of the words at all. No one in his right mind would call the ungodly worship of idols “not good.” He would call it very evil. So the fount of wisdom, the Lawgiver of godliness, the accuser of ungodliness, would not have called the worst ungodliness merely “not good,” since he calls it the very definition of wickedness. The text is hinting at something else. He means: I gave them statutes “which if a man does, he shall live by them,” and by these he means the Ten Commandments of the law. But they transgressed these and went on trampling them without fear. So I bound and nailed them to other ordinances, which could give them no life, but by observing them and being occupied with them they would stop transgressing those necessary laws. By these he is hinting at the commandments about leprosy, a dead bone, carrion, a man with a discharge, and other such things, together with the frequent sprinklings these required and the sacrifices offered for them. Once they were caught up in keeping such rules, they could no longer despise those necessary and beneficial laws so freely. That is why he did not say he gave them evil ordinances, but ordinances that were not good. They did not teach wickedness, and in themselves they did not produce virtue, but they made the people go often to the divine temple and attend on God. Whoever believed he had been defiled ran to be purified, and when he arrived he was reminded of God. This remembrance drove out his impious frame of mind and persuaded him to keep the divine laws. In themselves, then, these ordinances were not good, since they did not match God's purpose but were suited to the weakness of those who received the law. So they were neither good nor necessary, yet they led to what is good and necessary. To this he adds: 26. “And I will defile them in their gifts, when I pass through every one that opens the womb, that I may destroy them, so that they may know that I am the Lord.” This resembles what God said through the blessed David: “And I sent them away according to

the pursuits of their hearts; they will walk in their own pursuits.” He means: Since I saw that they gained no benefit from my exhortations, I let them follow their own reasonings from then on and no longer bore to steer them. He hinted at this here too by saying, “I will defile them in their gifts.” Aquila translated this more clearly: “And I defiled them in their decrees, in making every one that opens the womb pass through.” He means: I allowed them to be defiled by their own practices when they made their children pass through fire and offered their firstborn children to demons, and after that I brought on them the punishments they deserved. 27–28. “Therefore speak to the house of Israel, son of man, and say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: In this too your fathers provoked me by the transgressions they committed against me. I brought them into the land that I had lifted my hand to give them, and they saw every high hill and every shady tree, and there they sacrificed to their gods, there they set out the provocation of their gifts, there they offered their sweet-smelling savour, and there they poured out their libations.” He means: They were not content with their defiance in Egypt and their transgressions in the wilderness. When they entered the land promised to them, they filled it with great ungodliness. They built altars on every hill and in the groves, set up idols, and offered them libations and all kinds of sacrifices. “There they set out the provocation of their gifts” means: with those lawless gifts of theirs they stirred up my anger. 29. “And I said to them, What is Abama” (or, as Symmachus put it, “What is Bama”), “that you go in there? And they called its name Bama to this day.” This place became notorious for its impious worship of idols. So he said to them: What do you gain from it? What benefit will Bama bring you, that you have made it so famous that its name has lasted until now? 30–31. “Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Do you defile yourselves with the iniquities of your fathers, and go whoring after their abominations? With the firstfruits of your labours and with your offerings, by making your children pass through fire, you defile yourselves, and with all your devices to this day,

and shall I answer you, house of Israel? [?] I will not answer you, and this shall not come up into your spirit.” He means: Do you expect to receive some answer from me while you live by your ancestral lawlessness and ungodliness and dare all the things I have described? Do not deceive yourselves. It is impossible for me to answer your inquiries while you dare such ungodliness. And through what happens to you I will also cast away this hope of yours. That is what he meant by saying, “And this shall not come up into your spirit.” 32. “And it shall not be as you say: We will be like the nations and like the tribes of the earth, to serve wood and stones.” He means: Nor will you achieve this aim of yours, that by making gods of wood and stones just as all the nations do, you will give them the honour that belongs to God. He again uses his customary oath, for, as the blessed Apostle says, since he had no one greater by whom to swear,

33. “Therefore, as I live, says Adonai the Lord, with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and with fury poured out, I will reign over you.” He means: I will no longer use my customary long-suffering, but I will lay bare my kingship and authority through chastisement. By “the mighty hand and the outstretched arm” he indicated both his power and his punishing justice. Then he explains the manner of the chastisement. 34. “And I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you from the countries in which you were scattered, with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and with fury poured out.” He means: First I will free you from the captivity that now holds you and bring you back to your former land. 35–36. “Then I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face. As I entered into judgment with your fathers in the wilderness of Egypt, so I will judge you, says Adonai the Lord.” He calls the nations a wilderness of peoples because they were long empty of God. By this he foretold that when godliness was brought to the nations, these people too would turn away from the worship of idols, shamed by the change in the nations that had once been impious. “I will enter into judgment with you face to face” points to the conviction that comes through events. He means: At that time events themselves will all but cry out and convict your disobedient and lawless mind, displaying the ready obedience of the peoples who had long been deprived. So just as I entered into judgment with your fathers in the wilderness and handed them over to utter

destruction, so I will bring punishment on you too. He made this clearer by what follows: 37–38. “And I will make you pass under my rod, and I will bring you in by the number of the covenant. And I will pick out from among you the ungodly and the rebels.” He means: Using my rod, I will scatter the ungodly and those who abandoned my law. But those worthy to be counted, who have kept my covenant, I will bring in and count worthy of my providence. By this he meant the company of the apostles and those who believed the divine preaching through them. Then, pressing his threat against the wicked, he adds: “For I will bring them out of the land where they sojourn, but they shall not enter the land of Israel; and you shall know that I am the Lord.” He means: After bringing them back from captivity, [I will] scatter these very men who behaved impiously among all the nations once more. This was fulfilled after the cross of our Saviour, for the Romans enslaved them, scattered them throughout the world, and drove them out of their royal city. After foretelling these grievous things, the Lover of mankind again offers them exhortation and counsel, for he remembers his own promises. He has said that he does not desire the death of the lawless so much as that he turn and live. So he says: 39–40. “And you, house of Israel, thus says Adonai the Lord: Let each of you put away his practices. After this, if you listen to me, you will no longer profane my holy name with your gifts and your practices. For on my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel, says Adonai the Lord, there the whole house of Israel shall serve me forever in the land, and there I will accept them, and there I will look upon your firstfruits and the firstfruits of your offerings among all your holy things.” He means: If you are willing to be persuaded and stop profaning my holy name, you will return to your ancestral land. (By being called by my name while living lawlessly and offering gifts to idols, you bring on me the blasphemy of your ungodliness.) You will enjoy my customary providence, gratefully offering the firstfruits of the good things you receive and seeing me accept them graciously. 41–42. “For with a sweet-smelling savour,” he says, “I will accept you, when I bring you out from the peoples and gather you from the countries in which you were scattered, and I will be sanctified among you in the sight of the peoples. And you shall know

"...that I am the Lord, when I bring you into the land of Israel, into the land over which I lifted up my hand to give it to your fathers." He has put "I shall be sanctified" in place of "I shall be glorified." For when all see both my benefactions and your gratitude, they will reap great benefit: they will see the weakness of their so-called gods, and behold my power through my benefaction toward you. 43. "And there you shall remember your ways and all your practices by which you defiled yourselves, and you shall strike your faces for all your evil deeds that you have done." For recognition of sin is the beginning of shame; that is why, when conscience pricks us, we are accustomed to strike our foreheads. This is what he has indicated here too. For when you have turned away, he says, from your former lawlessness, and embraced my service, and enjoy my providence, you will become aware of your former impieties and will strike your faces, reckoning in what great evils you were entangled...

44. "And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have dealt with you in this way, so that my name may not be profaned, and not according to your evil ways, nor according to your corrupt practices, O house of Israel, says the Lord God." I will deem you worthy of this care, he says, because I wish, through my benefaction toward you, to turn all other people to the knowledge of me; for you are not worthy of kindness or of pardon, having been reared in lawless practices. Having learned, then, how impious it is to profane the divine name, let us take care not to bring blasphemy upon the Master. For those who have been granted his name but live unworthily of it stir the tongues of the foolish to blasphemy against him. God said this about the Jews as well: "And you profaned my name among the nations, when it was said of you, 'These are the people of the Lord, and they have come out of his land.'" But we have received the very name of the Master, for we are named after Christ. Therefore it befits all of us, according to the apostolic legislation, "whether we eat or drink or do anything, to do all to the glory of God," and to give no offense "to Jews or to Greeks or to the Church of God," to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

45, 46. "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face toward Teman, and look toward Darom, and prophesy against the leading forest of Negeb." In Greek, Teman means "midday" (the south); Darom signifies the southwest; and Negeb the south wind. Symmachus also translated it this way: "Son of man, set your face toward the south, the way of the southwest, and prophesy concerning the forest of the southern country." By all these he hinted at Jerusalem, for Jerusalem lies to the south, the midday and the southwest of Babylon. And since it does not lie due south but inclines a little toward the west, he necessarily added "southwest" as well, since that is its position. He called Jerusalem a "leading forest" because of its unfruitfulness, for such is a forest; and because of the hardness of its mind, for such is the nature of the oak; and besides, because the trees in a forest are not planted in order, but there is great disorder among them; and moreover because the forest is a dwelling-place of wild beasts. All these things one would have found in Jerusalem at that time. 47. "And you shall say to the forest of Negeb: Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am kindling a fire in you, and it shall devour in you every green tree and every dry tree; the flame that has blazed up shall not be quenched." He has persisted in the figure: since he called Jerusalem a forest, he fittingly names the enemies' army fire, and those slain by them burning trees; and by "green tree" and "dry tree" he means those flourishing in wealth and those living in poverty. Then he teaches that the nations lying in between will also share in the calamity, for he says: "And every face shall be burned in it from the east to the north. 48. And all flesh shall know that I the Lord have kindled it, and it shall not be quenched." Here again Symmachus rendered "from the east" as "from the south." He teaches that from the land of the Chaldeans to Jerusalem he will use the fire of the army and will consume the nations lying in between, so that at least through this [?]

...calamity all may learn that he himself is Master of the world. 49. "And I said: By no means, Lord God! They are saying to me, 'Is this not a parable that is being spoken?'" When these things had been said, he says, I made known to the Master the people's unbelief, saying that they supposed the words to be a parable and not the truth; and then the Master himself commanded me to say more plainly what had been said in parables. He speaks as follows:

1, 2. "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Therefore prophesy, son of man, and set your face toward Jerusalem, and look toward their holy places, and prophesy concerning the land of Israel." Since, he says, they suppose that what was said is merely a parable and not the truth, show them clearly that the forest of Negeb—that is, the southern, meridional forest—is Jerusalem. 3. "And you shall say to the land of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I will draw my sword out of its sheath, and I will destroy from you the unrighteous and the lawless." It is clear that he calls the punishment a sword; and the sheath, that is, the case of the sword, is his name for longsuffering. When that ceases, the punishment is brought bare upon those who deserve it. And showing the justice of the punishment, he fittingly added, "I will destroy from you the unrighteous and the lawless." Then he also teaches what would befall at that time the other nations lying in between. 4. "Because," he says, "I will destroy from you the unrighteous and the lawless, so shall my sword go out of its sheath, and it shall not turn back again." For because of the lawless deeds in you, he says, I will bring out the army of the Chaldeans like a sword from its sheath and hand over to the same punishment those who lie between you and the Chaldeans as well; and I will cause all to know by experience that I have authority over all, and that I have justly surrounded them with this calamity. 6. "And you, son of man, groan with the breaking of your loins, and groan in anguish before their eyes." Let your own compassion also accompany what is said, he says, and teach them by your groaning that the words are true. 7. "And if they say to you, 'Why are you groaning?' you shall say, 'Because of the tidings, for it is coming; and every heart shall be broken, and all hands shall go slack, and all flesh and every spirit shall faint, and all thighs shall be defiled with wetness. Behold, it is coming, and it

shall be,' says the Lord God." When you groan, he says, they will inevitably ask, wanting to learn the cause of your suffering. So answer those who ask: "Foreseeing the evils to come, and the grievous tidings, and the fear that will thereupon come upon everyone, I groan and lament the calamities of my kinsmen." 8–10. "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord God: Say to the sword: Sword, be sharpened and be enraged, so that you may slaughter victims; be sharpened, so that you may be made to gleam, ready for destruction; slaughter, set at nought, put away every tree." Once again he figuratively calls a sword the punishment brought through the Babylonians upon both the Jews and the other nations in between. He seems to me himself to urge it to be whetted, to be polished and to slaughter, and to tear up every tree by the root, teaching that these things will happen by his permission, and that each of them is accomplished not by the power of the Babylonian but by his own working. Of the same kind is what God himself said in Deuteronomy: "For I will whet my sword like lightning, and my hand shall lay hold on judgment, and I will take vengeance and repay justice to my enemies, and repay those who hate me; I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh." For there too he called his punishing activity a sword and arrows, as he exacts their due penalties from the guilty. Then he adds: 11. "And he gave it ready for his hand to grasp; it has been sharpened; it is a sword ready to be given into the hands of those who pierce." For this sword, he says, once it was made ready, he entrusted to those suited to inflict punishment; he means the Chaldeans. Of the same kind is what God said in Isaiah against the Babylonian, or rather the Assyrian: "Shall the axe be glorified without the one who cuts with it? Or shall the saw be exalted without the one who draws it? Likewise if one lifts up a rod or a stick." And again: "Woe to the Assyrians; the rod of my wrath and of my anger is in their hands." What he there called a rod of discipline, an axe and a saw—instruments that destroy plants—he has here named a sword, whetted and polished for the punishment of those being chastised, and placed in the hands of the Babylonians as executioners, so to speak. Above he also called this punishment fire, wishing to frighten them with many names and to bring to repentance those devoted to impiety. To these words he adds:
