12. "Cry out and wail, son of man, for this has come upon my people, upon all the leaders of Israel; those who dwell beside me have fallen to the sword together with my people." What goodness could rival this? He punishes justly, and [?] "they have fallen to the sword together with my people." For the priests, having shared in the people's lawlessness, shared in the punishment as well. These are the ones he called "those who dwell beside me," since they spent their time within the divine temple and were entrusted with the priestly ministries. 13. "Therefore clap your hands, for it has been justified; and what if even the tribe is thrust away? It shall not be, says the Lord God." By clapping your hands, he says, signify the onset of the calamity, and marvel at the justice of the punishment. [?] ...the benefit will come to them; for this will be established as the beginning of their [?] return. For even if the tribe that has been set apart from the other nations is now thrust away (by this he means the whole Jewish people), yet it will exist again and will obtain recall; for it is enough to confirm what is said that the Master and Lord himself says these things. 14. "And you, son of man, prophesy and clap hand upon hand, and double the sword; the third sword is a sword of the wounded, the great sword of the wounded." He calls "the third sword" the campaign against Jerusalem that took place in the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign. In number it is actually the fourth; but since the one under Jeconiah was bloodless (for the king went out of his own accord to Nebuchadnezzar with his mother and his wife and his officials, and so was led away captive to Babylon), he fittingly calls the one under Zedekiah the third sword, counting the engagements and pitched battles and not simply the incursions. That is why he also says, "The third sword of the wounded is the great one." Then he teaches why he commands him to clap his hands. 15. "And you shall dismay them, so that their heart may be broken and the weak may be multiplied at every gate of theirs; they have been handed over to the slaughter of the sword." Do and say, he says, things that can frighten them, so that their hearts may be

broken—that is, so that the resistance of their heart may be softened and, as it were, crushed by the prediction of painful things. And it is enough to terrify them that they will be handed over to slaughter, and that all the gates will be full of the slain. Then, by a kind of personification, he signifies the permission he gave: "Well done! It has become sharp for slaughter; well done! It has become gleaming; go through like lightning. 16. Be sharpened on the right and on the left, wherever your face is set." He says the sword is two-edged, whetted on both sides, very well sharpened to a fine edge, sending out flashes like lightning. Therefore he says: Turn to whichever side you wish, right or left, for you will have me also working with you. This he indicated by adding: 17. "And I too will clap my hand against my hand and let loose my wrath; I the Lord have spoken." That is why the blessed Jeremiah also said, "I know, O Lord, that a man's way is not his own, nor shall a man walk and direct his own way," teaching that none of these things happens without working or permission from above. He works what is fitting, and permits the rest by another mode of dispensation, both yielding to the free will of human beings and in this way exacting the penalty for sins. 18–20. "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, mark out for yourself two ways for the sword of the king of Babylon to enter; from one country two roads shall go out; prepare a pointing hand at the head of the way of each city. You shall set a pointer at the head of the way for the sword to enter upon Rabbath of the sons of Ammon and upon Judah in Jerusalem." Draw, he says, as in a picture, a single road dividing in two, one branch running straight to Jerusalem, the other stretching to Rabbath of the sons of Ammon. For since Nebuchadnezzar, setting out from Babylon, campaigned against both Judea and the Ammonites, God foretells these things through the prophet. He said "Rabbath of the sons of Ammon" since there is also another city of the same name, the Rabbath of Amman. Some say that this city of Amman is the one now called Philadelphia in Arabia, which to this day is called Amman in the local language. To this he adds: 21. "Therefore the king of Babylon shall stand on the ancient road, at the head of the two roads, to practise divination, to shake up rods, to inquire of the carved images, and to

inspect livers." For when he reaches the road that divides in two, he says, one branch of which leads to Judea and the other to Rabbath, he will use divination by rods, and likewise the inspection of the entrails of victims, wishing to learn where he should march first. And when he has done these things, he says: 22. "On his right hand the oracle fell upon Jerusalem: to throw up a palisade, to open the mouth with a shout, to raise the voice with the blast of the trumpet, to set palisades against its gates, to throw up a mound, and to build emplacements for siege engines." It should be understood that the demons know nothing of the future, but they attempt to foretell it by conjecturing from events; and sometimes they hit the mark, but often they miss it. One can see this not only from events but can also learn it from the divine Scripture. For when, through Zedekiah the false prophet, they foretold Ahab's victory, they fell away from the truth: he was not only defeated in battle but also killed. And here too, knowing the law given to Israel, and seeing the people's way of life at odds with its commandments, and moreover having heard the prophetic predictions, they learned from every quarter of the divine indignation. So through the oracles they foretold this to the impious king: that he must first march against Jerusalem and use palisades and mounds and all the other engines of war. But while he is doing these things, he says, the besieged hold them in contempt, not because they trust in virtue but because they are sick with insensibility. And teaching this he said: 23. "And he was as one divining a divination for them before them, keeping weeks of weeks for them." They are disposed, he says, as though the oracles portended good things for them. This is what he hinted at by "before them," that is, as though the oracles had been given in their favor; and they go on as though celebrating week upon week. Now one of their three greatest feasts was the feast [of weeks] [?]. But events will not follow their opinions. "And he," he says, "recalling their iniquity, [that they may] be taken." For the remembrance of their lawlessness will be the cause of their capture. 24. "Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have brought your iniquities to remembrance, in that your impieties have been uncovered, so that your sins are seen in all your deeds and in all your practices—because you have brought these to remembrance, in them you shall be taken." You, he says, have become the cause both of the enemies' boldness and of the demons' truthfulness;

for the wickedness of your practices and the excess of your impiety have both stripped you of my grace and made you fall under the enemies, who, as they make their attacks on you by divination, see events following their divinations. Since, then, you have also become the agents of their truthfulness, you will rightly be taken and handed over to punishment. From here he passes on to the rulers, both the king and the priests, and says: 25, 26. "And you, profane and lawless leader of Israel, whose day has come in the time of iniquity—an end. Thus says the Lord God: Take off the turban and put away the crown; this shall not be such." You, the priest, he says, have been stripped of the priestly turban because of your lawlessness; and you, the king, having lived in impiety, have deprived yourself of the crown. So let each office put away its own insignia. For this siege, he says, is not like those of old: your kingdom has come to an end. And teaching the cause, he says: "You have humbled the lofty and exalted the lowly by iniquity." For using iniquity as your accomplice, you humbled the one who was lofty through virtue, and with your words exalted the one who was lowly through iniquity, perverting justice.

27. "Iniquity, iniquity, I will make it." For this reason, he says, I will exact from you the penalty for this iniquity. Then he adds: "Nor shall this be such, until he comes to whom it belongs, and I will give it to him." For this siege, he says, is more grievous than the earlier ones; yet I will not entirely quench the spark of the royal line until he comes to whom it is due and to whom it is fitting, and to him I will hand over the kingdom. The blessed Paul also says this: "until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made; and it was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator." And Jacob the patriarch, blessing Judah, said: "A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes for whom it is laid up, and he is the expectation of the nations." Here too, then, he has hinted at the kingdom of Christ the Master, saying, "Nor shall this be such, until he comes to whom it belongs, and I will give it to him." For even though Jerusalem endured siege and sack at the hands of Nebuchadnezzar, it was not such as it suffered at the hands of the Romans after the saving cross. For after the first capture, when seventy years had passed, it was rebuilt and regained its former prosperity; but after the saving cross it suffered utter desolation, and the Jews themselves do not even dare to set foot within its borders, being barred by law. That is why he said, "Nor shall this be such," meaning: such as the one to come. For I will preserve the race, until

"…until the one comes to whom it belongs, and I will hand it over to him." For when, he says, the one to whom the promises refer appears, then, after handing the kingdom over to him, I will give these people up to utter destruction. From here he turns the prophecy against the Ammonites, who were hostile to the Jews and gloated over their misfortunes. (28–29) "And you, son of man, prophesy and say: Thus says Adonai the Lord concerning the sons of Ammon and concerning their taunting. And you shall say: Sword, sword, drawn for slaughter and drawn for destruction! Rouse yourself so that you may flash, in your vain vision and in your divining of falsehoods." It was not the sword that divined, but those who used it. He called the divination and the vision false because they were foreign to the truth. For even if it did foretell true things at that time, it only seemed to announce beforehand what it had heard from the divine prophets, who were proclaiming God's sentence. The accursed demons, who live in wickedness, passed on to Nebuchadnezzar through his divinations what came from the prophets, while to the Jews, through the false prophets, they proclaimed the opposite, promising them peace and the flight of their enemies. The aim was that the Jews, disbelieving [?] God and contradicting him, would be stripped of his usual providence and handed over by justice to their enemies, and that the demons' oracles would be shown to be true. Having thus commanded the sword to be laid on the necks of those who had lived lawlessly and wickedly, since their limit and end had arrived, he gives the order, saying: (30) "Return to your sheath. Do not stay in this place in which you were born; in your own land I will judge you." As for you, he says, O Babylonians, whom I call a sword: you have done what I commanded, but I will exact the penalty for your impiety not here but in your own land. (31) "And I will pour out my wrath upon you; with the fire of my wrath I will blow upon you." By this he showed how easily the divine power acts. For just as blowing is easy, he says, so it is effortless and very easy to hand you over to every kind of punishment. "And I will hand you over into the hands of barbarous men who craft destruction. (32) You shall be fuel for the fire; your blood shall be in the midst of your land; there shall be no memory of you, for I the Lord have spoken." By this he hinted at the uprising of the Medes and Persians against Babylon. In their siege they brought every kind of engine against the walls, and when they had got inside the city by night during a festival, they subdued the whole city, burned most of it, and filled the houses and all the streets with blood.

CHAPTER 22. (1–3) "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Will you judge the city of blood? Show her all her lawless deeds, and you shall say: Thus says Adonai the Lord." He has turned his discourse back to Jerusalem, and he bids the prophet to act like a judge and expose the lawless deeds she has dared to commit. He calls her a city of blood because she has carried out many unjust slaughters. For this reason he again uses the same titles, and cries out: "O city that sheds blood in her midst, so that her time comes, and that makes plans against herself to defile herself!" You yourself, he says, draw these misfortunes upon you, O city: you devise wicked schemes and put them into action, you rage through them, and you are filled with unjust blood. By "time" he meant the misfortune. [?] (4) "In your blood which you shed you have fallen, and in the plans you have made you were defiled; you have brought your days near and brought on the time of your years." For when lawlessness grows greater, it cuts short the term that divine longsuffering has measured out. One can see this happening also in the time of Noah. God had given the people of that time a term of one hundred and twenty years for repentance, but seeing their impiety increase, he cut the term short and brought the punishment of the flood in the hundredth year. He hinted at this here too, saying, "You have brought your days near and brought on the time of your years." Then he recounts the [?] of her lawlessness. "Therefore I have made you a reproach to the nations and a mockery to all the lands, (5) those near you and those far from you." For this reason, he says, I will make you a disgrace and a laughingstock to all your neighbours and to those living nearby, and not only to them but also to those who live far away. "And they shall mock you and shout [?] against you: Unclean, notorious, and abounding in lawlessness!" For they will gloat over your troubles and call you unclean and lawless and notorious for wickedness. Then he lists the kinds of wickedness. (6) "Behold, the leaders of the house of Israel, each with his own kinsmen, mingled together in you so as to shed blood." He began the accusation with the rulers, since subjects [follow] their rulers; for when the head is in a bad state, the body must share in its sickness. He says, then, that they did not even keep their hands off their own relatives, but trampled on the rights of kinship and carried out unjust slaughters. And further,

(7) "Father and mother," he says, "they reviled in you." This too is one of the things forbidden by the law. "And toward the stranger," he says, "they behaved unjustly in you." The law had forbidden this too, saying: "You shall not mistreat a stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt." Learn kindness, he says, from what you yourselves suffered. But they broke this law too without any fear. Then another charge: "They oppressed the orphan and the widow in you." But the good God commands the very opposite: "Defend the orphan," he says, "and vindicate the widow." And in the law: "You shall not glean your vineyard a second time," he says, "and what is left shall be for the orphan and the widow and the stranger." These people, however, not only gave them no share of any good thing but even treated them badly. And there are things worse than these: (8) "They despised my holy things and profaned my sabbaths in you." For they trampled on my laws, he says, and outraged the day honoured by rest with unlawful work. And things more impious still: (9) "There were robbers in you, so as to shed blood, and they ate on the mountains in you." For you had living in you, both those who live in lawlessness, murderers and men stained with blood, and those who honour the demons on the mountains and feast in the idol shrines. "And they did unholy things," he says, "in your midst." Then he [?] each of these

(10) "They uncovered their father's shame in you, and in you they humbled the woman set apart in her uncleanness." They had intercourse with their stepmothers, he says; this is what he called uncovering a father's shame, for that is what he called it in the law as well: "You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's wife; it is your father's nakedness." Being utterly lustful and extremely licentious, he says, they did not even keep away from women suffering their flow, which is not only unlawful but also extremely unclean. Then he continues accusing them of lust. (11) "Each one did lawlessness with his neighbour's wife, and each one defiled his daughter-in-law in impiety." This is a heightening of the lawlessness. To have intercourse with another man's wife is not the same as plotting against one's own son's marriage: just as adultery is worse than fornication, so intercourse with a daughter-in-law is more impious than adultery. "And each one humbled his sister, his father's daughter, in you." Here too he has clearly shown how extreme the abomination was, by pointing out that the man and the woman were the offspring of one father. From here he moves on to the charge of greed. (12) "They took bribes in you so as to shed

blood." They were continually selling justice, he says, and selling unjust slaughters for money. Then at the very end he puts what is, as it were, the crowning touch on these evils: "They took interest and increase in you." Even if this had not been placed last as the more grievous sin, but had simply been listed alongside the others, that would be enough to frighten those who practise it and persuade them to flee this kind of greed, since it is yoked with the most impious and lawless deeds; for it has been counted alongside murderers and idolaters and the most lustful and licentious. Having thus described the kinds of wickedness, he next teaches the punishment that is to come. "And you brought to completion the full measure of your wickedness, the wickedness of oppression; but me you forgot, says Adonai the Lord. (13–14) Behold, I will strike my hand against my hand at what you have accomplished and what you have done, and at your blood that has been shed in your midst. Will your heart endure, or will your hands be strong, in the days when I act against you?" He speaks of striking the hands as a master and a judge would, to show his anger. Since you forgot me, he says, and refused to remember either my benefits or my laws, I will bring such terrors upon you that your hands will go slack, and your heart, filled with every kind of turmoil, will despair of salvation. Then comes the [confirmation] of what has been said: "I the Lord have spoken, and I will do it." The dignity of the speaker, he says, confirms what has been said; for it is enough for you to learn who has spoken in order to believe his words. (15) "And I will scatter you among the nations and disperse you through the lands." Then the benefit that comes from this: "And your uncleanness shall depart from you. (16) And I will take possession of my inheritance in you before the eyes of the nations, for I am the Lord." For when you become captives and exiles, he says, you will then be taught by experience to be self-controlled. You will cease from your former lawlessness and learn that I am your God and Lord, and you will be called my inheritance; and through you the nations among whom you live as strangers will learn my dignity and power. (17–18) "And the word of the Lord came to me: Son of man, behold, the house of Israel has become to me all mixed with bronze and tin and iron and lead; they are mixed in the midst of a furnace of silver." This people, he says, O prophet, is like debased silver with a large admixture of bronze and iron and tin and lead. God says this also through the prophet Jeremiah: "Call them rejected silver, for the Lord God has rejected

them." Through the metals mentioned he indicated the various kinds of wickedness. This too one can [learn] from the prophet Jeremiah, for he made the same accusation against the Jews when he said: "The bellows has failed from the fire, the lead has failed; in vain does the silversmith refine the silver; their wickedness has not been melted away." Then he added: "Call them rejected silver, for the Lord God has rejected them." He called the divine working a bellows. By fire he means sometimes the word that instructs and purifies, and sometimes punishment carried out in deeds, for the divine power works through both. Again, he called the prophetic teaching a silversmith and the punishment lead. For just as lead is thrown into silver while it is being smelted so as to consume the dross in it, so punishment is brought on those who deserve it, so that they may be shown to be pure of sin. He threatens to do this here as well. (19–22) "Therefore say: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Because you have all become one mixture, therefore, behold, I will gather you into the midst of Jerusalem. As silver and bronze and iron and lead and tin are gathered into the midst of a furnace to blow fire upon it and smelt it, so I will gather you in my wrath and in my anger; I will bring you in and smelt you, and I will blow upon you in the fire of my wrath, and you shall be smelted in its midst. As silver is smelted in the midst of a furnace, so you shall be smelted in its midst, and you shall know that I the Lord have poured out my anger upon you." Since you took in the admixture of wickedness, he says, and like untested silver were shown to be debased through every kind of wickedness, I will make Jerusalem a smelting furnace for you, and [?] like lead [?] the [?], setting my working and will in motion like a kind of bellows,

(25) "Her leaders in her midst are like roaring lions seizing prey, devouring souls by force, taking wealth and honours; they have multiplied her widows in her midst." For when the men were being killed, widowhood clearly took their place. From here he turns his accusation against the priests. (26) "And her priests have set aside my law." This is the greatest lawlessness of all, for those who ought to have guided the others were themselves continually blind. "And they profaned my holy things." They performed the services unlawfully, he says. Then come the kinds of this lawlessness: "They did not distinguish between holy and profane, and they did not distinguish between clean and unclean." They did not discern and teach, he says, what is holy and divine and what is profane and human. Here he calls "profane" not what is accursed, but what is common and separate from divine things. Clean and unclean are the things the law sets apart and, again, the things the law forbids. These concern not only foods and sacrifices but also clothing and the other things that happen, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: discharges and menstruation, touching leprosy and touching a corpse, animals that die of themselves or are killed by wild beasts, and everything else the law lays down. To these he adds: "And they hid their eyes from my sabbaths, and they profaned me among them." For when they saw the sabbath day openly outraged and unlawful work done on the day of rest, they refused to rebuke those who dared to break the law. Instead, as if shutting their eyes, they pretended not to see what they kept on seeing. Returning again to the rulers, he says: (27) "Her rulers in her midst are like wolves seizing prey, shedding blood and destroying souls so that they may make greedy gain." Those who had obtained power, he says, made unjust slaughters a source of profit, and those who should have been champions of the wronged joined the side of the wrongdoers. From here he passes on to the prophets, saying: (28) "And her prophets daub them." [?] As he also said above, the wall the people had built badly was daubed even worse by the false prophets [?]. The so-called prophets, he says, gave their approval to the wrongs the rulers did, using flattering words, since they had learned to court those in power. Then he teaches their punishment: "They shall fall, seeing vain visions, divining falsehoods, saying, 'Thus says Adonai the Lord,' when

the Lord has not spoken." For in imitation of the true prophets, they attached their false oracles to the person of God and fastened the lie onto the very fountain of truth. And these things, he says, they said: (29) "Oppressing the people of the land with injustice, seizing plunder, oppressing the poor and needy, and not dealing justly with the stranger." They used lying speech, he says, and gave oracles to please the rulers, wanting to gain freedom to act against the poor, and making the lie a source of profit [?]

[?] "…living uprightly and standing in the breach of the wall before my face at the time of the land's trial, so that I might not wipe it out completely; and I did not find one." He teaches this also through Jeremiah, saying: "Go through the streets of Jerusalem and see, and search in her squares, to see whether you can find one man who does justice and seeks faithfulness, and I will be merciful to them." Here too, then, he says that among the rulers, among the priests, and among all the others, he looked for at least one man who could stand in the breach of the wall. That is, he looked for someone who could hold back the punishments being brought upon them through [his] righteousness [?], and who could block and wall off the breach made by lawlessness and [the onslaught] of punishment; and he did not find one. Therefore he says: (31) "I poured out my anger upon her in the fire of my wrath, to make an end of them." And to show that the punishment was just, he added: "Their ways [?]…" For since they walked badly and lawlessly, he says, the end followed in keeping with their own way. From this one can learn not only how great God's goodness is but also how great the impiety of the Jews [?] was. For there [in Sodom?] he promised that if he found [?] righteous men he would keep the whole city untouched by punishment; but here he looked for one and did not find him. Therefore he handed it over to the enemies and had it laid waste. It is fitting, then, for us, knowing that divine mercy is yoked with judgment, ('mercy and judgment,' they say [?]) [?] of sin [?] God's longsuffering [?]

CHAPTER 23. (1–3) "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, there were two women, daughters of one mother, and they played the harlot in Egypt." In the passages already interpreted, he called the whole people a single harlot, since from the beginning it had been considered one people. But since the division took place under Rehoboam, and some were called Ephraim and Israel while others were called Judah, it is fitting that he uses the parable and figure in a divided form. He names them after their capital cities: the ten tribes after Samaria, and Judah and Benjamin after Jerusalem. He says they were of one mother, not only because the race had one root, but also because in impiety they had one mother, Egypt; for earlier too he figuratively called their mother a Hittite and their father an Amorite. These, then, he says, played the harlot in Egypt. Then he also indicates the time: "In their youth they played the harlot; there their breasts fell, and there they lost their virginity." For their fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, were outstanding in piety, and Jacob's sons too remained strangers to idolatry; but those descended from them learned impiety instead during their stay in Egypt. By their youth he means the beginning of their growth into a multitude; by the corruption and the falling of the breasts, their learning of impious doctrines. For just as the breasts sag after virginity is lost, so the governing faculty within us collapses after a falling away from God; for the breasts are, as it were, its coverings and defences. Then, since he had called them women in a parable, he also gives them the names of certain Egyptian women who were notorious for their licentiousness. He says: (4) "And their names were Oholah the elder, and Oholibah her younger sister." Having said the earlier things in riddles, he brought the discourse to greater clarity and mentioned those courtesans. In this way he heightened the accusation, wanting to give them, through this example, a sense of their impiety. Then [he recounts] the [?] that came to them from him

[?] …he recounts the kindness [?]. "And they became mine, and bore sons and daughters; and as for their names, Samaria is Oholah, and Jerusalem is Oholibah." By "union" and "partnership" he means the agreement made with them through the law: he gave the law, and they promised to keep it. "They bore me sons and daughters" shows that, living under the law, they for a time raised their children in piety. Up to this point, then, he has brought a common accusation against both. From here on, since the tribes were divided, he first brings his accusation against Samaria, which he named Oholah. For when the kingdom was split in two, she was the first to run aground on the impiety of the heifers. 5. "And Oholah," he says, "played the harlot away from me, and doted on her lovers." He used the word "lovers" as one would of a woman, but he is hinting at the demons, whom she served without ceasing. Then he also sets out the kinds of impiety:

"And on the Assyrians," he says, "who were near to her. (6, 7) Clothed in blue, leaders and generals, all of them chosen young men, horsemen riding on horses. And she bestowed her harlotry on them, on the choice sons of the Assyrians. With all on whom she doted, in all her thoughts, she was defiled." When he speaks in riddles of "chosen young men clothed in blue," he means the idols painted and shaped by them in that fashion. All the impious of old were accustomed to dress their own gods in the costume current among themselves. The Greeks and Romans arm Ares in the style of their own equipment, the Persians in theirs, the Indians in one way and the Ethiopians in another, and likewise each of the nations we know of. Yet he also teaches that they themselves were the first to call the Assyrians to their aid, despising God's alliance. For they summoned Pul, who was king of the Assyrians, to help them against the Syrians, and promised to pay him tribute and tax. From then on the intermingling brought in impiety. Then he adds: 8. "And she did not give up her harlotry from Egypt, for they lay with her in her youth, and they deflowered her and poured out their harlotry upon her." Having joined herself to the Assyrians, he says, and having taken the stamp of their superstition, she did not neglect the Egyptian teachings either, but went on keeping those too with great care. Having thus described the kinds of impiety, he goes on to show [?] the justice of the punishment:
9. "Therefore I delivered her into the hands of her lovers, into the hands of the sons of the Assyrians, on whom

she doted." Since she would not bear my laws, he says, but though dedicated to me she loved others, I stripped her of my providence and handed her over to those whom she preferred to fellowship with me. 10. "They," he says, "uncovered her shame; they took her sons and daughters, and killed her with the sword; and she became a byword among women, and they executed vengeance on her for the daughters." So, he says, once I gave her up, she learned by experience what fellowship with me is, and what the wickedness of her lovers is. As soon as they had her in their power, they first laid bare her harlotry by punishing her, and then slaughtered her with great savagery and without mercy. They carried off her sons and daughters as captives, and every city talks about what happened to her. Here again he has figuratively called cities "women." And they showed their cruelty not only to her but also to her daughters, by which he means the cities and villages subject to her. The ten tribes suffered these things, first under Tiglath-pileser and then under Shalmaneser, both kings of the Assyrians. Having thus recounted what befell Samaria, he turns his discourse to Jerusalem and says: 11, 12. "And her sister Oholibah saw it, and was more corrupt than she in her doting (Aquila rendered 'doting' as 'longing'), and multiplied her harlotry beyond the harlotry of her sister. She doted on the sons of the Assyrians, leaders and generals near her, clothed in garments with fine borders, horsemen riding on horses, all of them chosen young men." Jerusalem too, he says, did the same things as Samaria. In the same way she trampled on her covenant with me and honored the gods of the Syrians above me, trusting in their alliance and despising my help. By the leaders and generals he hinted at the alliance they made. 13. "And I saw," he says, "that one way of the two was defiled." Their practices, he means, are alike and rival each other. 14–16. "And she added to her harlotry, and saw men painted on the wall, images of Chaldeans painted in colors [?] with a stylus, girded with embroidered cloths about their loins, with dyed tiaras on their heads; all of them had the look of officers, like the sons of Babylon, of the land of the Chaldeans, their native country. And she doted on them at the sight of her eyes." Well and very aptly has he mocked the impotence of idols, teaching that they are nothing but colors and shapes and the products of craftsmanship. And "all had a threefold look"

signifies their many forms. Symmachus rendered it "[?] all of them plunderers." When she saw these, he says, though she saw nothing but figments of the painter's art, she fell in love with lying with them. Everywhere he is hinting at idolatry. "And she sent messengers," he says, "to them in the land of the Chaldeans. 17. And the sons of Babylon came to her, to a bed of lodgers, and defiled her with their harlotry; and she was defiled by them, and her soul turned away from them." Having summoned them to her aid, he says, and having taken on impiety through mingling with them, she then turned away from them again. Here he does not mean turning away from the demons, but from the Babylonians themselves; for Jehoiakim, Jeconiah and Zedekiah broke the treaties they had made with the Babylonians. 18. "And she uncovered her harlotry and uncovered her shame, and my soul turned away from her, as my soul had turned away from her sister." Seeing, he says, how far her impiety went, he stripped her of my providence. Again he has used "soul" in the manner of allegory. This is not because the Divine is divided into soul and body, for it is incorporeal and not composite. Rather, he speaks in human fashion and in the way humans are used to, condescending to human weakness. Up to this point he seemed to be speaking to the prophet. From here on, as though recounting what she had dared to do had brought it back to mind, he turns his words to her. 19. "And you multiplied," he says, "your harlotry, recalling the days of your youth, in which you played the harlot in Egypt." I had given your offenses in Egypt over to oblivion, he says, but by your later practices you have made their memory bloom again. For doing the same wrong again often calls earlier sins to mind. Then once more, allegorically and figuratively, he brings the charge of idolatry. 20, 21. "And you doted on the Chaldeans, whose flesh is like the flesh of donkeys, and whose members are like the members of horses. And you revisited the lawlessness of your youth, which you committed in Egypt in your lodging, where the breasts of your youth fell." Even while you mingled with the Chaldeans, he says, you did not neglect the Egyptian practices, but served both their gods and those of Egypt. Their great godlessness and polytheism he likened to the members of horses and donkeys, since he also calls idolatry harlotry. For souls that were joined and dedicated to God, and then abandon him and embrace union with demons, are rightly called adulteresses.

22–24. "Therefore thus says the Lord Adonai: Behold, I will rouse your lovers against you, those from whom your soul turned away, and I will bring them against you from every side: the sons of Babylon and all the Chaldeans, Pekod and Shoa and Koa, and all the sons of the Assyrians with them, chosen young men, leaders and generals, all of them officers and men of renown, riding on horses. And they will all come against you from the north, with weapons and chariots and wheels and a multitude of peoples. They will put on breastplates and shields and helmets against you, and set a guard around you." Through them, he says, you will learn from events what I am and what your lovers are. Though you despised me, I remained patient. But these, as soon as they learn of your revolt, will come in full armor of every kind, using horses and chariots and bringing all their subjects with them, and will wall off your entrances with siegeworks. This is what he meant by saying, "They will set a guard around you." Then he adds: "And I will set judgment before them, and they will punish you with their judgments. (25) And I will set my jealousy against you, and they will deal with you in the wrath of my anger." Since you preferred them to my care, he says, I will use those very men to exact from you the penalty for your transgression against me, and I will hand you over to their punishments. He also describes the kinds of punishment: "They will cut off your nose and your ears, and your survivors will fall by the sword. They will take your sons and your daughters, and fire will devour your survivors. (26) And they will strip you of your clothing and take your splendid ornaments." Some, he says, they will carry off as captives, others they will spear in battle, and others they will mutilate, acting with harshness and cruelty. They will plunder everything that belongs to you and give most of your possessions to the fire. He also shows the benefit that will come from the punishment. 27. "And I will turn your impieties away from you, and your harlotry from the land of Egypt; you will remember it no more." Once you have fallen into those evils, you will come to see your own transgression, and you will utterly loathe the things that brought this calamity upon you. 28, 29. "For thus says the Lord Adonai: Behold, I am delivering you into the hands of those you hate, from whom your soul turned away. (29) And they will deal with you in hatred, and will take all your labors and your toils." [Apparatus: others read "threefold," less well. "From the north" is placed in B before "against you." B: "they will call." After "of my anger": "and you will not lift your eyes to them, and Egypt."]

[?] "…and you will be naked and disgraced, and the shame of your harlotry and of your impiety will be uncovered." You loved the Chaldeans, he says, and then hated them in turn; but I will hand you over to them. Through them I will exact the penalty from you, and through the punishment I will show your whole impiety laid bare. For those who see your calamities will learn that your transgression was their cause. Therefore he fittingly added: 30. "Your harlotry did these things to you, when you went whoring after the nations and were defiled by their thoughts." You followed, he says, the practices of the nations, which devised impiety by their own reasonings. And not only, he says, did you imitate the impiety of the other nations, but also: 31. "You walked in the way of your sister, and I will put her cup into your hands." What Samaria suffered, he says, you too will suffer. He called the punishment a cup because it produces stupor and drunkenness in those who drink it. 32–34. "Thus says the Lord Adonai: You will drink your sister's cup, deep and wide; and what overflows will become a laughingstock and a mockery, to complete your drunkenness. You will be filled with faintness, a cup of ruin and destruction, the cup of your sister Samaria. And you will drink it and drain it, and gnaw its shards, and tear at your breasts." He called the cup deep because of the greatness of the calamity, and wide because of the period of seventy years. He named it a cup of destruction because of the desolation that came upon the city. He added "you will drain it" because she suffered the final siege. He said she would gnaw its shards because she would fall into the worst of evils, and tear at her breasts because of the repentance that her sufferings would produce. "And your feasts," he says, "and your new moons I will take away, for I have spoken, says the Lord Adonai." I will put out every festival of yours and every delight, and I will bring my words to fulfillment; for I am a true Master who does not lie. 35. "Therefore thus says the Lord Adonai: Because you forgot me and cast me behind your body, you too must bear your impiety and your harlotry." Since you preferred the pleasures of the body to my service, he says, receive the wages of licentiousness. By this he hints that lawlessness became the foundation of impiety; for being slaves to their pleasures, they rolled down into the worship of idols.

36. "And the Lord said to me: Son of man, will you judge Oholah and Oholibah, and declare to them their lawless deeds? For they committed adultery, and blood is on their hands; they committed adultery with their thoughts, and their children whom they bore to me they made pass through fire to them." For "Will you judge?" the other translators rendered "Enter into judgment." Take on my role, O prophet, he says, and conduct the trial against Samaria and Jerusalem, and declare [?] their transgressions. Declare how they abandoned me and mingled with idols, and how they offered to those idols as a sacrifice the children I had given them, despising my laws and profaning my Sabbaths. This is what he added: 38. "Even this they did to me: they defiled my holy things on that day, and profaned my Sabbaths." Then he teaches the manner of the profanation:

39. "And when they slaughtered their children to their idols, they also entered my sanctuary on that day and profaned it." Great is the extent of this impiety. First, slaughtering their children is the furthest limit of impiety. Offering such victims to demons makes the evil worse still. Daring to do this on the Sabbath, when even necessary work was forbidden, shows the impiety to be far greater. And then, after such a deed, to set foot on the divine threshold: what further extreme of impiety does that leave? That is why he put it last, and added once more: "And behold, this is what they did in the midst of my house." They dared this impiety, he says, in the consecrated house. 40. "And they sent for men coming from afar, to whom they sent messengers; and as soon as they arrived, you bathed at once, painted your eyes, and adorned yourself with ornaments. (41) And you sat on a spread couch, with a table set out before it." He has described all this as though of a courtesan. It signifies the alliance they made with the Assyrians and Chaldeans, and the impiety brought in from them. He also alludes to the finery at the festivals of the demons, the luxuries, the changes of clothing, and everything else they were accustomed to do at such festivals. This is also what the following words mean: "And my incense and my oil you set before them." That is, of the things [offered] to

42. "And they made merry among them." For the destruction of human beings is the merriment of demons. In addition he says: "And with a sound of harmony they [Apparatus: (?) Rec. (?). B: "you will declare."]

played music for men who came from a multitude of people, drunk with wine, from the desert." For what is more desolate than those who worship idols? From those desolate souls, he says, the lessons of impiety were brought to you, and you received them with musical instruments playing sweet melody. "And they put bracelets on their hands and a crown of boasting on their heads." For those who choose to serve idols receive nothing from them. Instead they offer them God-given gifts, decking them with every kind of ornament. 43. "And I said: Do they not commit adultery in these things? These are the works of a harlot, and she has played the harlot." I said, he says, using the prophets as my instruments, that your adultery was being committed with lifeless things, and that such practices of yours are those of a harlot. 44. "And they went in to her as men go in to a harlot; so they went in to Oholah and to Oholibah, the lawless women, to commit lawlessness." Their transgression gave license from then on, and so they went in to Samaria and Jerusalem as to courtesans open to all: both the demons, the destroyers of souls, and the Chaldeans who had been taught to worship them. So he now turns his words to these, and says: 45. "And these are righteous men." He used "righteous" not to bear witness to their righteousness, for they were utterly unjust and lawless and exceedingly impious. He used "righteous" by comparison with her impieties, meaning "compared with you they are righteous." He did the same earlier when addressing Jerusalem, for he said: "And you justified your sisters by your sins and by all the lawless deeds you committed." Here too he says, "These are righteous men," that is, more righteous than you. "And they will punish them with the punishment of adulteresses, and with the judgment [?] of blood, for they are adulteresses, and blood is on their hands." [?] Their adulteries, he says, and their murders [?]. For they will pay the penalty at the hands of their lovers, and they will suffer what adulterous and murderous women suffer. Having thus completed the riddling narrative, [he pronounces?] the sentence against them. 46. "Thus says the Lord Adonai: Bring up a multitude against them, and give them over to turmoil and plunder. (47) And let them be stoned with the stones of crowds, and let them pierce them through with their

swords. They will kill their sons and daughters and burn their houses with fire." Then he shows the benefit that will come of this. 48. "And I will turn impiety away from the land, and all women will be instructed and will not act according to their impieties." For when these women suffer these things and are given over to stones and swords and fire, he says, every city will reap a benefit, learning what the wages of impiety are. Here again he has called cities "women." 49. "And your impiety will be laid upon you, and you will bear all the sins of your desires, and you will know that I am the Lord." You will reap the fruits of your impiety, he says; for you did not take it up under compulsion, but by choice and desire. Yet from the punishment you will harvest the greatest benefit, the knowledge of my lordship. May we enjoy this knowledge, not by being taught through suffering evils, but by perceiving the divine benefits. May we loathe an ungrateful mind, be renewed each day by the remembrance of God, and be set aflame with the love of God by the working of the all-holy Spirit. And may we await the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory to the Father, with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

CHAPTER 24. CHAPTER XXIV. 1, 2. "And the word of the Lord came to me in the ninth year, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, saying: Son of man, write down for yourself the name of this day, the day on which the king of Babylon set himself against Jerusalem, from this very day." He has told us the time at which the Babylonian marched against Jerusalem. While he was besieging the city, the prophet foretold to those already taken captive the evils that were about to overtake them. So the Master, to show that the prophecy did not lie, commands him to mark the day on which the enemy began to attack the city, so that both from the time and from the outcome of the events [?]… [col. 875] Verses 1, 2. And the word of the Lord came to me

…so that both those who have already been taken captive and those under siege may learn that God foretold these things about them long before, and that they were defeated not because of the strength of their enemies but because they were paying the penalty for their own sins. 3. "And speak a parable to the rebellious house." After marking the date, the prophet is commanded to teach in parable and riddle what was going to happen to the city. Because what was said was obscure, the hearers would become more eager to ask about it, and so would learn the divine oracles more exactly. "And you shall say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: (4, 5) Set on the cauldron, set it on, and pour water into it, and put pieces into it, every good piece, leg and shoulder, the flesh stripped from the bones, taken from choice cattle, and kindle the bones under them." He calls the city a cauldron, and the water poured in stands for calamities of every kind. The pieces, the legs and shoulders from choice cattle, are those who were eminent in [?], wealth and power, the rulers, leaders and priests, all handed over to the calamities alike. The bones burning underneath are those who lived in poverty, who were the first to be handed over to famine. The fire is the Babylonian king and his army. To this he adds: "It has boiled, it has boiled, and its bones have been cooked in its midst." For once the fire was set, he says, the bones burning underneath were consumed by it: they became the prey of famine. And those who escaped the onslaught of the famine came to the very height of the evils, enduring the assaults of the besiegers. 6. "Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: O city of blood, a cauldron that has rust in it, and the rust has not gone out of it; it has brought it out piece by piece; no lot has fallen upon it." Here he has taught us that earlier, too, he called the city a cauldron, and he calls sin the rust of the cauldron. And the gravest charge is that even so great a fire of calamities did not consume the cauldron's rust. "It brought it out piece by piece; no lot fell upon it" shows that no one escaped the calamities that were brought on. Nor were some assigned by lot to destruction and others to safety, as had happened in earlier sieges. Instead all alike were handed over, some to famine, others to plague, and those who survived these were either killed fighting or, being besieged, were sold into slavery. He also teaches the cause of the evils. 7. "For her blood was in her midst." They suffer these things, he says, as the penalty for their excessive bloodshed. "I have set it on a bare rock; I did not pour it out on the ground, to cover it with earth."

(8) "So that wrath might rise up for vengeance, to be avenged, I have given her blood; I have set it on a bare rock, so that it is not covered." I will not cover up, he says, the lawless deeds they dared to commit. I will lay them bare and show them to everyone, like blood that is not poured on the ground and soaked up but is cast on smooth rock and kept there forever, as an accusation against those who dared to shed it. 9–12. "Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: O city of blood, I too will make the firebrand great. And I will pile up the wood and kindle the fire, so that the flesh may melt away and the broth be boiled down, and the bones be roasted together. And it shall stand empty on its coals; it has been kindled so that it may be scorched and heated, and its bronze be burned, and its uncleanness be melted in its midst, and its rust fail. Its rust shall be brought low, and it shall not go out from it." "I will make the firebrand great," he says, that is, I will increase the beginning of the evils. "And I will pile up the wood" means: I will supply many occasions and much fuel for the fire of evils, so as to kindle it. And I will make "the flesh being boiled," that is, the people in the city, melt away. Some will be consumed by famine, roasted together like bones, and others will be burned up by calamities of every kind, like flesh being boiled. Under the great onslaught of the fire the broth will also be consumed, and with it every necessary supply and every means of relief, so that in the end the bronze itself, left alone in contact with the fire, melts down and is consumed together with the rust. For once the city's defenders were defeated, it was captured, finally laid waste and given over to fire. And yet, he says, even though so many evils fell upon it, it was not rid of its rust, but [?]

"Its rust is great; its rust shall be put to shame. (13) In your uncleanness is a seething." It was you, he says, who by your lawlessness stirred up this seething and kindled the flame of the fire. For you had much rust of sins, and now that it has been laid bare it will be covered with shame. "Because you were defiled and were not cleansed of your uncleanness, you shall not be cleansed any more until I have spent my wrath on you." Since you refused to heal your wounds by repentance, you will not obtain pardon or enjoy cleansing until you have paid the penalty for your transgressions. Then he shows that what was said is true by the identity of the one who speaks. 14. "I the Lord have spoken." And he shows that what is to come cannot be gainsaid:

"And it shall come, and I will do it; I will make no exception, I will not spare, and I will not relent." For I will not let some go free; I will hand them all over to the evils I have threatened. He also shows that the punishment is just: "According to your ways and according to your devices I will judge you, says Adonai the Lord." And the same thing [?]: "Therefore, behold, I will judge you according to your devices, and according to your blood I will judge you, O unclean one, notorious and much given to provoking." You have become notorious for wickedness, he says, and the cause of your lawlessness is that you followed evil thoughts. He indicated this by saying, "According to your devices and according to your blood I will judge you." For we first reason about things, whether good or bad, and only then do we add the deed to the reasoning. From here he moves the prophecy into another form, and says: 15–17. "The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, behold, I am taking from you the desire of your eyes violently. You shall not beat your breast or weep, nor shall tears come to you. Groan in silence; it is a groaning of blood, a mourning of the loins." By "desires" or "devices" of the eyes (for some copies read it this way) he means his wife, his partner in marriage. When she died, the prophet was ordered neither to weep nor to lament but to groan in silence, even though the mourning touched his loins. For by "the loins" he indicated the desire to beget children; for so also [?]

…to enjoy something. The prophet also seems to have been a Nazirite, for it says, "Your hair shall be braided upon you." And earlier he was commanded to drink water, not wine. Both of these are marks of Nazirites. 18. "And I spoke to the people in the morning, as he had commanded me; and my wife died in the evening, and in the morning I did as I had been commanded." Here the prophet takes the place of the God of all. The people of Israel had been joined to the Master as a bride, and they were about to be handed over in this way to slavery and slaughter, and the divine temple to be burned. So God makes the prophet a figure of what was to come. When his wife died suddenly, God charges him not to lament or weep, not to put on mourning dress, not to share in the meal of consolation, but to groan in silence. In this way he shows that he himself will grant no kindness to those joined to him, yet will bring punishment on them against his will. "For he does not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he should turn and live." That is why he tells the prophet to groan in silence. By this he signifies that he too, against his will, bears the calamities brought on the people: his goodness is great and on its account he leans toward kindness, but the excess of their lawlessness compels him to punish. 19–24. "And the people said to me," he says, "Will you not tell us what these things mean that you are doing? And I said to them: The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Say to the house of Israel: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I am profaning my holy places, the pride of your strength, the desires of your eyes, and the things your souls hold dear; and your sons and your daughters whom you have left behind shall fall by the sword. And you shall do as I have done: you shall not be comforted by their mouth, and you shall not eat the bread of men. And your hair shall be on your heads and your shoes on your feet; you shall not beat your breasts or weep, and you shall waste away in your hearts, and you shall not comfort each his brother. And Ezekiel shall be a portent for you; you shall do all that he has done when these things come, and you shall know that I am Adonai the Lord." I have shown you the prophecy through deeds, he says, and sketched in my own person what will happen to you. When my wife came to the end of her life, I did none of the things usually done for the dead: no lament, no tears, no mourning dress. So too with you. Your sons and daughters will be slaughtered, and the holy temple will be profaned by the entry of the unholy barbarians, the temple in which

you have boasted until now and have gone on vaunting yourselves. On top of this you will meet with countless other evils, yet you will not even be free to lament or be allowed to do the customary things: not to shave your head, not to bare your feet of sandals, not to relieve the weight of your grief with streams of tears, not to share in the meal of consolation, not to perform any other of the customary rites. And you will remember what the prophet did, and learn from the outcome of events that the prophet became a portent and a sign for you, giving you through his deeds a prediction of what was to come. 25–27. "And you, son of man, will it not be on the day when I take from them their strength, the pride of their boasting, the desires of their eyes and the pride of their soul, their sons and their daughters? On that day the one who escapes will come to you to tell it in your ears. On that day your mouth will be opened to the one who escaped, and you will speak and be mute no longer, and you will be a portent for them, and they will know that I am Adonai the Lord." You will teach them these things not only now, but also later. When the prediction is fulfilled, when the holy things are handed over to the unholy barbarians and their sons and daughters are given up to slaughter, and someone arrives from there to tell what has happened, you are to remind them of the prediction and not keep silent. Then they will learn that these things happened because I willed and permitted them, and that they are paying the penalty for their impieties; and that they suffered not because of the strength of their enemies but because of my just wrath. From here he now turns the prophecy to Israel's neighbors, who were gloating over them, and he brings forward the sons of Ammon first.

CHAPTER 25. 1–5. "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against the sons of Ammon and prophesy against them. And you shall say to the sons of Ammon: Hear the word of Adonai the Lord. Thus says Adonai the Lord: Because you rejoiced over my holy places when they were profaned, and over the land of Israel when it was laid waste, and over the house of Judah when they went into captivity, therefore, behold, I am handing you over to the sons of Kedem as an inheritance, and they shall encamp with their baggage in you and pitch their tents in you; they shall eat your fruits and drink your richness. And I will make the city of Ammon a pasture for camels and the sons of Ammon a pasture for sheep, and you shall know that I am Adonai the Lord." The other translators rendered "sons of Kedem" as "sons of the East." These are the people who trace their descent from Ishmael.

So the God of all says through the prophet to the sons of Ammon: Since you gloated when you saw the temple consecrated to me trampled by foul and unholy men, the land of Israel laid waste, and the tribe of Judah taken captive, I will make you subject to people far inferior to the Babylonians and far weaker. They will surround you with many calamities, pitching their tents in your cities and grazing their herds of camels in your land, and they will make you yourselves shepherds of sheep. When these things happen to you, you will learn that my people suffered what they suffered not because of any weakness of mine but because of their own lawlessness. 6–7. "Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Because you clapped your hand and stamped your foot and rejoiced in your soul over the land of Israel, therefore, behold, I will stretch out my hand against you and give you up as plunder among the nations, and I will wipe you out from among the peoples and destroy you utterly from the lands, and you shall know that I am Adonai the Lord." Because, he says, you gloated and exulted over the sufferings of my people, clapping your hands and stamping your feet as you leaped and danced, you will suffer harsher things, and through the events themselves you will learn my sovereignty. From here he moves the prophecy on to Moab, who was Ammon's brother and neighbor. 8–11. "Thus says Adonai the Lord: Because Moab and Seir said, 'Behold, the house of Israel and Judah is just like all the nations,' therefore, behold, I am disabling the shoulder of Moab, from his cities, from his frontier heights, the choice land, the house of Beth-jeshimoth above the spring of the city by the sea, Baal-meon and Kiriathaim. I have given the sons of Kedem against the sons of Ammon as an inheritance, and I will give it up to be removed, so that there may be no remembrance of the sons of Ammon among the nations. (11) And on Moab I will execute vengeance, and you shall know that I am the Lord." He joined Seir to Moab because Seir too was one of the neighbors. By Seir he means those descended from Esau. Esau was also called Edom, which means "ruddy" or "red," and Seir means "shaggy" and "hairy." Esau, Jacob's brother, had both of these features: "For the first came out red," it says, "all hairy like a hide." And the patriarch Jacob said of him to his mother: "Esau my brother is a hairy man, but I am

a smooth man." Seir and Moab, he says, reveling in my people's sufferings, dared to say that my people is no different from the other nations. This blasphemy reached even to me, implying that I was as weak as the idols of the other nations and could not defend my people. For this reason "I am disabling the shoulder of Moab, from his cities," that is, I will destroy their strength. And I will lay waste not only the cities that lie on the heights but also his coastal cities. By "coastal" he means the cities lying along the Dead Sea, for the Moabites lived far from the other sea. He also gives the names of the cities, of which a small remnant has survived to this day; some belong to this part of Arabia, others to that. He adds that he will hand these too over to the same enemies to whom he handed their brothers, the sons of Ammon. And they will learn by experience that the Master is powerful and able to defend his people, but because of the people's lawlessness he will not consent to do so. That is why he added, "And they shall know that I am the Lord." Having foretold in this way what would happen to Moab, he turns his discourse to Seir, also called Edom. 12–14. "Thus says Adonai the Lord: Because Idumea acted in taking vengeance on the house of Judah in wrath, and they bore a grudge and exacted vengeance from them, therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: I will stretch out my hand against Idumea and cut off from it man and beast, and I will make it a desert, and those pursued from Teman and Dedan shall fall by the sword. And I will lay my vengeance on Idumea by the hand of my people Israel, and they shall deal with Idumea according to my anger, and they shall know my vengeance, says Adonai the Lord." Like the Moabites and Ammonites, they gloated, but they also showed their wickedness in deeds, nursing their old grudge: "For Esau bore a grudge against Jacob," it says, "because of the blessing with which his father blessed him." So, he says, I will hand them over not to other enemies but to my own people, whom they wronged, so that through utter desolation they may learn the power of my sovereignty. Teman is a city of Idumea, and so is Dedan. Their founders were among the descendants born to the patriarch Abraham by Keturah, and the cities were named after them. Dedan lay near Idumea and bordered on it. Having foretold in this way what concerned these peoples, he turns the prediction to the foreigners. For the Idumeans were not foreigners, being descendants of Isaac; nor were the Ammonites and Moabites, who trace their descent from Lot. The Tyrians and Sidonians

were indeed foreigners, as were all the others who were their neighbors. But the divine Scripture gives the name "foreigners" especially to the people of Ashkelon and Gaza, of Gath and Ekron, and of Ashdod, because their land adjoined that of the tribe of Judah and they were its very close neighbors. So he also tells what would happen to them. 15–17. "Thus says Adonai the Lord: Because the foreigners acted in wrath and rose up to take vengeance, rejoicing with their whole soul, to destroy in everlasting enmity, therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I will stretch out my hands against the foreigners, and I will wipe out the Cretans and destroy the remnant who live along the coast. And I will execute great vengeance on them with rebukes of my wrath, and they shall know that I am Adonai the Lord, when I lay my vengeance upon them." He charges these too with wrath, as he did the Idumeans. They bore a grudge against my people, he says, because it had conquered them and established its own kingdom, and so they made the time of its calamity a time for revenge, rising up and inflicting countless evils on it. For this reason I will exact from them the penalty for their grudge and hand them over to blows sent by God. I will destroy the subjects together with their rulers and give them over to evils they cannot escape, so that through what they endure they may come to know the power of my sovereignty. But let us not wait to come to know our Master through the experience of evils. Let us instead receive the knowledge of him through his ever-flowing gifts and be grateful for his benefits. Let us flee the passion of resentment, having learned what destructive fruits it bears. And let us keep the apostolic commandment, not waiting for the sun to go down on our grievances against one another, but quenching our anger before it sets. In this way we shall also put an end to the anger of the just Judge against us and reap that lovely and thrice-longed-for favor. May we all obtain it, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

"Because Sor said against Jerusalem, 'Aha! She is broken, she has perished; the nations have turned to me; she who was full has been laid waste.'" In the eleventh year of Jeconiah's captivity and of Zedekiah's reign, in the fourth month, on the ninth of the month, Jerusalem was taken by the Babylonians. So a few days before the capture the prophet is ordered to utter his prophetic words against Tyre, for in the local language Tyre is called Sor. Tyre too had rejoiced at the siege of Jerusalem, and supposed that once that most illustrious city was destroyed, she would rise to power over all the neighbouring nations. (3–6) "Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I am coming against you, Sor, and I will bring up many nations against you, as the sea comes up with its waves. They will tear down your walls and demolish your towers, and I will sweep her dust from her and make her a bare rock. She shall be a place for drying nets in the midst of the sea, for I have spoken, says Adonai the Lord, and she shall be plunder for the nations. And her daughters that are in the plain shall be slain by the sword, and they shall know that I am the Lord." With these words he threatens her with the campaign of the Babylonians. He says that her ramparts will be destroyed and she will become desolate, so that she will look like the smooth rocks on which fishermen usually spread out their nets. He also says that the cities and villages subject to her will be laid waste, for these are what he calls her daughters. And he points out the gain that comes from these calamities: "For they shall know," he says, "that I am the Lord." (7–8) "For thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I am bringing against you, Sor, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the north (he is king of kings), with horses and chariots and horsemen, and a host of very many nations. He will slay your daughters in the plain with the sword; he will set a siege post against you and build around you; he will dig a trench against you, and raise a palisade around you on every side, and a ring of arms; and he will set his spears against you." By "siege post" he means the bases that invading enemies usually build, so as both to plunder the surrounding country and to wear down the besieged through want of necessities. By "build around" he means the walls the enemy builds on the outside. To this encircling wall, he says, he will add palisades and trenches and earthworks, so that no one will dare to come out, and missiles of every kind can easily be hurled. Then he adds:

(9–14) "He will tear down your walls and your towers with his weapons. The dust of his many horses will cover you, and at the noise of his horsemen and the wheels of his chariots your walls will shake as he passes through your gates, as one enters a city from the plain. With the hooves of their horses they will trample all your streets; he will slay your people with the sword and bring the foundation of your strength down to the ground. He will plunder your power and despoil your possessions; he will throw down your walls and demolish your pleasant houses, and cast your stones and your timber and your dust into the midst of the sea. He will put an end to the throng of your musicians, and the sound of your harps will be heard no more. And I will make you a bare rock; you shall be a place for drying nets, and you shall never be built again, for I have spoken, says Adonai the Lord." All that I foretell, he says, is true. So accept this prediction as one that does not lie: the Babylonians will tear down your walls, and after demolishing your houses they will fill the places nearby [?] with their stones. So loud will be the clatter of horses and chariots that the city will seem to be shaken by an earthquake. They will plunder your possessions and sell your inhabitants into slavery. And such desolation will seize you that fishermen will dry their wet nets in you; what they usually do on the smooth rocks near the sea, they will do in you because of your utter desolation. As for "You shall never be built again," we shall learn its meaning from the prophecy of the blessed prophet Isaiah. That prophet too foretold grievous things for Tyre, but he limited them to a fixed period: "Tyre shall be left," he says, "for seventy years, like the time of one king, like the lifetime of a man. And after the seventy years God will visit Tyre, and she will be restored again to her former state, and will be a market for all the kingdoms of the world on the face of the whole earth, and her trade will be holy to the Lord," and so on. So "She shall not be built" hints at a change in her ways: she will not be built according to her former impiety, but will receive another building, the direct opposite, which, according to the prophet Isaiah, will be holy to the Lord. The facts bear witness to this, as does the piety that prevails there now. For she turned to God from her former superstition and her error concerning idols, and received the light of the knowledge of God. (15–16) "For thus says the Lord to Sor: Will not, at the sound of your fall, when your wounded groan, when they are slain with swords in your midst,

the islands quake? All the rulers of the nations of the sea will come down from their thrones; they will take the turbans off their heads and strip off their embroidered robes. They will be seized with astonishment; they will sit on the ground and fear their own destruction, and groan over you." Tyre was renowned from of old, not only in Asia but in Europe too; so the calamity that befell her inevitably became widely known. When the islanders learn of it, he says, they will be terrified, and their kings, out of dejection and grief, will bare their heads of their diadems (for these are what he called turbans), will put off their costly clothing, and will take on the garb of mourning, expecting to suffer the same. This is what he meant by saying, "And they will fear their own destruction." The news of your misfortunes will distress them so much that they will even take up a lament over you and say: (17–18) "How you have perished and been destroyed from the sea, O city that was praised, which was strong in the sea, she and her inhabitants, she who laid the fear of her on all who dwell in her! And the islands will be afraid from the day of your fall, and the islands will be troubled by your power in the sea." Reflecting on your former power, he says, and seeing the calamity that has now overtaken you, they will lament you, who were once so celebrated and famous, and they will be anxious about their own affairs, fearing that they may fall into the same. (19–20) "For thus says Adonai the Lord: When I make you a desolate city, like the cities that will never be inhabited, when I bring the deep up over you and many waters cover you, then I will bring you down with those who go down to the pit, to the people of the ages past, and I will make you dwell in the depths of the earth, like an everlasting wasteland, with those who go down to the pit, so that you may not be inhabited, nor rise up on the land of life." He called the Babylonian army a "deep" because of its vast numbers. Since Tyre is surrounded by water and like an island, lying entirely within the sea and having a single approach from the land, he aptly used this figure, calling the host of enemies water and a deep. "I will bring you down with those who go down to the pit, to the people of the ages" signifies death, which all who pass through life undergo in this present age; so by "the people of the ages" he meant the dead. And "that you may not rise on the land of life" points to that saying of the psalm: "Therefore the ungodly shall not rise

in the judgment, nor sinners in the council of the righteous." Since those who inhabited Tyre at that time were ungodly, they will not rise into the land of life, which the blessed David calls the land of the living: "For he has delivered my soul from death," he says, "my eyes from tears, and my feet from stumbling, that I may be pleasing before the Lord in the land of the living." And the Lord in the holy Gospels makes the same distinction: "These," he says, "will rise to eternal life, and those to eternal punishment and shame." So he threatens those who then inhabited Tyre and lived in impiety not only with the Babylonian's assault and the ruin it brought, but also with painful and grievous things in the life to come. For what could be more painful than not to rise on the land of life? To this he adds: (21) "I will give you over to destruction, and you shall not exist forever, says Adonai the Lord." All the divine prophets and the holy apostles were granted the same Spirit; therefore they do not say things that contradict one another, for the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of truth. If the divine prophets were granted the same Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of truth, then the oracles of the blessed prophets agree with one another. So if we find Tyre's desolation limited in time in Isaiah, and then hear the prophet Ezekiel saying to Tyre, "You shall be sought and not found forever, says Adonai the Lord," [?] we shall not accuse the prophets [of contradiction], but shall resolve the question from the idioms of Scripture. Divine Scripture is accustomed to call even a short time an "age." Such is the saying of the blessed David: "Our age is in the light of your countenance." And yet the same David says: "The days of our years are seventy years, and if in strength, eighty years, and most of them are toil and trouble." Knowing that human life is that long, he called it an age. So "You shall not be found for the age" means: for the age [?] of the desolation; and a period of seventy years was set for it through the prophet Isaiah. And if someone wishes to understand the passage more spiritually, he will find the prophecy true in this way as well. For if anyone looks for Tyre, he will not find that former city. That one was impious; but the one that blossomed and flourished again after that desolate city is seen to be pious, shining with the light of the knowledge of God. So whether one wishes to understand the prophecy literally, he will find that the time appointed for her is called an age; or if in

(1–3) "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, take up a lament over Sor, and say to Sor, who dwells at the entrance of the sea, the market of the peoples from many islands." These words show the surpassing love for humankind and the goodness of God. The passage also teaches us that when we inflict some correction on sinners, we should not do it out of hostility and hatred, but with sympathy and deep grief. For he himself, though he judges justly and most righteously, commands the prophet to lament the city being punished, thereby showing the disposition with which he punished it. "Thus says Adonai the Lord to Sor: You said, 'I have clothed myself with my beauty.' [?] In the heart of the sea, to Baalim." By these words he exposes her ingratitude and arrogance. Having received from God the means of her splendour, she was ungrateful to the giver of these good things, and credited her own wisdom and power with the abundance of good things that had come to her. She even dedicated it to Baalim, which is what divine Scripture calls the idols. Her impiety, then, was twofold: not only did she fail to acknowledge the giver of good things, but she dared to ascribe their bestowal to things utterly powerless, which cannot even clothe themselves with visible beauty. Then he recounts how many and what kind of gifts she enjoyed, and from how many nations the sources of her wealth were brought to her. (4–6) "Your sons clothed you with beauty. Cedar from Senir was built for you; strips of cypress planks were taken from Lebanon to make your fir masts; from Bashan they made your oars." These are mountains that produce various kinds of timber. So he lists what was brought to her from every quarter: that you cut your masts in Lebanon and shipped them over, your oars from Bashan, and your building timber from Senir. To this he adds: "They made your sacred things of ivory, houses of wood from the islands of Kittim."
