Instead of "your sacred things," the other translators have put "your sailyard," in keeping with the sequence of what was said before, for the sailyard goes with the mast and the oars. But if it were said of the idols, it would not be unlikely: she fashioned ivory idols, he says, and "houses of wood," that is, panelled with planks, for that is how Aquila translated it too. And to show how precious the timber was, he also named the places it came from: "For you brought these," he says, "from the islands of Kit-

tim." By Kittim he means the Greek islands. For through Jeremiah too God says: "Cross over to the islands of Kittim and see, and send to Kedar and consider carefully whether such things have happened, whether nations will change their gods, though they are no gods." By Kedar he indicates the nations lying to the east, and by Kittim those to the west. Kition is a small town in Cyprus that is still called by that name today; pronounced with an aspirate, as is the Hebrew idiom, it shows its kinship with "Chettiim" [Kittim]. And at that time Cyprus ruled over the islands. That is why he calls the Greek islands Kittim. From these islands, he says, your precious timber was brought to you. To this he adds:

(7) "Fine linen with embroidery from Egypt became your bedding, to give you glory and to clothe you; blue and purple from the islands of Elishah became your coverings." Egypt, he says, supplied you with bedding of many colours and of every kind; he means carpets and the other goods brought from there. And Greece sent you coverings of every kind, some dyed purple, others hyacinth blue. For by Elishah he means Greece.

(8) "And your rulers who dwell in Sidon, and the Aradians, became your rowers." The Hebrew and the Syriac do not have "your rulers" but "your neighbours." But so that we may also make sense of the translation of the Seventy, let us take it this way: the Sidonians, once your rulers, now together with the inhabitants of Arad man your fleet, rowing your ships, while the skilled men among you serve as pilots. "For your wise men, Sor," he says, "who were in you, these were your pilots. (9) The elders of Byblos and their wise men, who were in you, these strengthened your counsel." They did not strengthen their own city, but offered you the best counsel and advice. "And all the ships of the sea and their rowers were in you, trading in exchange with you, and they were yours as far as the west of the west." Merchants flocked together from every side, he says, some selling, others buying; for this is what "trading in exchange with you" means. And not only did those near you put in at your harbours, but also those who lived in the very farthest reaches of the west. That is what "the west of the west" means: not only those who live to the west of you, he says, but also those to the west of them

(10–11) "Persians and Libyans and Lydians were in your army, your men of war; they hung light shields and helmets in you; these gave you your glory. The sons of the Aradians, and your army, were on your walls all around; and Medes too were guards in your towers; they hung their quivers on your shoulders all around; these perfected your beauty." Having described the different kinds of timber, the variety of clothing, the sailors and pilots, the counsellors who showed what had to be done, and the merchants arriving from everywhere, he also lists her military roll, drawn from various nations and trained in civic affairs [?]: Persians, Lydians, Libyans, Aradians and Medes. He also names the kinds of armour: quivers, light shields and helmets. The pelta is the small shield that light-armed troops carry in war; it is also used by those who perform the pyrrhic war dance. (12) "The Carthaginians were your merchants because of the abundance of all your strength; silver and gold, bronze and iron, tin and lead they gave as your merchandise." Carthage (the metropolis of what was once called Libya and is now called Africa) is called Tarshish by the Syriac and the Hebrew. By naming the metropolis, he indicated the trade in the metals mined there that was brought from the whole nation. (13) "All Greece, and the lands bordering on it, traded with you in human lives, and gave bronze vessels as your merchandise." Slaves, he says, and bronze vessels were brought to you from Greece and the neighbouring lands. (14) "From the house of Togarmah they gave horses and horsemen and mules as your merchandise." Horses, he says, and their riders, and mules, Phrygia sent you; for that is how they interpret "the house of Togarmah." (15) "The sons of the Rhodians were your merchants; from the islands they multiplied your trade, horns and ivory tusks." The "horns" Symmachus translated as ebony wood, from which the so-called ebony wares are made. These, he says, the Rhodians brought you, sailing across the sea, and they filled up for you their

[?] setting out from [other] nations, yet choosing to live with them. (16) "Stacte and purple and embroidered work and fine linen from Tarshish, and Raamoth and Choth, they gave as your merchandise." Besides what has already been mentioned, you also had other good things from Carthage, which not only adorned you with clothing and wrapped you in embroidered garments, but also spices that gave you a rich fragrance. By stacte he means what is called balsam; by Choth, onycha; and by Raamoth, the other aromatics. (17) "Judah and Israel, these were your merchants in the sale of grain, and of perfumes and cassia; and they gave the finest honey and oil and resin to your mixed multitude." So great, he says, was the abundance brought to you by trade with Judea that those who lived with you, the foreigners and resident aliens among you, enjoyed the goods imported, using some for food and others for the luxury of their fragrance

(18) "Damascus was your market for the multitude of your works, from the abundance of all your power." What was produced among you, he says, Damascus bought; so you traded with her too, selling off your surplus and collecting gold from her in return. "Rich wine from Helbon, and bright wool from Miletus. (19) And Dedan and Javan and [?] gave wine as your merchandise." By Javan he means Ionia, and by Dedan a city of Idumea; Helbon was a village near it. Good things were brought to you from every side, he says: sweet and fragrant wine from this nation, and the finest wool from Miletus, a city that once belonged to Ionia and now belongs to Caria. Symmachus translated [Helbon?] as Chaldane. "From Asel came wrought iron, and wheels are in your mixed multitude. (20–21) Dedan were your merchants in choice beasts for chariots. Arabia and all the rulers of Kedar, these were merchants at your hand, in camels and rams and lambs; in these they traded with you." Some, he says, brought you wrought iron, others mules and horses for chariots, others camels and rams and lambs, so that some might carry your loads and others feed and clothe you. [?] By Kedar he means those descended from Ishmael [?] [?] and of the

…a city of Idumea, as we have already said. For both in Jeremiah and in Ezekiel himself, in the vision against Idumea, we have found Teman joined to Dedan. Some took Asel to be Asia, which has excellent ironworkers and makes iron vessels very well. 22. “The merchants of Sheba and Raamah, these were your merchants, with the finest spices and precious stones, and they gave gold as your market.” Sheba and Raamah trace their descent from Cush, and Cush was Ham's firstborn. These, then, are Ethiopian and Indian nations. The goods brought from there also show this: precious stones, gold, and [?].

23. “Haran, Chalan and Dedan, these were your merchants.” Haran is Carrhae, and Chalan is Chalanne, where the tower was built. We have often explained Dedan. “Sheba, Asshur and Charman were your merchants, 24. bringing merchandise in Machalim and in Galima: blue cloth, embroidery, and choice treasures stored in manozois, bound with cords, [?] in cypress ships; in them was your merchandise.” By Sheba he means an Indian nation, for we find this name in the genealogy of Shem as well. Asshur is the Assyrian, and Charman is the region called Carmania. Aquila translated the words “In Machalim and in Galima, blue cloth, embroidery, and choice treasures stored in magozois” as follows: “In finely made wrappings of blue and embroidery, and stored in matozois.” The phrase “in magozois” is a Greek transliteration of the Hebrew, and it means “in hidden vessels.” The Syriac translator also understood it this way when he translated it. He is saying that costly, embroidered clothing, covered with very valuable wrappings, stored in vessels of excellent workmanship and bound with cords, was brought to you. 25. “The ships of the Carthaginians were in your trade, in the multitude of your mixed throng.” You also used the ships of the Carthaginians for trade, and you had a countless population, not only native but brought in from abroad. “And you were filled and became very heavy in the hearts of the seas. 26. Your rowers brought you into much water.” He is saying: “Your surfeit made you frisk about, and while you enjoyed good things you ignored your benefactor.” He made the same accusation against Israel: “Jacob ate,” he says, “and was filled, and the beloved one kicked.”

He means: “Since you reaped no benefit from your prosperity, I will teach you to be sensible through its opposite. For the south wind has shattered you in the heart of the sea.” This was his figurative name for the Babylonian. The south wind naturally raises the greatest waves and stirs up a dangerous surge against those at sea, so, as he is speaking to a coastal city, he figuratively calls the enemies' attack a south wind. Then, so that we need not dwell on the same points, he says that utter destruction will overtake you and your resident aliens, your rowers, your pilots, your counselors, your merchants, and those who fill your military roll. He meant this when he said: “They shall fall in the midst of the heart of the seas.” He adds that once the siege and capture have taken place, your pilots who sail from far away will be seized by great fear and turn to flight. The sailors and the bow officers will do the same: they will abandon their boats and go ashore lamenting and wailing. They will sprinkle earth on their heads and lie down on the ground itself, smearing themselves with its dust. They will strip their heads of the beauty of their hair, put on sackcloth, and go on lamenting and mourning. Then he gives the lament that they make: “Who is like Tyre, silenced in the midst of the sea?” He means: “You spent all this time in quiet and peace, and no one dared to stir up trouble against you.” 33. “How much reward did you find from the sea?” This is enough to teach everyone not to be proud of apparent prosperity, because of the reversal that follows. He is saying this to Tyre: “What have you gained in all this time from your great trade?” And yet he says: “From your mixed throng and your commerce you enriched all the kings of the earth. 34–36. But now you are shattered in the sea, in the depth of the water. Your mixed throng and all your assembly have fallen in your midst, and all your rowers. Those who live in the islands will be gloomy over you, and their kings will be utterly astounded, and their faces will weep. The merchants of the nations will hiss at you. You have come to destruction, and you will be no more forever.” He is saying: “Consider how your toil in trade did you no good, nor did the coming of all the nations. Like a boat swamped by the sea, you were overwhelmed by the sudden onset of disaster, as if you had taken waves upon you: the blizzard of the armies. For this reason all the islanders and coastal peoples, together with their kings,

lament you, seeing that the city once most illustrious has suddenly vanished from sight and is gone. Amazed at your change to utter desolation, they will show the shock in their minds by hissing.” We will understand the words “you will be no more forever” according to the interpretation we have already given. But if another must be added to what has been said, we will not shrink from it. We have heard the God of all say through the prophet Jeremiah: “At one moment I will speak against a nation and a kingdom, to uproot, pull down and destroy them; and if that nation turns from their evils, I will repent of the evils I planned to do to them. And at another moment I will speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to build it up and to plant it; and if they do evil before me, so as not to listen to my voice, I will repent of the good things I said I would do for them.” Does the Master, then, pronounce sentence and then revoke it, and does the truth lie? He pronounces sentence against those who [do not?] make use of repentance; but for those who accept the medicines of repentance the verdict of punishment lies idle. This is what happened with the Ninevites. He condemned them to utter destruction, saying: “Three days more, and Nineveh will be overthrown.” But when they repented he accepted them and revoked the sentence. So here too the change in the descendants revoked the verdict of perpetual punishment.

1–2. “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, say to the ruler of Tyre: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Because your heart was lifted up and you said, ‘I am a god; I have dwelt in the dwelling of God in the heart of the sea’—yet you are a man and not God, and you have set your heart as the heart of God.” These kinds of sin are abominable, but pride is the most abominable of all. For Scripture says, “Everything lofty is an abomination before the Lord,” and, “The Lord opposes the proud.” And the divine Apostle says: “Not a recent convert, lest he become puffed up and fall into the condemnation of the devil.” The ruler of Tyre also had this disease, both the visible ruler and the invisible one. We who are pious are ruled, properly and truly, by the God of all, but we are also ruled by men adorned with piety. So too Tyre now, like us, has God as its king and the men whom he has appointed to reign. But in the past, suffering from ignorance of God and enslaved to impiety, it had as its ruling king the devil, the inventor and teacher of wickedness and impiety. It also had a visible ruler, who was wickedly driven by him and

enslaved to impiety. The words, then, are addressed to both, but not everything fits either the one or the other. Some things fit both, some fit only one of them, and the passage just read fits each. For the devil ran aground on that madness: in his frenzy he called himself God and persuaded people to offer him that worship. And the visible ruler of the Tyrians, sick with the same conceit and looking at his great prosperity, imagined that he was God. That is why God says to him: “But you are a man and not God.” And he makes a comparison: 3. “Are you wiser than Daniel? The wise did not instruct you in their knowledge.” He means: “Far from comparing what you have with the divine nature, I will show that it falls short even of intelligent men. Daniel had divine wisdom and also acquired the learning of the Chaldeans; but you have been deprived of divine grace and did not acquire knowledge from wise men.” Then comes the refutation from the facts: 4–5. “Was it by your knowledge or your understanding that you made power for yourself and acquired silver and gold in your treasuries? Or was it by your great knowledge and your trade that you multiplied your power, and your heart was lifted up in your power?” He is saying: “Learn from the facts themselves that you obtained this trade and this abundance of goods not by your own wisdom but by my provision. For if I wish, I will strip you of all of it at once and set experience over you to teach you the facts. If you had gained these possessions by your own wisdom, you would have used that same wisdom and not been stripped of what you acquired. But when you are stripped and left bereft of all of it, throw away your foolish reasonings and know that it was I who gave you these things and took them back again. Since you did not know me when you received, you will learn me when you are stripped.” 6–10. “Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Since you have set your heart as the heart of God, behold, I am bringing against you foreigners, pests from the nations, and they will empty their swords upon you and upon the beauty of your knowledge, and they will lay your beauty low in destruction. They will bring you down, and you will die the death of the slain in the heart of the sea. Will you really say, ‘I am God,’ in front of those who kill you? You are a man and not God, in the hand of those who wound you. You will die the deaths of the uncircumcised at the hands of foreigners, for I have spoken, says Adonai the Lord.” He means: “When the enemies I send against you strip you of your royal authority and

send you to death by the sword, will you swagger and boast and call yourself God again, as if to frighten them with the divine title? That cannot happen. The change in your circumstances will bring about a change in your thinking, and you will learn that you are a man and not God when you are wounded and killed and slaughtered like your uncircumcised subjects. For my sentence is firm and cannot be gainsaid.” This is what he meant by “For I have spoken, says Adonai the Lord.” These words also fit the avenging demon that worked wickedness in the visible ruler of the Tyrians. That is why he threatens him with destruction by foreigners, pests and nations. Such were, in former times, those who through the preaching of the gospel were changed and came to the knowledge of God. That is why the divine Apostle says: “For we too were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, hating one another.” And God himself says through the great Moses: “They provoked me to jealousy with what is no god; they angered me with their idols. So I will provoke them to jealousy with what is no nation; with a foolish nation I will anger them.” Through these people, then, who were once foolish, senseless, led astray, hateful, pests, foreigners and gentiles, the prophetic word foretells the overthrow of the devil. One can also find the name “foreigners” applied to the pious who have believed: “For you,” he says, “who once were far off have been brought near.” He says that with their own swords these will destroy the beauty of the devil's knowledge and make it vanish. In other words: “They will overthrow your devices and put a stop to your plots against human beings; they will tear up from their foundations the shrines that they had built for you; and they will hand you over to oblivion as to a kind of death, having received authority ‘to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all your power.’ And through the facts themselves you will learn that you persuaded people in vain that you are God. You will suffer this because your mind was uncircumcised and you did not cut away the grievous passion of your arrogance.” 11–13. “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, take up a lament over the ruler of Tyre, and say to him: Thus says Adonai the Lord: You are the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and a crown of beauty. You were in the delight of the paradise of God. You have been bound about with every precious stone: sardius, topaz, emerald, hyacinth, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper, silver,

gold, ligure, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl and onyx. And you filled your treasuries and your storehouses within you with gold, from the day you were created.” One might force these words to apply to the visible ruler of Tyre, but properly and truly they fit the wicked demon that worked in him. If we take them of the visible ruler of Tyre, we will understand them as follows. “You are the seal of likeness”: for man was formed according to the divine image. “Full of wisdom”: for he is rational and honored with reason. “And a crown of beauty”: for he is superior to all irrational creatures, whether they walk, fly, live in water or both on land and in water. “And you were in the delight of the paradise of God”: you trace your descent from a forefather who, as soon as he was formed, was placed in the paradise of delight to work it and keep it. It is also fitting that he calls Jerusalem, which is named the holy and divine city, a paradise, since it has the plants of God's prophecy and high priesthood, which bestow life and salvation. In former times there was friendship between the king of the Tyrians and the king of the Israelites, and they had dealings with each other; this is easy to learn from the books of Kingdoms. The words “You have been bound about with every precious stone” are clear when understood literally and taken to refer to a king. He means: “I adorned you with countless good things and brought you materials of every kind from everywhere. From them you made diadems and crowns, brooches, belts and rings, and you filled your storerooms; [?] now you have done the opposite, because of their abundance and splendor.” With regard to the devil, however, we will not understand these words in this way. Instead we will take “You are the seal of likeness” to refer to the rule and authority once given to him. For the divine Apostle says: “According to the ruler of the authority of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience.” So it is clear that he was once entrusted with the administration of this air, but having fallen from his command through arrogance, he displays his own working in those who do not believe the word of the preaching. “Full of wisdom and a crown of beauty, and you were in the delight of paradise”: by these words he hints at his former virtue. For Scripture says: “God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good.” And he too was one of the things that were made, before his will had undergone its change for the worse. By the stones mentioned he signifies his manifold wisdom and knowledge. For the high priest, wearing on his breast the oracle of judgment, which held these very stones,

entered the Holy of Holies; and the breast is a kind of storeroom and safeguard for the heart. Everything that follows fits not the visible ruler of Tyre but the invisible one. 14. “For you were made,” he says, “with the cherub, anointed by God [?].” He means: “Together with those holy and [?] powers you were deemed worthy both of creation and of anointing.” Here he calls “anointing” the sanctification that the divine Spirit supplies to the incorporeal and holy powers. “And I set you on the holy mountain of God; you were in the midst of fiery stones.” By the holy mountain of God he means the height of knowledge, and by fiery stones the most holy powers, for they have both preciousness and a luminous nature. The divine Scripture often calls pious human beings holy stones as well: “For holy stones,” it says, “roll upon the earth.” But these are holy, not fiery. Concerning the powers above, let us hear the divine David saying: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire.” None of this fits the visible ruler of the Tyrians, even if some contentious people should argue a thousand times over that the fiery stones are the Jews and that the Tyrians had dealings with them. For the Jews are not fiery stones. And even if someone should call the prophets among them fiery stones, the interpretation still will not stand. For the Tyrians, who lived in impiety, had no fellowship with the prophets. They carried on their trade with the earthbound and base among the Jews, whom no one in his right mind would dare to call fiery stones, since they broke the divine law and made contracts with gentiles contrary to its will. Nor can “I set you on the holy mountain of God” be seen to fit him. For he did not live in Jerusalem, so that we might grant that this was said of Mount Zion. What follows also shows this clearly. 15. “You walked,” he says, “blameless in your days, from the day you were created until iniquities were found in you.” Such was the devil before his fall. But of human beings we hear: “No one is pure from filth, not even if his life on earth lasts a single day.” He, however, being incorporeal, was blameless at the beginning; but when he inclined toward the worse, he set out on the road diametrically opposed. 16. “From the abundance of your traffic you filled your storehouses with lawlessness, and you sinned, and

you were wounded.” He means: “Not content with the wisdom and authority given you, but longing for greater things, you became full of lawlessness and received the wounds of sin.” The prophet Isaiah says this about him: “How has the morning star, who rose at dawn, fallen from heaven? He who sent out to all the nations has been crushed to the earth?” For although he had all as his subjects, he fell from his tyranny through the saving cross. Then he describes his former madness and his overweening arrogance: “You said in your mind, ‘I will ascend to heaven; I will set my throne above the stars of heaven; I will sit on a lofty mountain, on the lofty mountains toward the north; I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High.’” By the mountains toward the north he means the occasions of wickedness. For according to the prophet, “from the north evils will be kindled upon all who live on the earth.” Having thus laid bare his conceit, he also foretells his overthrow: “But now you will go down to Hades, to the foundations of the earth.” The divine Ezekiel is taught by God to say the same thing: “For the overshadowing cherub brought you down from the mountain of God, from the midst of the fiery stones.” At that time it was the cherub, deemed worthy to bear the divine glory, that separated him from the holy powers, which are indeed called fiery. But now those who are worthy of God's visitation through purity of soul, in whose hearts are the ascents of God, as the divine prophet says, have received authority to trample him under their feet. 17. “Your heart was lifted up at your beauty.” He means: “You thought highly of yourself when you saw the good things I had supplied to you.” “Your knowledge was corrupted together with your beauty.” He means: “You were stripped of everything when you abandoned the rank given to you.” “Because of the multitude of your sins I cast you to the earth; I have given you up before kings to be made an example.” He means: “Because you practiced great wickedness, you fell from the rank above and were cast down below, to be laughed at by those who keep the rank given to them and know how to rule well over the passions within them.” 18. “Because of the multitude of your sins and the injustices of your trade, you have profaned your sanctification.” Let those who disagree tell us what sanctification the impious king of Tyre had. They would not be able to show any. But the one now under discussion, when he was one of the holy archangels, shared in every kind of holiness. Yet he profaned that sanctification himself by engaging in wicked trade, and in desiring more he fell even from what he had been given.

He also brought man to suffer this. For man too had been made in the image of God; but he was led astray by the devil's chattering words and wanted to become God, and so he lost even what he had been before, the image of God. “And I will bring forth fire from your midst.” This fits both: the one who worked the wickedness and the king of Tyre in whom it was worked. Both of them gave occasion for the punishment brought on them. What was said to the Jews through the prophet Isaiah is similar: “Behold, all of you kindle a fire and make the flame strong; walk in the light of your fire and in the flame you have kindled.” So here too he says: “I will bring forth fire from your midst; it will devour you.” That is, I will use your own transgressions as the fuel for the punishments against you. “And I will make you ashes on your land before all who see you.” This too fits both. For man fell in his own land and became dust. And the devil, who imagined that he ruled the world, was overthrown by our God and Savior and, like ashes, by the pious [?]

19. “And all who know you among the nations will be gloomy over you.” Those who still remain in your service see that the idols have ceased and that their sanctuaries have been utterly destroyed, so they live in dejection, despondent and continually distressed. “You have become destruction, and you shall be no more forever.” By these words he showed its complete destruction. Having thus finished the lament for Tyre, he passes on to Sidon, [?] since it borders on Tyre, and briefly [foretells] what will befall it as well.

[?] “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against Sidon and prophesy against it, and say: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I am against you, Sidon, and I will be glorified in you; and you shall know that I am the Lord, when I execute judgments in you, and I will be sanctified in you. And I will send death upon you, and blood into your streets, and the wounded shall fall in your midst by swords, in you and all around you, and they shall know that I am the Lord.” He means: since you did not know me when you prospered, O Sidon, I will surround you with many evils of every kind, with famine and with slaughter by enemies, so that through your calamities you may learn my lordship. He also gives the reasons for the destruction. 24. “And there shall no longer be for the house of Israel a thorn of bitterness or a briar of pain from all those around them who treated them with contempt; and they shall know that I am Adonai the Lord.” He means: I will bring these things on Tyre, on the foreigners [?]

and on all who live nearby, so that my people may no longer have you as a model of impiety, nor have enemies continually attacking and constantly tormenting them. Having foretold these grievous things, he now foretells good things for Israel, and so makes the grief of those nations even sharper, since in their hostility they found Israel's prosperity a source of pain. 25–26. “Thus says Adonai the Lord: I will gather the house of Israel from the nations among which they were scattered, and I will be sanctified in them before the peoples and the nations, and they shall dwell on their own land, which I gave to my servant Jacob. And they shall dwell in it in hope, and they shall build houses and plant vineyards and dwell in hope, when I execute judgments on all among those around them who treated them with contempt; and they shall know that I am the Lord their God and the God of their fathers.” The God of the universe does not chastise all sinners in the same way. He treats those who belong to him as a physician treats patients, but the others as a judge treats the accused. That is why the prophet prayed: “Chastise us, Lord, but with judgment and not in wrath.” Blessed David asked for the very same thing: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor chastise me in your anger.” This difference can also be seen in the passage just interpreted. For to the others he has so far promised nothing good. But to Israel he promised recall and restoration to his favor, the building of houses, the tilling of land and the planting of trees, the hope of good things, and the sum of all good things, the knowledge of God. For when these things happen, he says, “they shall know that I am their Lord too, and the God of their fathers.” May we too always have this knowledge, so that we may love him with all our heart, with all our soul, with all our power and with all our strength. Let us not divide our love but devote it wholly to him, so that we breathe him and carry with us an unquenchable remembrance of him, when we sit and when we rise, when we lie down and when we walk on the way. For so we shall continually enjoy his providence and obtain the good things promised, in Christ Jesus our Lord, with whom be glory to the Father, with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

CHAPTER 29. 1–2. “In the tenth year, in the twelfth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against the king of Egypt and prophesy against him, and speak against all Egypt.” Having brought the predictions about Tyre to a close, he turns his discourse to Egypt. 3. “And say: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the dragon that lies in the midst of the rivers, who says: The rivers are mine, and I made them.” Some of the translators said “the river” in the singular, but the Seventy used the plural. Both are true: the Nile is one, but its canals are very many, and the local people call each canal a river. So he exposes Pharaoh's arrogance, showing him boasting of the rivers as though he had made them. He calls him a dragon because of his tyranny and his hostility to God. For divine Scripture also gives this name to the devil: “For on that day,” it says, “God will bring his holy sword, great and strong, upon the dragon, the serpent,” and so on. [4. ?] “[?] your [jaws], and I will make the fish of the river stick to your fins, and I will bring you up out of the midst of your river, and all the fish of your river will stick to your scales. 5. And I will cast you into the desert [?], you and all the fish of the river, and I will quickly throw you down, and all the fish of your river. You shall fall on the face of the plain, and you shall not be gathered up or laid out for burial. I have given you as food to the beasts of the earth and the birds of heaven. And all who live in Egypt shall know that I am the Lord.” The threats are fearful and full of horror. He threatened to hand over to slaughter not only Pharaoh but his subjects as well. For by the fish sticking to him

he meant his subjects. And just as with Tyre he drew the material for his allegory from the sea (since the city is on the coast), so here he takes his figure from the river. By the king's scales and fins he meant his rule and authority, and because of these his subjects necessarily shared in the king's punishment. And by the bridle he plainly hinted at the bucking that came before it. He threatened to send some into a desert land as captives of war, and to hand others over to slaughter and leave them as food for the beasts. Then he adds the reason: “Because you became a staff of reed to the house of Israel. 7. When they took hold of you with their hand, you were crushed; and every hand clapped against them; and when they leaned on you, you were broken, and you broke all their loins.” Tyre and the foreigners we discussed above were threatened with calamities because they rejoiced over what had befallen Israel. Egypt is not blamed for this but for quite the opposite. It led the people to trust in its help and so stripped them of God's providence, yet gave them no benefit by its own aid. He indicated this by the reed staff, broken through weakness and crushed. So too in Isaiah, Sennacherib described the help of the Egyptians this way: “For you trust,” he says, “in the staff of reed, the broken one, in Egypt; if a man leans on it, it will pierce his hand. So is the king of Egypt and all who trust in him.” He said the same here: “They took hold of you with their hand, you were crushed, and every hand clapped against them.” He means: they became a laughingstock and an object of glee to their enemies when you, like a reed staff, were crushed and defeated. [?] and you promise to help others, you will learn by experience that you cannot defend even your own land when I bring the punishment upon you; and my people will recognize my power. Then, recalling once more their boastful words (“For you said,” he says, “The rivers are mine, and I made them”), he threatens Egypt with desolation. Not all of it, however, but only from Magdol and Syene to the borders of the Ethiopians. And even for these cities the desolation is not permanent, but for a time
[?] … A: “man”, placed after “from you”. A: “the land of Egypt destruction and desert”. For “but”, B has “for”. B: “him”.

10–12. “Therefore, behold, I am against you and against all your rivers, and I will give the land of Egypt over to desolation, sword and destruction, from Magdol and Syene to the borders of the Ethiopians. No foot of man,” he says, “shall pass through it, and no foot of beast shall pass over it, and it shall not be inhabited for forty years. And I will give its land over to destruction in the midst of a desolated land, and its cities shall vanish in the midst of desolated cities for forty years; and I will scatter Egypt among the nations and winnow them in the countries.” God's loving-kindness is beyond words. He brings punishments in due measure and weight, and then heals what he has struck. For his is the voice that says: “I will kill and I will make alive; I will strike, and I will heal.” So here too he threatens the Egyptians with captivity, dispersion and desolation, but he limits the desolation to a short time. For forty years, he says, Egypt will be untrodden, and not all of it, but only from Magdol and Syene to the borders of the Ethiopians; and at once he promises their return. 13–14. “For after forty years,” he says, “I will gather the Egyptians from the nations among which they were scattered. And I will turn back the captivity of the Egyptians and settle them in the land of Pathros, the land from which they were taken.” Having thus promised release from captivity, he foretells how small that kingdom would later be. 15. “And it will be,” he says, “a lowly kingdom, lower than all kingdoms; it will be the lowliest, so that it is never again exalted over the nations; and I will make them few, so that they are no longer numerous among the nations.” The events confirm the truth of the prophecy. The kingdom of the Egyptians was overthrown by Nebuchadnezzar. It flourished again under Cyrus the Persian but did not recover its former power. Much later, Cambyses son of Cyrus overthrew it again, made it subject and forced it to pay tribute. Later still it received Macedonian kings, and the Egyptian kings ceased altogether. 16. “And they shall no longer be for the house of Israel a hope that brings their iniquity to mind when they followed after them; and they shall know that I am the Lord.” He means: I will reduce their kingdom so far that my people will no longer trust in their help or take occasions for impiety from them, but will seek my providence; for they will learn my lordship.

17–18. “And in the twenty-seventh year, on the first day of the first month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made his army labor at a great labor against Tyre. Every head was made bald and every shoulder rubbed bare, and neither he nor his army received any wages for Tyre, for the labor with which he labored against it.” Those earlier prophecies he spoke in the tenth year of Jehoiachin's captivity, or the twelfth, as the Hebrew and the Syriac have it. These he spoke in the twenty-seventh year, after the capture of Tyre and the long siege. Because of that siege, he says, every head became bald and every shoulder rubbed bare. Living in the open air usually does such things, since the heat often flays the bare parts of the body that are exposed to it. He promises to give Nebuchadnezzar Egypt as wages for the [?] he had suffered in the siege of Tyre. This was not because Nebuchadnezzar had done this deliberately, in service to the divine will, for he marched against all these nations on his own impulse. Rather, God shows by this that nothing will happen without his consent. “For two sparrows,” it says, “are sold for a penny, and not one of them will fall without your Father in heaven.” Nothing that happens escapes his notice. Some things he directs himself, and others he permits to happen. Sometimes he gives way to human free will, and sometimes he allows those who deserve it to be punished by others. Wishing, then, to show that Nebuchadnezzar received this power by his permission, he promises to give him the enslavement of the Egyptians as wages for the siege of Tyre. 19–20. “Thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he will carry off its multitude, plunder its spoils and seize its booty, and that will be the wages for his army. In return for the service he performed against Tyre I have given him the land of Egypt, because of what he did.” He said the same things again, confirming the prediction by repeating it. “Thus says Adonai the Lord: 21. On that day a horn will spring up for all the house of Israel, and to you I will give an open mouth in their midst, and they shall know that I am the Lord.” Divine Scripture sometimes uses “horn” for piety, sometimes for power, sometimes for kingship. The phrase “a horn will spring up” is a metaphor taken from calves, which are weak

before their horns grow out, but gain great strength once the horns have grown. So, he says, when Egypt is overthrown my people will flourish and acquire piety, since they will no longer have wickedness for a teacher. And having learned my lordship, they will lend their ears to the words of the prophets. He showed this by saying: “And to you I will give an open mouth in their midst.” For through Ezekiel he meant the whole choir of the prophets.

CHAPTER 30. 1–3. “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy and say: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Wail: Alas, alas for the day! For the day of the Lord is near, and is drawing near [?]” He uses everything said here to frighten them, urging them to lament and mourn. By “day” he means the time of punishment. By “cloud” he means the darkness that the calamity brings on souls. And by “time of the nations” he means the punishment brought on the nations. He means: not only will my people fall into these evils, but the nations too will pay the penalty for their impiety. 4–5. “And a sword will come upon the Egyptians, and there will be turmoil in Ethiopia, and the wounded will fall in Egypt, and its multitude will be taken, and its foundations will collapse. And Persians [?], Cretans, Libyans, Ethiopians, Lydians, all Arabia and all the mixed peoples, and some of the sons of my covenant, will fall by the sword in it, together with it.” What will befall Egypt will throw Ethiopia into turmoil too, for as a neighbor it will be anxious that it may suffer the same. Then he lists the allies of the Egyptians who will perish along with them: Cretans, Libyans, Ethiopians, Lydians and Arabs. Greek histories also tell of the alliance between the Lydians and the Egyptians. By Persians he does not mean men who came from Persia to help them. How could they have had Persians as allies when Assyrians and Chaldeans were at war with them [?]? He means those who had long ago emigrated from there and settled in Egypt. They say that this is also why the Egyptian Babylon has the same name as the Persian one, because Persians lived there. By “sons of the covenant” he means the Jews who went down to Egypt after the siege of Jerusalem, taking the prophet Jeremiah with them. He threatens them with punishment too, because they left Judea against his will and went to

Egypt. These things were also spoken through the prophet Jeremiah: “For all the remnant of Judah who are living in the land of Egypt shall know whose word will stand, mine or theirs. And this shall be the sign to you, says the Lord: Behold, I give Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hands of those who seek his life, just as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hands of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, his enemy, who sought his life.” So the predictions of the divine prophets agree with one another, for they are the words of one Spirit. Having thus foretold once more the desolation of Egypt and its limits, and having called the Assyrian king “fire,” he adds: 9. “On that day angels will go out from my presence in Seim, hastening to destroy Ethiopia, the hope; and there will be turmoil among them on the day of Egypt, for behold, it is coming.” He called Ethiopia “hope” because the Egyptians trusted in the Ethiopians' help. “Seim” means “in strength” in Greek. He means: while the Egyptians endure these things, the Ethiopians, their allies, will be thrown into turmoil. This will be not only because of the evils that have come upon the Egyptians, but also because of the calamities that will overtake the Ethiopians themselves through angels whom I send and who hasten to carry out what they have been commanded. 10–12. “Thus says Adonai the Lord: I will destroy the multitude of the Egyptians by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, he and his people with him, pestilences sent from the nations to destroy the land; and they will empty all their swords upon Egypt, and the land will be filled with the wounded. And I will make their rivers desolate, and I will sell the land into the hands of wicked men, and I will destroy the land and all that fills it by the hands of foreigners. I the Lord have spoken.” He means: I will hand Egypt over to the Babylonians, the cruelest of all nations, so that their whole land is filled with slaughter and the rivers are emptied of those who live along them. He wrote “I will sell the land into the hands of wicked men” in place of “I will hand over.” This too fits what was said earlier, for he said he would give Nebuchadnezzar the enslavement of Egypt as wages for the toil he endured in the siege of Tyre. Then he foretells that their abominations, that is, their idols, which are full of abomination, will be destroyed by the enemy. 13. “And the rulers of Memphis will cease.” At that time those entrusted with the reins of Egypt

[?] And fear will fall on all the Egyptians, as Tanis is set on fire, Diospolis suffers utter destruction, and Sais, the most powerful of their cities, meets the gravest calamities. In short, the enemy will spread over all Egypt like fire, so that even Syene, which lies farthest inland, will hear the uproar they make. He also made the suddenness of the attack clear enough when he said, “There will be wars in Memphis in a single day”; for the battle will arrive together with the news. The words “In Diospolis there will be a breach, and waters will be poured out” hint at the destruction of the walls and the entry of the enemy, who flow in like water and spread through all its streets and houses. To this he added: 17. That the young men of Heliopolis and Bubastis will fall by the sword. Clearly these too took great pride in themselves as champions and mighty men. But “the women too,” he says, “will go into captivity.” Then he adds: 18. That in Tahpanhes the day will grow dark. By this he means the darkness that comes with calamities. He signified the same thing again when he said, “And a cloud will cover her.” For those who fall into misfortune do not see the light as others do; they think the day gloomier than any darkness. Then he showed the purpose of what was happening. 19. And I will execute judgments in Egypt, and the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord. I will allow all this to happen, he says, so that the Egyptians too may learn not to be proud of themselves, but to acknowledge my sovereignty. 20. And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the first month, on the seventh of the month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying. The same pattern is found in the prophet Jeremiah. He too sets down the dates out of order: he first places the events under Zedekiah, who was the last to reign, and then goes back to relate those under Jehoiakim, who held the kingship before him. The reason is that they are not simply writing history but recording prophecies delivered at particular times. Here he had good reason, indeed every reason, to mention this date. Having threatened Egypt with so great a cloud of calamities in the twenty-seventh year, he teaches us that the punishment is just. For in the eleventh year, he says, the Lord said to me: 21. Son of man, I have broken the arms of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and behold, he was not bound up so that he might be healed, nor was a poultice put on him, nor was he bandaged

so as to grow strong and take hold of the sword. I brought a moderate punishment on him, he says, and he would not use the remedies of repentance in order to regain his former power. 22–24. Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and I will break his arms, the strong and outstretched ones as well as the broken ones, and I will knock the sword out of his hand. And I will scatter Egypt among the nations and winnow them through the countries. And I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon. Since he refused to be brought to his senses by moderate chastisement, I will subject him to the heaviest punishments and strip him of all his strength, so that he cannot even use the weapons of war; but I will fill the Babylonian with all strength and power. In the case of both the Egyptian and the Babylonian, he used the arms to signify power, since it is with the arms that the work of war is done. “And I will put my sword,” he says, “into his hand, and he will bring it against Egypt, and he will take her plunder and seize her spoils.” I, he says, will put the power to punish into his hands, so that he may do to Egypt everything that was foretold. He has added these words again, confirming the earlier ones by repeating them. Since they are clear and already evident from what has been explained, I have left them without comment. [Chapter 31] 1, 2. And it came to pass in the tenth year, in the third month, on the first of the month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, say to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his multitude: Whom have you likened yourself to in your loftiness? Since Pharaoh would not make proper use of God's patience, but persisted in his conceit and arrogance, God addresses him with a question. Tell me, he says, O king of Egypt, whom do you compare yourself to? Which of the kings do you think you resemble, that you hold yourself so high? Then he adds: 3. Behold, Assyria was a cypress in Lebanon, beautiful in its shoots, tall in its size, and dense in its shade, and its top reached into the midst of the clouds. He is again speaking figuratively. He says that the king of the Assyrians resembled the cypress that grows in Lebanon in the greatness of its height, in the dense and spreading multitude of his subjects, and in the splendor of his governors and generals, whom he called “shoots.” He wrote “its top reached into the midst of the clouds” not only as a hyperbole in keeping with ordinary speech (many people say, “So-and-so has gone up to the clouds”), but also

to expose the arrogance of the king's thoughts. For his are the words: “I will go up above the clouds; I will set my throne above the stars of heaven.” This can be learned from every part of divine Scripture. Sennacherib cried out, “The Lord will not deliver Jerusalem out of my hand”; and Nebuchadnezzar made a golden image and ordered all his subjects, rulers and ruled alike, to worship it. Here too, then, the prophet has revealed the king's proud mind through riddles. To this he adds: 4. Water nourished him, the deep made him tall; it led its rivers around his plants, and sent out its channels to all the trees of the field. By water and the deep he meant the countless nations he had enslaved. By bringing tribute and taxes to his army, like irrigation, they nourished it as one nourishes plants, and they equipped its channels, that is, its military divisions, to be sent out to all the trees of the field. This means against those not yet subdued or enslaved, so that they too might become his subjects. 5. Therefore his size was exalted above all the trees of the field, and from there his branches spread wide, and his shoots [?] from abundant water as he stretched out. This, he says, became the cause of both his boasting and his pride: receiving irrigation from countless nations, he grew together with his shoots. 6. In his shoots, he says, all the birds of heaven made their nests. By this he indicated the more rational of men, who are winged, as it were. “And under his branches all the beasts of the field gave birth.” By these he signified the barbarian nations, who are beastlike and groveling in soul. He explained this himself when he said, “In his shadow dwelt a multitude of nations.” What he said above piecemeal and figuratively, he has added here plainly and clearly. By his shadow, his shoots and his branches he meant not only his governors and generals but also the satraps who ruled the nations, whom the subject peoples continually served. Nebuchadnezzar himself saw these things in a dream, and blessed Daniel interpreted the [vision] of the tree.

7. And there was beauty in his height, he says, because of the multitude of his branches. Blessed Daniel too teaches us about this multitude. [Notes:] A: “nourished.” “its”: Hebrew “flowing” [?]. “the” supplied [?]. “the”: [?] B. “from” supplied. A: “beautiful,” omitting “in.” “multitude”: A “length.”

when he says that Darius, who succeeded to Belshazzar's kingdom, had a hundred and twenty satraps. Then he explains the cause of this multitude: “For its roots were in much water.” Having stretched out his roots everywhere, he says, and received abundant irrigation, he nourished these branches. And continuing the figure, he says: 8. Cypresses did not surpass him in the paradise of God. None of those who reigned in the world at that time, he says, was more illustrious than he. Here he called the world “paradise,” since for now he is saying everything figuratively. “And pines,” he says, “were not like his branches, and firs were not like his shoots.” Not only was he himself more illustrious than the other kings, he says, but his branches and shoots too far surpassed the kings of the other nations in height and density. By pines and firs he figuratively meant the kings of lesser nations, over whom he set the satraps, who forced them to obey. He says, then, that he became greater than the greatest kings, while over the lesser ones not only he but also his officials became more powerful and more illustrious. Then he adds: “No tree in the paradise of God was like him in his beauty, 9. because of the multitude of his branches.” By beauty he means what is seen, what pertains to the body: the purple robe, crowns, jeweled thrones, bodyguards, shield-bearers, and everything else that usually makes kings splendid to the eye. He says, then, that none of those who reigned on earth at that time equaled him. And he adds that all of them envied him: “For all the trees of delight in the paradise of God envied him,” he says. Then he lays bare the conceit of his soul: 10, 11. Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Because he grew great in size and set his top in the midst of the clouds, and his heart was lifted up in his height, I saw it when he was exalted. And I handed him over into the hands of the ruler of nations, and he brought about his destruction in keeping with his impiety. Since, he says, he was not content with dominion over men but turned his arrogance against me as well, “I handed him over,” he says, “into the hands of the ruler of nations.” He means Cyrus, who was a Mede on his mother's side and a Persian on his father's

and so sprang from two nations. He destroyed the kingdom of the Assyrians and Babylonians. “And he brought about his destruction,” he says, “in keeping with his impiety”: he suffered what his lawless deeds deserved. In terms of the history, then, these things befell Nebuchadnezzar, who was sick with such cruelty and arrogance, together with impiety. But anyone who looks closely will find that these words also point to the devil, the common scourge of mankind, God's foe and enemy. He was created fair and good, equal to the ruling powers and more illustrious than the lesser ones (for by the paradise of delight and the trees in it, according to the laws of allegory, he meant the incorporeal natures). Yet he raged against the one who made him and gave him such beauty and power, and, plotting tyranny and dreaming that he would be God, he fell. Blessed Paul also hints at this when he says, “Not a recent convert, lest he be puffed up and fall into the condemnation of the devil.” For one who does not know how to use honor properly will suffer the same as the devil, who made the honor given him an occasion for arrogance and conceit. It is he, the prophet says, who “will be handed over to the ruler of nations.” And who is this ruler of the nations, if not the only-begotten Word of God, Christ the Master? To him the prophet says, “Who will not fear you, O King of the nations?” And blessed Jacob says: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes for whom it is reserved, and he is the expectation of the nations.” Isaiah too proclaims this: “For there shall be,” he says, “the root of Jesse, he who rises to rule the nations; in him the nations will hope.” And the Father says to him: “I have given you as a covenant to the race, as a light to the nations, that you may be salvation to the end of the earth.” And the same prophet says to him again: “Egypt has toiled, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians, and the Sabaeans, men of stature, will come over to you and be your slaves; they will follow behind you bound in fetters, and they will pray to you, because God is in you, and there is no God besides you,” and so on. And he himself says through blessed David: “A people whom I did not know served me.” Countless other testimonies teaching the same thing can be found. It is to him, then, that the prophet says the common scourge and enemy was handed over, and by him that his destruction came about in keeping with his impiety. To this he adds: And I cast him out, 12. and foreign pestilences from the nations destroyed him utterly, and threw him down on the mountains. When the Lord had conquered him and stripped him of his power and tyranny, those from the nations who were once pestilences and strangers to God, having believed the divine preaching, (1 Tim. 3:6)

destroyed him utterly, tore up his tyranny by the roots, and threw him down on the mountains. Where he once had his sacred precincts and altars, they set up the monuments of the philosophic life. “And in all the ravines his branches fell, and his trunks were broken in every plain of the earth.” By his branches and trunks he meant the idol temples of every kind, which owed their founding to him. Through those who were once pestilences but afterwards became faithful nations, these were made to vanish completely from the mountains and the plains. “And all the peoples of the earth came down from his shelter and leveled him to the ground.” For once they recognized his deceit, they not only fled his rule but brought him down to the very ground, fulfilling the Lord's command that says, “Behold, I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy.” 13. Upon his fall all the birds of heaven rested, and all the beasts of the field were upon his trunks. Whoever is winged, he says, and keeps the eye of his mind fixed on heaven rejoices to see his overthrow and the stripping bare of impiety. And those who were once beastlike will rush against his branches and tear down the precincts of the idols with their own hands; for these are what he called trunks. 14. So that none of the trees by the water may be exalted in their size, or set their top in the midst of the clouds, and that none who drink water may stand up to him in their height. His ruin, he says, and the overthrow of his power will benefit others and give them reason for caution. Seeing what befell him, they will not dare to think more highly of themselves than they deserve, nor try to seize a rule that in no way belongs to them, using the honor I have supplied them, like irrigation, as provision for tyranny. “For all were given over to death.” Not only the devil himself, but also the demons who shared his tyranny suffered utter destruction. But it is time to return to the history again. What has been said is enough to show that these words were spoken not only about Nebuchadnezzar but also about the one who worked in him and taught him his own arrogance. He says, then, that Nebuchadnezzar himself and those with him will be handed over to death, suffering the same as other men. “Into the land of the deep,” he says, “in the midst of the sons of men who go down to the pit.” To this he adds:

15. Thus says Adonai the Lord: On the day he was brought down to Hades, the deep mourned for him; it covered and stopped its rivers and held back the abundance of water. By the deep he meant the subject nations, who fought alongside him and mourned, not for his slaughter, but for their own defeat and destruction. That it was not him they mourned he showed clearly enough by saying, “It held back the abundance of water,” meaning, “It will no longer consent to send you tribute.” “Lebanon grew dark over him; all the trees of the field fainted over him.” By Lebanon he means not the mountain but the density of the kingdom, and by the trees of the field the officials under him who ranked below the governors and were planted, as it were, in a plain. He means the satraps who were subordinate to the governors and generals, while those planted in Lebanon are the greater officials. Just as we do not take Lebanon here to mean Lebanon, or the plain to mean a plain, or the trees to mean trees, so we do not take the paradise of delight called God's paradise literally either. In Nebuchadnezzar's case it means the kingdoms of the world; in the devil's case, the intelligible and incorporeal powers. 16. At the sound of his fall, he says, the nations were shaken, when they brought him down to Hades with those who go down into the pit. This happened in both cases. When the king of Babylon was killed, the news ran everywhere and threw the subject nations into turmoil. And when the devil was overthrown, the nations were shaken and moved from their former deception to the truth of the saving doctrines; for blessed Paul too calls such a change a shaking. “And in the lowest part of the earth all the trees of delight comforted him, the choice and finest of Lebanon, all that drink water. 17. For they too were brought down with him to Hades, with those slain by the sword.” By the lowest part of the earth, the pit and the trench, he means death in Nebuchadnezzar's case and utter humiliation in the devil's. He says, then, that those who shared power with each of them will share their destruction; for when a kingdom is overthrown, the governments subject to it must also undergo change. The words “They will comfort him” are drawn from our own experience, since shared calamity somehow naturally brings the disheartened a measure of consolation. Not only, he says, will the rulers he appointed be overthrown,
[Notes:] A: “I stopped.” A: “and I held back.” B: “and it surrounded.” [?] “trees” [?]. A [?]. A: “below.” “and the” added.

but also “his seed, those who dwelt under his shelter, perished in the midst of their life.” Belshazzar, Nebuchadnezzar's seed and son, was not allowed to reach old age because of his great impiety; he was given over to slaughter when the span allotted to men was only half spent. In the devil's case, we should understand the seed as the teaching of impiety that he sowed. It too will be utterly wiped out, along with those who are eager to champion it. Then he turns to address him:

18. Whom did you resemble in power, in glory and in greatness among the trees of delight? Go down, and be brought down with the trees of delight into the depth of the earth. Since you would not be like the trees planted alongside you, he says, but wanted to be like the one who planted them, I command you to be cast down with these trees, which had the same ambitions as you, and to be thrown into the depth of the earth. This too fits both of them. To this he adds: “In the midst of the uncircumcised you will lie with those slain by the sword.” He speaks of uncircumcision not of the body but of the heart. For not only the New Testament but also the Old knows of circumcision of the heart, and God says this through the prophet: “For all the nations are uncircumcised in the flesh, but the house of Israel are uncircumcised in their heart.” Since, then, you refused to circumcise your arrogance, and the excess of arrogance remained in you, you will suffer the same as those who did such things. Then he completes the thought: “So it is with Pharaoh and all the multitude of his strength, says Adonai the Lord.” Having said above, “Whom have you likened yourself to in your loftiness?” and having related the story of the Assyrian, that is, the Babylonian, he added: “So it is with Pharaoh and all the multitude of his strength.” For if that king, he says, who was far greater and more illustrious than you, will suffer these things, you too should expect the same punishment, since you share the same impiety.

CHAPTER 32. 1, 2. And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, on the first of the month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, take up a lament over the king of Egypt, and say to him: You were likened to a lion of the nations, and you were like the dragon in the sea; you butted with your rivers, stirred up the water with your feet, and trampled your rivers. Here again he denounces the king's arrogance and conceit, and says that he imitated the pride of the dragon in the sea. We have been taught that this is the devil, who long ago [?] the nations bitterly [?] [Notes:] “of delight”: missing in A. “the”: [?] prefixes “the.” “trees”: B prefixes “the.” AB: “but to the very.” [?] A adds “your.” “uncircumcised”: B places it after “heart.” [?] A: “twelfth”; so it had to be emended from A [?]. “you butted with your rivers”: Hebrew “you burst forth from your rivers.” “with”: A “the”; B “in the.” “water”: A prefixes “the.” “the”: missing in B.

…and who has lived with a briny cast of mind. Isaiah too says that God will bring his holy sword upon the dragon in the sea. And he says that he attempted to be likened even to a lion. But we have learned that the lion who reigns over the nations is the Lord: "For having lain down," it says, "he rested like a lion and like a lion's cub; who will rouse him?" So he says: Because you tried to be likened to the lion of the nations, just like the dragon in the sea, and took up an arrogant mind against the God of all, trusting in the river and its canals, as if you needed neither clouds nor rain nor providence and care from above, but used your feet, stirring up the water and channeling it for irrigation — for this reason, he says, "I will cast my nets over you in an assembly of many peoples, and I will haul you up with my hook." Fittingly and very aptly he mentioned a hook and nets in connection with the river. And he explained these too by saying, "In an assembly of many peoples." For as with a net, the army of the enemies, and as with a hook, my will, I will catch you and hunt you down like a fish. 4–6. "And I will stretch you out," he says, "on the land, and the plains will be filled with you, and I will make all the birds of heaven settle upon you, and I will fill all the beasts of the whole earth with you. And I will give your flesh to the mountains, and fill the plains with your blood. And the land will be watered with your discharges from the mountains, and I will fill the ravines with you." When, he says, you are caught and slain by the enemies, you will lie unburied and fill the bellies of the beasts and of the birds; and the streams of blood and the fluids of decay — for these are what he called "discharges" — will fill both the plains and the mountains. 7–8. "And when you are extinguished I will cover the heaven and darken its stars; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not show its light. All the lights of heaven I will darken over you, and I will put darkness upon your land, says Adonai the Lord." He does not say that these things happen in nature, but in the state of mind of those in distress; for people in calamity think the day darker than night. And to teach this he said, "And I will put darkness upon your land" — not upon the whole earth. But if anyone says that darkness really did come upon Egypt at the time of the war, God showing that it was he himself who used the Babylonians to punish the Egyptians, he will not stray from the pious sense.

9–10. "And I will provoke the heart of many peoples when I lead your captivity among the nations, into a land you did not know. And many nations will be gloomy over you, and their kings will be utterly astonished when I draw my sword before their face, awaiting their own fall from the day of your fall." When your captivity takes place, he says, some, remembering your former insolence, will show themselves pitiless toward you; others will lament and grieve, inferring from what has befallen you the evils that will overtake them. Then he teaches that the army of the Babylonians will come, with certain champions fighting in the front ranks — for these are the ones he called "giants." And since they are crueler than all the nations, they will exact from you, O Egypt, he says, the penalty for your arrogance [?] — for this is what he called "insolence," since the boaster is insolent. He says that they will destroy their strength, lead the people away captive and plunder the cattle, and that for a long time the stream of the river will remain unmuddied, with neither beast nor man stirring it, because of the desolation resulting from the captivity; and that the canals, no longer being diverted this way and that, will flow like oil, he says, that is, quietly and gently, with nothing obstructing them. These things, he says, will happen when desolation has overtaken the land and its inhabitants have been led away as prisoners of war. "And they will know," he says, "that I am the Lord." For through the experience of evils they will be taught their own worthlessness and will recognize my lordship. Then he says that also 16. "The daughters of the nations" — he means the cities and the villages — "will lament him; over Egypt and over all its strength they will lament him, says Adonai the Lord." Not only the nation of the Egyptians, he says, but also the cities of the other nations will lament their king, reckoning up their former prosperity and seeing the sudden reversal. 17–18. "And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the first month, on the fifteenth of the month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, lament over the strength of Egypt, and, turning him aside, drag him down." By the word, he says, of

prophecy turn him aside from his position, sweep him off the royal throne and bring him down. "And the nations will bring down her daughters as corpses into the depth of the earth, to those who go down into the pit." By "daughters" he again means the cities and the villages, which he says will be handed over to death; for he called death "the pit," taking the name from the grave.

19. "Go down from the comely waters, and lie down with the uncircumcised." You who once, he says, luxuriated in the waters of the river and gained your comeliness from the fruits that grow by them, but did not circumcise the impiety of your heart, share the slaughter with those like you. Then, having said the same things again, he added: 21. "And the giants in the depth of the pit will say to you: Be! For whom are you better than? Go down, lie down with the uncircumcised in the midst of those wounded by the sword." Blessed Isaiah too says this about the Babylonian: "And the rulers from of old will say to you: You too have been taken, just as we were; you have been counted among us. Your glory has gone down to Hades, and your great gladness; beneath you they will spread rot, and the worm will be your covering." And here too he says: Those who became famous for their power and died long ago will say to you — for these are the ones he called giants — "Be," that is, a corpse like us; for whom are you better than, that you try to be [?]? Go down, then, receive the end of life, and receive the same slaughter as those who dared the same things as you. Then he names those who were distinguished for their power. 22–23. "There is Assur and all his assembly; all the wounded were placed there. And their burial is in the depth of the pit, and his assembly was around his tomb." Who, he says, was ever so much talked of as the king of the Assyrians? And yet even he, he says, met the end of life, and his whole army shared in his death. "All the wounded who have fallen by the sword, who set their graves in the thighs of the pit." This is what he called the shape of the tombs; for tombs are oblong and resemble thighs. "And an assembly was around his burial place, all the wounded who fell by the sword." For they too, like their king, met slaughter, and were handed over to slaughter beside his monument. And these things, he says, were suffered by men "who had seen their terror upon the land of life." Yet all those who struck terror and fear will receive, he says, their disgrace along with those brought down into the pit; for, stripped of that glory, they will end their lives in shame, meeting slaughter just as those they slaughtered did. Then he speaks of the nation of

"…its multitude, and all the wounded who fell by the sword, and who went down uncircumcised into the depth of the earth." In wars it was the custom for tombs to be made nation by nation; for their countrymen gathered their own dead and committed them to a single burial. This, then, is what he has shown here that the nation of Elam did; and this nation borders on the Assyrians. He teaches too that they met death uncircumcised, never having been freed from impiety. Then, having said again that those who were once fearsome to all received their own torment and died just like the others, he added: 25. "Around each one is his burial, all uncircumcised, wounded by the sword." He means the other nations that met this slaughter. 26. "There Meshech and Tubal were placed." The Iberians are called Tubal, and the Cappadocians Meshech. Having again said the same things he had said about the Elamites, he added: 27. "And they laid their swords under their heads." For weapons are useless once those who used them have been slain. He also states the cause of the slaughter: "And their iniquities were upon their bones." They paid, he says, the penalty for impiety. Then he also indicates the form their impiety took: "For they terrified giants in their lifetime, and became a terror to the mighty in the land of the living." For they practiced such cruelty and boldness, he says, as to strike fear not only into [?], but also into those who pride themselves on strength and power. Therefore, he says, you too have met the same slaughter as those you slew. The other nations too endured these things. 29. "For there is Edom, and its kings, and all its rulers, who gave their strength to wounds of the sword." That is, those who used their strength for bloodshed. And having shown that these too were slain in the same way, in the same way

30. "There are the rulers of the north, all of them, all the generals of Assur, who were brought down with the wounded, with their terror." "For his spirit will go forth, and he will return to his dust," as the divine David says; "on that day all his thoughts will perish." This is what God said here too: "Who were brought down with the wounded, with their terror"; for with death the [?] of their power too [?] … "of their strength," that is, they are naked and bereft of

strength. "In shame they lay down uncircumcised." For nothing fills a person with shame so much as the accusation of an evil conscience. Again he called "uncircumcised" those who do not cut away the superfluities of sin. Then, having said that they received their torment with those who go down into the pit — that is, their punishment — he added: 31–32. "King Pharaoh will see them and be comforted over all their strength; wounded by the sword are Pharaoh and all his host, says Adonai the Lord. For he put his terror upon the land of life, and he will lie down in the midst of the uncircumcised wounded by the sword, Pharaoh and all his multitude, says Adonai the Lord." For looking at those who had become greater and far more powerful, he says, Pharaoh will receive some consolation, and his subjects with him. Yet he will pay the penalty for his impiety, because, having laid great fear upon his subjects, he himself did not accept my law but left his soul uncircumcised. For this reason he too, and those who shared his mind, will meet the same slaughter as those who lived as he did. Having learned these things, then, and come to know through the divine oracles what penalties are paid by those whose soul is uncircumcised, let us receive, I beg you, the circumcision of the all-holy Spirit, not made with hands, of which blessed Paul says: "And circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; its praise is not from men but from God." And we have been taught that circumcision of the heart is the removal of sin and the cutting out of the evil impulses of the mind. To teach this the Master said: "If your right eye causes you to stumble, cut it out and throw it away from you." And he said the same about the hand and the foot, and added: "It is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body be thrown into Gehenna." Here he called the activities of the members "members"; these we ought to circumcise and cut out, cleansing the rational part and dedicating and consecrating it wholly to the divine laws. For in this way we shall become strangers to fellowship with the adversary, and shall receive as our indweller our Master and Benefactor, to whom glory is fitting to the ages of ages. Amen.

CHAPTER 33. 1–2. "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, speak to the sons of your people." When God is gracious, he calls the people his own; but when he turns away from them because of their transgressions, he no longer uses the name that expresses kinship. This

also happened in the case of the great Moses. For before the transgression he said to Pharaoh, "Send out my people, that they may serve me"; but after the worship of the calf he says to Moses: "Hurry, go down from here quickly; your people have acted lawlessly." So here too he calls the people not his own, but the prophet's people. "And you shall say to them: A land — if I bring a sword upon it, and the people of the land take one man from among them and set him as a watchman for themselves, 3–5 and he sees the sword coming upon the land and blows the trumpet and warns the people, and the one who hears hears the sound of the trumpet and does not take heed, and the sword comes and overtakes him, his blood shall be upon his own head. Because he heard the sound of the trumpet and did not take heed, his blood shall be upon him." By "sword" he means war, and by "watchman" the lookout. The passage teaches us that he himself grants people peace out of his goodness, but permits war to happen because of the transgressions of people who bring troubles upon themselves.
