If, then, he says, when war is waged against a city, those under attack post a lookout on some [?] place, and he, seeing the army advancing, sounds the alarm with the trumpet, and does not despise or neglect those who appointed him to this task, he himself, he says, will be guiltless, having fulfilled the work entrusted to him; but the one who would not take heed and see to his own safety will become the cause of his own slaughter and captivity. [?] he says: "His blood shall be upon him"; let him lay the blame for the slaughter on himself, he says. "But this one, because he took heed, has saved his life." But if, he says, he takes heed, he will become the cause of his own safety. 6. "And if the watchman sees the sword coming and does not blow the trumpet, and

does not warn the people, and the people do not take heed, and the sword comes and takes a life from among them, that one has been taken because of its own iniquity, but its blood I will require at the watchman's hand." But if, he says, the appointed lookout neglects to warn the people of the enemy's approach, those who perish will pay the penalty for their own negligence, but the watchman himself will be held to account for the betrayal he committed. He said this to make the prophet more zealous in the ministry of the word. Therefore he adds: 7. "And you, son of man, I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel, and you shall hear a word from my mouth and warn them from me." What the lookout usually does in wartime, he says, you too, prophet, ought to do, and pass on with all eagerness what I say. 8. "When I say to the sinner, Sinner, you shall surely die, and you do not warn the sinner — the ungodly man — to take heed, to turn him from his way so that he may live, that lawless man shall die in his lawlessness, but his blood I will require at your hand." If, he says, I decree death for someone, and you do not make known to him the sentence passed against him, so that he might annul the sentence through repentance, he will meet an end of life that he deserves, but I will hold you to account for his destruction. But if, he says, you make all my words plain to the one who lives lawlessly, and he despises your words and persists in his own wickedness, he will suffer just punishment, while you will free yourself from accountability. 10. "And you, son of man, say to the house of Israel: This is what you have said: Our errors and our iniquities are upon us, and we are wasting away in them; how then shall we live?" While I, he says, do everything for the salvation of Israel and do not want them to despair, they use the language of despair and think salvation through repentance impossible, saying that they bear a very heavy burden of sins and still today persist in error and transgression; and they consider it impossible for people in such a state to obtain salvation through repentance. 11. "Say to them, then: As I live, says Adonai the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he turn from his way and live." Who could marvel worthily at the Master's goodness? Though treated with ingratitude and great thanklessness, he cares for the ungrateful and makes every provision for them,

wishing to see them change. Therefore he adds a fatherly exhortation full of affection: "Turn, turn back from your evil way; why will you die, house of Israel?" The doubling is a feature of the Hebrew language, and it shows the genuineness of the turning. 12. "And you, son of man, say to the sons of your people: The righteousness of the righteous will not deliver him on the day he goes astray, and the lawlessness of the lawless will not kill him on the day he turns from his lawlessness." Wishing to convince them that he accepts the sinner's repentance, he demonstrates it from the opposite case. For just as, he says, if someone who has lived in virtue were to abandon that road and choose the road of vice, he must necessarily meet an end worthy of that road, so if someone brought up in lawlessness should wish to return to the road of virtue, he will be entirely freed from the punishment appointed for the lawless. 13–15. "When I say to the righteous man, You shall surely live, and he trusts in his righteousness and commits lawlessness, none of his righteous deeds shall be remembered; in the injustice he has committed, in it he shall die. And when I say to the ungodly man, You shall surely be put to death, and he turns from his lawlessness and does justice and righteousness, and returns a debtor's pledge, and pays back what he has seized — the lawless man — and walks in the ordinances of life so as to do no wrong, he shall surely live and shall not die." Neither, he says, will my promise of good things benefit the righteous man unless he persists in doing good; rather, he will pay the penalty his life deserves. Nor will the sentence of punishment harm the sinner who wishes to use the remedies of repentance, ridding himself of all injustice, treating his neighbor with kindness, and in short choosing to keep what I have commanded; for by his change he will annul the sentence and enjoy life. And the loveliest thing of all: 16. "All his sins," he says, "which he has committed shall not be remembered against him, because he has done justice and righteousness; in them he shall live." Having thus shown his own goodness, he exposes the ingratitude of the people. 17. "And the sons of your people say: The way of the Lord is not straight; yet it is their own way that is not straight." Though I have set such goodness and kindness before them, he says, they dare to slander my dispensations as not right. And yet they ought to have perceived from the facts

that all my ways are upright and just, while their own are perverse. Then he says the same thing more clearly in the form of a question: 18 [?]. “Hear now, house of Israel: Is my way not straight? Is it not your ways that are not straight?” Then he repeats what he has said: the righteous man who chooses wickedness will be punished, and the sinner who returns to righteousness will obtain salvation. “But to you,” he says, “this did not seem just.” So he went on: 20. “And this is what you said: The way of the Lord is not straight.” Then he declares: “I will judge each of you according to your ways, house of Israel.” This is enough to persuade even the very hardest of hearts to love turning away from wickedness. 21, 22. “And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the tenth month, on the fifth of the month of our captivity, that one who had escaped came to me from Jerusalem, saying: The city has been taken. And the hand of the Lord came upon me in the evening, before the one who had escaped arrived, and it opened my mouth until he came to me in the morning; and once my mouth was opened, it was no longer kept shut.” The Syriac reads: “In the eleventh year and the twelfth month,” which fits the sequence better, for the city was taken in the eleventh year. He says that at the time stated someone came announcing the capture of Jerusalem. But the Master had acted beforehand and put the word of prophecy in him the evening before; and when that man appeared at dawn and brought the news, he no longer let me keep the prophetic words in silence, but commanded and enabled me to deliver them without ceasing. For the Master, above all, knows the time for silence and the time for speech. 23, 24. “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, those who live in these desolate places in the land of Israel keep saying: Abraham was one man, and he possessed the land; we are many, and the land has been given to us as a possession.” They suffer from an extreme lack of feeling. After so many punishments, and such great ones, they are still bold, and though they see Judea laid waste, they dare to say: “If Abraham, being alone, possessed this land, much more shall we, who are many, be its masters.” They ought instead to have considered Abraham's virtue and their own wickedness, and to have sought righteousness instead of trusting in numbers. That is why the Master also puts this [?] to them.
25, 26. “Therefore say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Since you eat with the blood,

A: “[?] to eat with the blood, and to lift up your eyes to your idols, and [?]” 15 “tenth”: so A [?]. 16 “before the one who had escaped [?]” 21 “Since [?]” 17 A: ἐγενήθη (“came to pass”). [?] “you eat with the blood, and lift up your eyes to your idols, and shed blood, and will you inherit the land?”

and you lift up your eyes to your idols, and you shed blood, and will you inherit the land? You have stood upon your sword, you have committed abomination, and each of you has defiled his neighbor's wife, and will you inherit the land?” Trusting in your own deeds, he says, you hope to take hold of the land of your fathers; yet your life is lawless, for you do what the law forbids. You eat blood, which I forbade when I gave the law to Noah as well, and which through Moses I commanded to be poured out on the ground. You set great store by the worship of idols, and you go on committing murders and adulteries. Since you dare such things, then, do not hope to inherit the land. 27, 28. “Thus says Adonai the Lord: As I live, surely those in the desolate places shall fall by the sword, and those on the open plain shall be given to the wild beasts of the field to be devoured, and those in the walled cities and those in the caves I will put to death. And I will make the land a desert.” The words “As I live” are the seal on what has been said. He says that those who live in the walled cities, in the caves, and in the deserted places will all pay the penalties he has described. And to show the cause, he adds: “And the arrogance of her strength shall perish, and the mountains of Israel shall be laid waste, because there is no one passing through. (29) And they shall know that I am the Lord; and I will make their land a desert, and it shall be laid waste because of all the abominations they have committed.” Through all this both they and we have been taught that, if we live in lawlessness, we should not trust even in many myriads beyond counting, but only in the remedies of repentance, which [?] showed beforehand

30, 31. “And you, son of man: the sons of your people talk about you by the walls and in the doorways of the houses, and they speak each to his neighbor and each to his brother, saying: Let us come together and hear what the word is that comes forth from the Lord. And they come to you as a people comes, and my people sit before you, and they hear your words, but they will not do them.” Everything said up to this point concerned those in Judea; but this concerns those already taken captive and living in Babylon. They wanted to hear the prophetic oracles, but they would no longer obey what was said. In their own gatherings they urged one another to run to the prophet and learn what God had declared, yet they went on contradicting it. That is why he says:

“And they will not do them. For falsehood is in their mouth.” The heart, he says, does not agree with the tongue. “For their heart goes after their defilements.” They listen to the word only for pleasure, not for benefit. Hence, fittingly:

32. “And you are to them like the sound of a sweet-toned, well-tuned harp.” Just as those who listen to some instrument producing a harmonious sound get enjoyment from it, he says, but no instruction from the notes, so too your words, O prophet, delight only their ears; they do not win over their soul, which lives in wickedness. For this is what he added: “And they will hear your words, but they will not do them, because falsehood is in their mouth.” But though they do not believe now, he says, when they see the outcome they will believe through experience. 33. “For when it comes,” he says, “they will say: Behold, it has come; and they will know that a prophet was among them.” What they now disbelieve they will believe through the events themselves, and then they will learn the power of prophecy. From here he turns his discourse to the shepherds. By shepherds he means not only the kings but also the priests, and he accuses them of shamelessness, of indolence, and of betraying the sheep.

Chapter 34. 2. “Son of man,” he says, “prophesy against the shepherds of Israel; prophesy, and say to the shepherds: Thus says Adonai the Lord: O shepherds of Israel, do shepherds feed themselves? Is it not the sheep that the shepherds feed?” Tell me, he says, what is a shepherd's proper task: to feed himself, or to feed the sheep? 3. “See, you eat the milk, and you clothe yourselves with the wool, and you slaughter the fat ones, but my sheep were not fed.” He says all this figuratively. You priests enjoyed the firstfruits, the tithes, and the portions set aside from the sacrifices; and you kings, who received tribute and taxes, were not content with these, but also slaughtered the wealthy and enjoyed their riches. Yet neither your priests nor you took any care to tend the sheep. Then he recounts their misconduct point by point. 4. “The weak you did not strengthen, the sick you did not heal, the broken you did not bind up, the ailing you did not restore to health, the straying you did not bring back, and the lost you did not [?]

seek; and, worst of all, the strong you wore down with toil, and you disciplined them with harshness and with mockery.” Not only did you fail to give the sick the treatment they needed, but you also laid many burdens on the healthy. This is easy to see from the histories. As for those who worshiped idols and lived in lawlessness, [?] those who tried to heal them, and who did so, they mocked, ridiculing what they said. Hence he says: “And you disciplined them with harshness and with mockery,” showing that [?] at the same time they inflicted grievous things on the saints and regarded it as sport and play [?].

5. Because of these bad shepherds, he says, I scattered my sheep, and they became food for all the wild beasts of the field. Again he speaks figuratively of beasts, since in the same discourse he called the people sheep. By beasts he means, in the spiritual sense, the demons, the destroyers of souls; and in the literal sense, those who attacked them from every side

6. “And my sheep were scattered and wandered over every mountain and on every high hill, and my sheep were scattered over the face of all the land, and there was no one to seek them or bring them back.” By mountains and hills and everything else he mentioned, he meant the worship of idols carried on there; for on mountains and hillocks and in every place they set up the precincts of idols, and neither the kings nor the priests prevented the impiety. That is why he said: “And there was no one to seek them or to turn them back.” Having made the accusation in this way, he threatens the shepherds with punishment, saying in effect: Since through idleness and neglect my sheep have become prey to beasts, and have enjoyed no care or forethought from you—for you cared only for your own luxury and the comfort of your bodies—9, 10. “Therefore, O shepherds, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will require my sheep at their hands, and I will make them cease from shepherding my sheep, and the shepherds shall no longer shepherd them; and I will rescue my sheep from their mouth, and they shall no longer be food for them.” By these words he foretold the end of both the kingdom of the Jews and the high priesthood
[?] 72 “and — no longer”: A “and they shall no longer feed.” 73 A: “they shall no longer be for them.”

[?] For I will free my sheep, he says, from their evil oversight; they never thought them worthy of any care, but only went on devouring them. Then he promises salvation through our Lord and Savior. 11, 12. “For thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I will seek out my sheep and visit them. As a shepherd visits his flock on a day when there is darkness and cloud in the midst of his scattered sheep, so I will seek out my sheep and rescue them from every place where they were scattered on the day of cloud and darkness.” By cloud and darkness he here means the gloom of ignorance that had spread over the world before the incarnation of our God and Savior. What he says, then, is this: Like a careful shepherd, who takes even greater care of his own sheep when he sees a mist coming down, since mist gives free rein to wolves and thieves, I too will care for my own sheep; I will gather them when they are scattered and make those that are separated into one flock. Such is the Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles. Then he makes the prophecy twofold. Its plain sense fits the Jews alone, but its mystical and hidden sense fits all people, especially since what happened to the Jews is a type of what concerns us. For their recall and release from captivity correspond to our return from the devil to God and our freedom from that tyrannical slavery. 13, 14. “And I will bring them out from the nations, and gather them from the countries, and bring them into their own land, and I will shepherd them on the mountains of Israel, and in the ravines, and in every inhabited place of the land. In good pasture I will feed them.” Yet the law is good, and the commandment, according to the Apostle, is holy and just and good; but he promises them another pasture, for they already had the pasture of the law. What, then, is this good pasture that surpasses the law? Clearly he is hinting at the teaching of the divine Gospels, in which God's sheep graze, are nourished and fattened, and enjoy salvation. And to show this more clearly he says: “On the high mountain of Israel shall be their splendor.” He had indeed mentioned many mountains and ravines, but [?] he singles out a certain high mountain, on which he foretells the splendor that those who graze there will have. Blessed David also mentions this mountain, saying: “The mountain of God is a rich mountain, a mountain [?] when there is. A: “of wandering.” “I will rescue”: A “I will drive out.” “from” (ἐκ): A “from” (ἀπό). “and”: B adds “and I will feed them into their land” [?] A [?] “on the mountains of Israel.” “good”: the text of the passage reads “holy.” “their splendor shall be”: lacking in [?]. “and”: B “but.” “David”: in B placed after “mentions.”

thick as curds, a rich mountain.” Then he says to the mountains of Israel, which envy this mountain: “Why do you suppose them to be mountains thick as curds? It is the mountain in which God was pleased to dwell; for the Lord will indeed dwell there to the end.” In vain, he says, do you envy this mountain, since God was pleased to dwell in it, and he will do so to the end. The other translators have taught us to understand it this way: Aquila says, “Why do you contend, you mountains thick as curds?” and Theodotion, “Why do you go to law over this mountain?” And Isaiah cries out, and Micah likewise: “In the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, and the house of the Lord on the tops of the mountains, and all the nations shall come to it,” and so on. And the Lord says in the holy Gospels: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden.” So here too he has called the lofty and conspicuous teaching of the Gospel a mountain, and on it he promised that the splendor of the sheep would come about. Then he adds: “And their folds shall be there.” This too plainly fits us, and not the Jews: they had one fold, the temple in Jerusalem, but we have churches beyond number throughout the whole world. “And they shall lie down and rest there, and they shall feed in good delight and in rich pasture on the mountains of Israel. (15) And I will shepherd my sheep.” By good and rich delight he means the divine oracles: “Take delight in the Lord,” it says, “and he will give you the desires of your heart.” By the mountains of Israel he means the prophetic books, on which we in turn graze, finding through them a way up to the greatest mountain; for through the prophetic oracles we are led to the teaching of the Gospel, to which they bear witness. And we have as our shepherd the Master and Lord himself, who cries out: “I am the good shepherd.” Foretelling this here too, he said: “And I will shepherd my sheep, and I will give them rest, and they shall know that I am the Lord.” For as we are shepherded by him and rest in his teaching as on green pasture, we come to recognize his lordship. 16. Thus says Adonai the Lord: “The lost I will seek out, and the straying I will bring back”—like Paul and those like him; “and the broken I will bind up”—like the tax collector, the harlot, the thief, and those like them; “and the weak I will strengthen”—like Peter after his denial; “and the fat and strong I will guard”—like the holy apostles and those who have chosen a life like theirs; “and I will shepherd

them with judgment,” supplying good things and disciplining when it is needed. Having thus concluded both his discourse against the bad shepherds and his prediction of the care that would come from himself, he turns his discourse to the sheep, teaching that the misconduct of the shepherds gives the sheep no excuse. For the sheep are rational: they have discernment and are able both to flee evil and to choose good. Hence he says: 17. “And you, my sheep, thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I will judge between sheep and sheep, between rams and goats.” For just as I judge between shepherds and sheep, he says, so I will also be judge among the sheep and will punish those who do wrong. 18, 19. “Was it not enough for you to graze on the good pasture, that the rest of your pasture had to be trampled under your feet? And to drink the clear water, that you had to muddy the rest with your feet? And my sheep grazed on what your feet had trampled, and drank the water your feet had muddied.” The word is addressed to the wealthy who have squandered their wealth in prodigality, taking from it not only what they need but what goes beyond need; and one might see this being done by some even now. The parable of Lazarus also bears witness, for it shows that rich man not sharing even the crumbs that fell from his table with the poor man. “You trampled the rest with your feet” is said figuratively, as of sheep that eat the grass and trample the rest, and that drink the water first and then muddy it with their feet. 20. “Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I am against you, and I will judge between the strong sheep and the weak sheep.” Then he describes the insolence of the strong. 21. “Because you shove with your sides and your shoulders, and butt with your horns, and you crushed all the weakening ones until you drove them out, and my sheep were scattered for every passerby [?]. 22. And I will save my sheep, and they shall no longer be plunder.” All this he said as of sheep—shoulders and horns and sides; but through all of it he exposed the unjust domination of those in power. Nevertheless he promises safety to the sheep. “And I will judge between sheep and sheep, and between ram and ram.” I will judge, he says, and I will not overlook
those who are wronged, but will exact justice from the wrongdoers. Then [he foretells?] the common salvation of all [?]

23. “And I will raise up over them one shepherd, who will shepherd them, my servant David; he will shepherd them, and he will give them rest, and he will be their shepherd.” Having said above, “I will shepherd,” he says here that David will be their shepherd, and he also calls him a servant. Who is this? Is it not clear that it is Christ the Master, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh? That is why he is also called a servant, as a man; and this is according to his nature, not according to his dignity. For if those who have believed in him are not servants but sons, much more is he himself, through whom the servants obtained their freedom, not a servant but a son. So too blessed Paul says: “Who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” And Isaiah also cries out in his person: “Thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb to be his servant, to gather Jacob; and Israel shall be gathered to him. Behold, I have given you as a covenant to the race, as a light to the nations, that you may be salvation to the end of the earth.” And again: “Jacob is my servant; I will uphold him.” In the Hebrew it reads, “My servant.” And the divine evangelist applied this testimony to our Lord Jesus. He is called servant, then, as a man, and this, as I said, not according to his dignity but according to his nature; for he took the form of a servant. As for the shepherd of the sheep being one, the Lord too said in the Gospels: “And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock, one shepherd.” Then he adds: 24. “And I the Lord will be their God, and my servant David a ruler in their midst.” And by what follows he shows that what has been said is true: “I the Lord have spoken.” For the [?] of the one who spoke is enough to confirm the words.

25. “And I will make a covenant of peace with David.” Paul is the interpreter of this, for he cries out concerning Christ: “He is our peace, who has made both one and has broken down the dividing wall of partition.” He said this above as well: “And I will raise up over them one shepherd.” For one shepherd tends both those from the Gentiles and those from the Jews who have believed. “And I will make evil beasts vanish from the land”: both the hordes of evil demons and the people afflicted with savagery, the ones [?] 30 “who”: A “and.” 31 “he — will give them rest” [?]

[?] being changed, and becoming rational, and [?] being entirely freed from being beasts, while others are brought to an end by death. "And they shall dwell in the wilderness confidently, and sleep in the forests." Both are unfruitful places. What he means is that they will occupy and cultivate the wilderness of the gentiles, and will find rest and healing in the forest of the Jews. Earlier, too, when he wanted to show how unfruitful Jerusalem was, he said: "Prophesy, son of man, against the forest of the Negeb." This means the south, as we have said before. 26. "And I will give blessing round about my mountain, and I will bring down the rain for you in its season; there shall be rains of blessing." This is what the teachings of the divine apostles are like: they bring water full of blessing to the souls of believers. Divine Scripture often calls teaching rain. The prophet Isaiah is a witness to this. Speaking for God, he threatens the old vineyard: "It shall not be pruned, nor dug; and I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it." 27. "And the trees in the field shall yield their fruit, and the earth shall yield its strength." Those who are earthly in soul, that is, those who come from the gentiles, and the Jews, who are as unfruitful as wild trees, will come to faith and enjoy this watering, and so they will give me the fruit of godliness. "And they shall dwell on their land in hope of peace." He did not say "in peace" but "in hope of peace." For the Lord said to those who had believed in him: "In the world you have tribulation; but take courage, I have overcome the world." The divine Apostle also says: "For in hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience." And again: "And not only so, but we ourselves also, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves as we wait for adoption, the redemption of our body." Then comes the most profitable thing of all: "And they shall know that I am the Lord, when I break the bands of their yoke and deliver them from the hand of those who enslaved them. (28) And they shall no longer be a prey to the nations, and the beasts of the land shall no more devour them." I have already said that the prophecy is twofold. One part fits the Jews themselves, and the other fits all people. For he freed the Jews from the Babylonian captivity, and he released all of us from the tyranny of the devil.

By "bands of the yoke" he meant the constraint of slavery. By "nations" and "beasts" he meant the savage enemies in the case of the Jews, and in our case the various ranks of demons, who [?] people like wild beasts. Then he shows the invincible weapon, by which I mean hope in him. "And they shall dwell in hope, and there shall be no one to terrify them." For "it is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in man." Whoever has this hope cries out: "All the nations surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I drove them back." 29. "And I will raise up for them a plant of peace for a name." The prophet Isaiah says this as well: "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from the root, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him," and so on. And again: "There shall be the root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope, and his rest shall be honor." The Lord explained this when he said: "I am the true vine, you are the branches." And in the Song of Songs we find the bride saying: "As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons." So here too he says, "I will raise up for them a plant of peace for a name," that is, one that is most renowned, glorious and widely celebrated. Perhaps the passage also hints at something else: that they will take their name from the plant. For all the godly are called Christians after Christ. "And they shall no longer be few in number in the land." That is, the godly will not be few, for they were very few before the coming of Christ. "And they shall no longer perish by famine on the land." [?] they will enjoy spiritual food, he says. For here he calls the lack of the word a famine. God threatened this famine through the prophets: "For I will bring," he says, "not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord." "And they shall no longer bear the reproach of the nations." This too fits both us and the Jews. We have grown into a multitude and filled the world, and we are no longer reproached by those who have remained in ungodliness; instead they envy and resent us. And the Jews, once they were freed from captivity and returned from Babylon, recovered their former spirit. 30. "And they shall know that I am the Lord their God, and that they are my people, the house of Israel, says the Lord Adonai." We must recall the Apostle's words: "Not all who are from Jerusalem are Israel, nor are they all children because they are the seed of Abraham." It is fitting to add [Critical notes: Psalm [?], 8. 87: "the prophet says": [?] "foretells." 88: "vine": [?]. 31: "and — land": [?]; in the Hebrew, "through them" [?]; [?] "with them." 57: "Jerusalem": the received reading.]

to these the words that the divine John the Baptist spoke to the Pharisees: "God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham." From this it is clear that all who have believed, and who see the God of the universe through faith, as far as it is possible to see him, will be called Israel, for this is what the name means. This happened to them after the return, but the prophecy fits us more properly and more truly, since what belongs to us is not a type but the truth. 31. "And you are my sheep," he says, "and the sheep of my pasture." To show that the word is addressed not only to Israel but to the whole of human nature, he had to add: "You are men, and I am the Lord your God, says the Lord Adonai." For you have been freed from your beastliness and have acquired the mind that befits human nature, and I will be your God and Lord, and I will take every care and thought for you. This, then, is the meaning of the prophecy. For my part, I see nothing new in the Jews' usual folly. But I am amazed that some of our own people dare to apply everything to Zerubbabel. They do not understand that most of what is said is directly contrary to what happened under him. Take these words: "I will make with David a covenant of peace, and I will remove evil beasts from the land, and they shall dwell in the wilderness confidently and sleep in the forests." And these: "They shall dwell in hope, and there shall be no one to terrify them, and I will raise up for them a plant of peace for a name, and they shall no longer perish by famine on the land, and they shall no longer bear the reproach of the nations." These are entirely contrary to the history about him. When he returned from Babylon and began to rebuild the divine temple, the neighbouring nations prevented him from finishing the work. That is why forty-six years passed before even the temple alone was completed, according to both the old history and the testimony of the Gospels. Another eighty-two years later the city received its walls, which Nehemiah built in the thirty-second year of the reign of Artaxerxes. And the book of Ezra tells us that such fear hung over the builders that they had to build while armed, carrying stones and shooting arrows at the enemy at the same time. How, then, can these words fit such people: "There shall be no one to terrify them," or "I will raise up for them a plant of peace," or "They shall not be few in number"? Ezra also tells us

that Nehemiah went to great trouble and could barely persuade the priests to leave their life in the villages and live in the city. Those who love learning can easily compare the rest with the history in the same way and see the discrepancy. So some things fit them, but most fit the salvation of the world. Let us leave the Jews, then, to their babbling. They have transferred to their soul the weakness of the bodily eyes of their own mother Leah, and they do not wish to see the truth. We urge our fellow believers to "test all things and hold fast what is good," as the divine Apostle says. With food we prefer the pleasant to the unpleasant, and indeed choose the more pleasant over the merely pleasant. Let us do the same with the divine oracles. For "the mind," as Job says, "discerns words, and the palate tastes food; and wisdom is found in a long time, and knowledge in a long and full life." Experience is an exact teacher when it takes the revelation from above as its co-worker. May we enjoy that revelation and be enlightened by its radiance, and so not miss [?] the truth, in Christ Jesus our Lord, with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. [?]

CHAPTER 35. 1–4. "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against Mount Seir, and prophesy against it, and say to it: Thus says the Lord Adonai: Behold, I am against you, Mount Seir, and I will stretch out my hand against you, and I will make you desolate, and you shall be laid waste. And I will make desolation in your cities, and you shall become a desolation, and you shall know that I am the Lord." Seir is a mountain of Idumea, as we have already said. The Idumeans traced their descent from Esau, and they were extremely hostile and ill-disposed toward the Jews. For this reason they even rejoiced at the calamities that came upon them. The God of the universe threatens these people with utter desolation. He used the words "I will stretch out my hand against you" as a metaphor drawn from people who strike with their hands,

to show how fierce his wrath is. Yet we know that the divine nature is free from passion, and that such words are measured to what the hearers can take in. Having threatened the punishment in this way, he adds the reason for it: 5. "Because there was in you an everlasting enmity, and you lay in wait for the house of Israel with guile, at the hand of enemies, with the sword, in the time of their affliction, and in the time of iniquity at the end." He accuses the Idumeans of nursing grudges and of plotting secretly against Israel. He pointed to these things when he said, "You lay in wait for the house of Israel with guile, at the hand of enemies, with the sword, in the time of their affliction." That is: when enemies came against them, you blocked their roads with ambushes and traps and did not even let them escape. The other translators rendered it the same way: "And you shut up," it says, "the sons of Israel to the hand of the sword, in the time of their affliction, in the time of lawlessness before me." He means: when the house of Israel was paying the penalty for the lawlessness committed against me (or the "iniquity," as the Seventy have it), their calamities were made worse by your deceits and your plots with the enemy. So the prophetic word teaches us not to trample on those who are being punished for their sins, but to weep with those who weep, as the apostolic admonition says. 6. "Therefore, as I live, says the Lord Adonai, you have surely sinned unto blood, and blood shall pursue you; since you hated your own blood, your blood shall pursue you." Here he uses "blood" to mean not war but kinship. He means: since you have made war on your own kin, you will rightly have war made on you by them, and I will raise up against you as enemies the kinsmen you hated. The Jews are kinsmen of the Idumeans, for both trace their descent from two brothers: the Idumeans from Edom, who is also Esau, and the Jews from Jacob, who is also [?]

7. "And I will make Mount Seir a desolation and a waste." Then he also describes how it will be laid waste: "And I will destroy from it man and beast, and the one who passes through and the one who returns." This shows how extreme the desolation will be. He will strip it not only of its inhabitants but even of travellers passing through. He also foretells how he will destroy its inhabitants. 8–9. "And I will fill your hills and your ravines with your slain, and all your plains; for those wounded by the sword shall fall in you. And an everlasting desolation

I will make you, and your cities shall no longer be inhabited, and you shall know that I am the Lord." Again, he used "everlasting desolation" and "shall no longer be inhabited" according to the idiom of Scripture. We will understand these words in light of what we have already explained about the desolation of Tyre. After threatening punishment in this way, he again lays bare their wickedness. 10. "Because you said: The two nations and the two lands shall be mine, and I will inherit them, and the Lord is there." Or, as the other translators have it, "And the Lord was there." This not only exposes their greed and grasping but also shows how extreme their ungodliness was, and it resembles the boastful words of Sennacherib. He said: "The Lord will not deliver Jerusalem from my hand." In the same way the Idumeans said boldly: "Let the Lord be in Jerusalem; we shall hold the two lands." And yet when the God of the universe brought Israel out of Egypt, he did not let them make war on the Idumeans. "You shall not make war on them," he told them, "for they are your brothers." So when they were barred from the road, they went around the mountain and the wilderness, as they had been commanded. And God said to Israel about that whole land: "I will not give it to you, for I have given it to the sons of Esau as an inheritance." Yet the Idumeans were not content with the good things God had given them. They hoped to inherit the land of the Jews as well. So it is fitting that the God of the universe both threatens punishments and confirms the sentence with an oath.

11. "For this reason," he says, "as I live, says the Lord Adonai, I will do to you according to your enmity and according to your jealousy, which you showed out of your hatred for them." He means: you will suffer what your envy and hostility deserve. "And I will make myself known to you when I judge you. (12) And you shall know that I am the Lord." He means: by bringing punishments on you I will make myself plain to you. Then you will not think that your troubles came from some other source, but you will learn that I am Master and gain some benefit from that knowledge. "I have heard the sound of all your blasphemies that you spoke about the mountains of Israel, saying: The mountains of Israel, the high ones, the everlasting ones, are desolate; they have been given to us for a possession. (13) And you spoke boastfully against me with your mouth, and multiplied your words against me, which I heard." He cannot bear even to repeat the blasphemous words. In this way he teaches us not to put other people's blasphemies on our tongues, even when we are only reporting them, but to remember the prophetic voice that says:

[Critical notes:] 88: A reads "they shall know." 89: B reads "will deliver" [variant form]. 90: B reads "he is your brother." 91: "possession": A reads "because you said, The mountains of Israel are desolate, they have been given to us for a possession [?]." 92: "and — them": missing in A. 93: [?] "and —": missing in A.

"so that my mouth may not speak of the works of men." In all this he showed not only their hostility and grudge-bearing but also their arrogance, and their rage and madness against God. He added something very useful: "You multiplied your words against me, which I heard." This teaches us that nothing we say or do can escape his power of sight or of hearing. 14–15. "Thus says the Lord Adonai: While the whole earth rejoices, I will make you an everlasting desolation. As you rejoiced over the inheritance of the house of Israel because it was destroyed, so I will do to you. You shall be a desolation, Mount Seir, and all Idumea shall be utterly consumed, and they shall know that I am the Lord their God." He threatened them with a punishment that has no consolation. He means: while everyone else lives in peace and contentment, I will surround you with calamities. Then you will not even have the comfort of sharing your misfortunes with others. Israel did have that comfort, for Nebuchadnezzar attacked not only them but also the Tyrians, the Sidonians, the Philistines and the Egyptians. Yet besides all this he promises a benefit through the punishment: "For they shall know," he says, "that I am the Lord their God." So discipline is beneficial. As the prophet Isaiah says, it "opens our ears" and prepares us to recognize our own Master, who strikes and heals.

CHAPTER 36. 1–3. "And you, son of man, prophesy to the mountains of Israel: Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord Adonai: Because the enemy said against you, 'Aha! The everlasting desolate places have become ours for a possession,' therefore prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord Adonai: Because you were made a ruin for all the nations, and because you were dishonoured by all those around you, so that you became a possession for the remaining nations, and you became a byword on the tongue and on the lips, and a reproach to the nations." Having foretold grim and gloomy things for the Idumeans, he turns his words to the mountains of Israel. He offers them a promise of good things and urges them to take heart, because the words the enemies spoke are false and empty. He means: the desolation will not last long. I will refute the taunts of the nations that live near you and put an end to their insolence against you. They will no longer tell the story of your calamities and your [?] misfortunes. To these

[?] of the Lord. Thus says the Lord Adonai to the mountains and to the hills, and to the torrents and to the ravines, and to the glens, and to the places laid waste and destroyed, and to the cities that have been abandoned, which became plunder and were trampled down by the remaining nations around them." It would have been easy and simple to promise the good things to the whole land of Israel in a few words. But he names each in turn, the mountains, the ravines, the hills, the cities and all the rest, to cheer those who were downcast because of the desolation. 5. "Therefore thus says the Lord Adonai: Surely in the fire of my jealousy I have spoken against the remaining nations and against all Idumea, because with gladness they took my possession for themselves as an inheritance, and with all their heart they despised souls, so as to destroy them by plunder." He means: the insolence of Idumea and of the other nations greatly provoked me. They used it against my land, rejoicing in its desolation, expecting to take control of it and to carry off as captives the souls who lived there. That is why I pronounced my sentences against them. 6. "Prophesy, then, O prophet, [?] concerning the land of Israel, and say to the mountains and to the hills and to the glens and to the ravines: Thus says the Lord Adonai: Behold, I have spoken in my jealousy and in my wrath, [?] round about you; they shall bear their own dishonour." He means: the reproach heaped on you has caused the sentence to be passed against those who reproached you, and they are reaping the fruits of their [?] against me and of their grudge and insolence against you. 8. "But you, mountains of Israel, [?] your grape and your fruit [?] my people [?]." He means: I will [?] the hope of the people and confirm their good expectation, and they will return and enjoy the fruits that grow among you. [?] it will enjoy. It is clear, moreover, [?] that he will speak to the mountains [?]. They are irrational and soulless, but by addressing them he comforts those who live in them, promising them good things. 9–11. "Behold, I am toward you, and I will look upon you, and you shall be tilled and sown." [Critical notes, largely illegible:] "and to the glens": missing in A. A reads "to those laid waste" [?]. [?] A reads "of wrath." [?] "possession": A [?]. [?] "again": A reads "Therefore prophesy" [?]. [?] "to bear" [?]. "Thus says — Lord": missing in A. [?] "and": missing in A.

"And I will multiply people upon you, the whole house of Israel, to the end, and the cities shall be inhabited, and the desolate places shall be built. And I will multiply upon you people and cattle, and they shall increase and multiply, and I will settle you as you were in your beginning, and I will do you good as in the years before you; and they shall know that I am the Lord." It is not the mountains that will know, but those who live in the mountains. These things were fulfilled after the return from Babylon, and the facts bear witness: the cities of Palestine are full of inhabitants, all of them have been rebuilt, and they shine with splendour. Only that one city has remained desolate in which the Jews, raging against the Master and Saviour, committed the outrage of the cross, gaining salvation for all people but destruction for themselves. The Master both promised that all Israel would obtain the return and fulfilled his own word. He arranged for Cyrus to permit the return to all. But they, sick with their usual disobedience, opposed the command and chose a foreign land over their own. 13–15. "Thus says Adonai the Lord: Because they said to you, 'You are a land that devours people, and you have been bereaved of children by your nation,' therefore you shall no longer devour people, and you shall no longer bereave your nation of children, says the Lord. And the reproach of the nations shall no longer be heard against you, and you shall no longer bear the insults of peoples, and your nation shall no longer be bereaved of children, says Adonai the Lord." These things too would have been fulfilled if the Jews had been willing. But since they went mad against the Master like raging dogs, they themselves left the prophecy unfulfilled, and even so the prediction remains true. For the God of the universe said beforehand through Jeremiah the prophet: "I will pronounce an end upon a nation and upon a kingdom, to rebuild and to plant it; and if they do evil before me, so as not to hear my voice, I will also repent of the good things which I spoke of doing for them." So the Jews are themselves to blame [?] for not obtaining what was promised through the prophecy [?]…

16–18. "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, the house of Israel lived on their land, and they defiled it by their way, and by their idols, and by their uncleannesses; their way became before my face like the uncleanness of a menstruous woman. And I poured out my wrath

upon them." The facts themselves, he says, bear witness to the justice of the punishment. They not only persisted in serving idols of every kind, but also practised every form of lawlessness, so that they were filled with every abomination and hatefulness. And since under the law the menstruous woman, that is, a woman with a flow of blood, was considered extremely unclean, he likens the abomination of their lawlessness to that discharge. Then, pressing the accusation further, he says: "Because they poured out blood on the land and defiled it with their idols. (19) And I scattered them among the nations and winnowed them into the countries." And again he shows the justice of the punishment: "According to their way and according to their practices I judged them." They reaped, he says, the fruits of what they had planted. By "blood" he means here not only their other murders but also the sacrifices of children which they offered to savage and wicked demons. For they were not content, he says, with the transgressions before the captivity; even after becoming captives and exiles they persisted in the same evils. 20. "And they went among the nations to which they went, and they profaned my holy name when it was said of them, 'These are the people of the Lord, and they have gone out of his land.'" By living in wickedness, he says, they brought blasphemy upon me. First the nations supposed that they had been defeated and fallen under their enemies because of my weakness. Then, having learned their wickedness by experience, they stirred up blasphemy against me, as if I delighted in such practices and called such wicked people my own people. Yet, taking thought for those very nations: 21. "And I spared them for the sake of my holy name, which the house of Israel profaned among the nations to which they went." Wishing to teach them my strength, he says, I will free these people from the [?] that beset them

22–23. "Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says Adonai the Lord: It is not for your sake that I act, house of Israel, but for the sake of my holy name, which you profaned among the nations to which you went. And I will sanctify my great name, which was profaned among the nations, which you profaned in their midst; and the nations shall know that I am the Lord, says Adonai the Lord, when I am sanctified in you before their eyes." You are not worthy of salvation, he says, but it is fitting that the nations should obtain healing, since they took from you an occasion to blaspheme me. The blasphemy will be undone through your salvation, for when they learn that my

name is great and sufficient for the help of [?], they will glorify and praise my lordship. This is what he indicated by saying: "And the nations shall know that I am the Lord God, when I am sanctified in you before their eyes." (24) "And I will take you from the nations, and gather you from all the lands, and bring you into your own land." This applies to all who returned, for those who chose to return obtained the return. But what follows no longer applies to all, only to those who chose to believe the preaching of the gospel. For he says: 25. "And I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your uncleannesses, and from all your idols I will cleanse you." By "clean water" he means the water of regeneration, in which we were baptized and received forgiveness of sins. And what follows confirms what has been said. 26. "And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will give you." By these words he signified a change of mind. Your heart, he says, will incline towards better things and will no longer lean towards worse things, as was its former habit. But "I will give" in no way harms free will. By words and deeds and countless [?] miracles he persuaded not only them but all the nations as well to come to true religion; he did not compel them. [?] The Holy Spirit and his grace were supplied through them, not to the Jews only but to all of the nations who came to the faith. By [a heart of stone?] he means one that is resistant and disobedient [?]…
28. "And you shall dwell in the land which I gave to your fathers." Again he turns the discourse to [?] what is common, and from spiritual things to bodily ones

"And you shall be my people, and I will be your God. (29–30) And I will cleanse you from all your sins, and I will call for the grain and multiply it, and I will not lay famine upon you. And I will multiply the fruit of the tree and the produce of the field, so that you may no longer suffer the reproach of famine among the nations." I know that each of these things can also be taken spiritually. Even so, I think that here the prophetic word is promising bodily things to the Jews. Since at that time great desolation held the land, he promises them an abundance of fruits of every kind, and he foretells the benefit that will come from this. 31. "And you shall remember," he says, "your evil ways and your practices that were not good, and you shall loathe yourselves in your own sight for your iniquities and for your abominations." When you enjoy these good things, he says, and learn what great fruits righteousness bears, you will remember your former wickedness and the punishment brought upon you because of it, and you will hate your former lawlessness intensely. He has put "you shall loathe" in place of "you shall abhor." David says something similar of the lawless man: "He set himself on every way that is not good, and he did not loathe evil," that is, he did not abhor wickedness. Having thus promised them good things, he humbles their pride again:

32. "It is not for your sake that I act, house of Israel, says Adonai the Lord; let this be known to you, house of Israel." You are not worthy of the promised good things, he says; rather, I do what befits my own nature. Then, exhorting and shaming them at once: "Be ashamed and be confounded because of your ways, house of Israel." Do not bear your many kinds of punishment, he says, without pain or feeling. Late as it is, take to heart the wickedness of your practices and blush for what you have dared to do. 33–34. "Thus says Adonai the Lord: On the day when I cleanse you from all your iniquities, I will also cause the cities to be inhabited, and the desolate places shall be built. And the land that was laid waste shall be tilled, whereas it had become a desolation in the sight of everyone who passed by." When I grant you forgiveness of sins, he says,

and show you to be clean by pardoning you, then I will provide buildings for the cities and plantings for the land, and in place of the former desolation, which all who passed by saw, I will make it inhabited. 35. "And they shall say: That land which was laid waste has become like a garden of delight, and the cities that were desolate, laid waste and razed sit fortified with walls." For just as all people once carried talk of your desolation on their lips, he says, so now you will be widely renowned and a wonder to all: your desolate land will be likened to the paradise of delight, and the cities that had been uninhabited and overthrown will be walled with strong ramparts. 36. "And the nations, as many as are left around you, shall know that I, the Lord, have built the ruined places and planted the desolate ones. I, the Lord, have spoken, and I will do it." The neighbouring nations will learn that it is I who sent the grievous things before and who now send the pleasing ones, and they will learn the certainty of what was said from the trustworthiness of the one who spoke. "I, the Lord, have spoken, and I will do it": for since I am Master and able to act, I will bring what I have said to fulfilment. 37. "Thus says Adonai the Lord: Yet for this I will be sought by the house of Israel, to do it for them." For "I will be sought" Symmachus said "I will be found." To my former benefits, he says, I will add this one too, and I will grant them to be called back. "And I will multiply them like holy sheep." For since [?] them like sheep [?]…

CHAPTER 37. 1. "And the hand of the Lord came upon me." Again he calls the divine activity a "hand." "And he brought me out in the Spirit of the Lord and set me in the middle of the plain." Again the vision is spiritual. He did not see what was shown to him with the eyes of the body; he received the revelation of the all-holy Spirit. "And it was full of human bones. (2) And he led me around them on every side, and behold, there were very many on the face of the plain." He receives revelations suited to the circumstances. Those taken captive from Judea had given up hope of better things because of the unbelief from which they suffered. So the God of the universe shows them his own power: he shows the prophet the resurrection of dead bodies, which is far more difficult than their recall from exile, and through him he teaches the whole people that all things are easy for him when he wills. Through this he taught the Jews and the other Israelites that it is very easy for God, when he wills, to lead those who had become captives back to their former freedom. And to us, and to all in general who have received the preaching of the gospel with faith, he shows how easily our bodies will be raised, and that at the divine word and nod the nature of things [?]…

"And he said to me: (3) Son of man, shall these bones live? And I said: Lord God, you know these things." The prophet did not doubt. He left the more exact knowledge to God, because he knew God's power exactly but did not know his will. 4–6. "And he said to me: Prophesy over these bones, prophesy, son of man, and say to them: Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says Adonai the Lord to these bones: Behold, I will bring the breath of life into you. And I will put sinews upon you, and bring up flesh upon you, and stretch skin over you, and I will put my spirit upon you, and you shall live, and you shall know that I am the Lord." He uses the prophet as an assistant and, as it were, an instrument of the resurrection in the

vision. Through the prophet's tongue he commands those lifeless and utterly dead bones to grow flesh, sinews and skin and to receive the breath of life. And these things took place as a type not only of the recall of the Jews but also of the resurrection of all. "For the trumpet will sound," says the divine Apostle, "and the dead will be raised incorruptible." 7. "And I prophesied as the Lord commanded me, and there was a sound as I prophesied, and behold, an earthquake, and the bones came together, bone to bone, each to its own joint." The prophet, serving the divine command, spoke the words he had been ordered to speak, and the deed followed the words. The earthquake signified the divine appearing, and the sound signified the activity of the angels who serve the divine will. I saw the bones, he says, running together, recovering their proper joining, and taking the structure they had at the beginning. 8. "And I looked, and behold, sinews came upon them, and flesh grew, and it came up upon them, and skin covered them over, and there was no breath in them." The second re-creation follows the pattern of the first creation. Just as the body of our forefather Adam was formed first and only then was the soul breathed into it, so here too both came together into their proper union. The bones grew flesh and sinews and were covered with skin, but they lay breathless and motionless; then by the divine will they obtain life and sensation once more. 9. "And he said to me: Prophesy to the breath, prophesy, son of man, and say to the breath: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe into these dead, and let them live." The passage teaches us how easily the divine power works, and that all things are in his hand. "For in his hand," it says, "is the soul of all the living." That is why he commands the prophet to charge the souls, wherever they might be, to return and take up their dwelling in their own bodies again. 10. "And I prophesied as he commanded me. And the breath entered into them, and they lived and stood on their feet, a very great assembly." When I passed on the divine command, he says, the bodies that had been joined together were brought to life and rose again, and there was, he says, [?]
[Notes:] 18 "and upon them": missing in A. 19 "were covered" [?]. 25 "into": B has "for in the hand."

[?] no small [number] of those who had risen. Having thus seen the revelation, he is taught its interpretation. 11. "And the Lord spoke to me, saying: Son of man, these bones are the house of Israel, and they say: Our bones have dried up, our hope has perished, we are lost." These things, he says, are a type of Israel, O prophet. They have despaired of their own situation, but the type has shown them the hope of good things. 12–14. "Therefore prophesy, son of man, and say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I will open your tombs, my people, and bring you up out of your graves, and bring you into the land of Israel. And you shall know that I am the Lord when I open your graves and bring you up out of your graves, my people. And I will put my spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land, and you shall know that I, the Lord, have spoken and will do it, says Adonai the Lord." If I have shown you, he says, that what seems to you far more difficult is done by me very easily, it is plain that I will do this with still greater ease. I will lead you out of the bonds of captivity as if out of tombs, and I will bring you back to your own homeland, for falsehood is foreign to the truth. Having thus promised the return, he foretells the harmony of the tribes after the return. 15–17. "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, take for yourself one rod, and write on it 'Judah and the sons of Israel joined to him'; and you shall take a second rod and write on it 'For Joseph, the rod of Ephraim, and all the sons of Israel joined to them.' And you shall join them to one another into one rod for yourself, to bind them, and they shall be together in your hand." Under Rehoboam the tribes were divided. The ten tribes kept to themselves and set up their royal seat in Samaria, one of the cities of Ephraim, while the tribe of Judah ruled itself and the tribe of Benjamin. But after the return they all came under one leadership. That is why God commanded the prophet to take two rods: to inscribe one with Ephraim, adding the tribes subject to him, and the other with Judah and those allied with him, and then to join the rods to each other, since the division would henceforth cease and there would be unity. Then, when the people asked and wanted to know the interpretation, he commands the prophet to say plainly:

"Behold, I will take the tribe of Joseph which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel joined to him, and I will put them under the tribe of Judah, and they shall become one rod in the hand of Judah." Those who long ago cut themselves off from the kingdom of Judah, he says, I will cause to acknowledge his leadership again. I will end the division that took place and make all the tribes obey Judah in harmony. And he explains the same thing again more clearly: "Behold, I take the whole house of Israel from among the nations to which they went, and I will gather them into the land of Israel. (22) And I will make them one nation in my land and on the mountains of Israel, and one ruler shall be king over them all." These things were fulfilled typologically in Zerubbabel, but exactly and truly in Christ the Master. Zerubbabel was not a king; he was a leader of the people and a general. "And they shall no longer be two nations, nor shall they ever again be divided into two kingdoms. (23–24) So that they may no longer defile themselves with their idols, and with their abominations, and with all their impieties; and I will deliver them from all their impieties in which they sinned, and I will cleanse them, and they shall be my people, and I will be their God. And my servant David shall be ruler in their midst, and there shall be one shepherd for them all." The words spoken by Christ the Master in the holy Gospels also fit these: "And I have other sheep which are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock, one shepherd." He calls Christ the Master "David" because he traces his descent from David according to the flesh, and "servant" because of his human nature: "being in the form of God, he took the form of a servant." So, to point to the nature he assumed, he called him "servant," meaning that according to the flesh he was born of a servile nature. For the Only-begotten, the Master of all, is not a servant. As God he is not called David either; he is called David because he is from David, and servant because of the nature he assumed. And though God the Word, becoming man, took this nature from a servant, he did not cast off what he was; rather, by its union with the divine nature he glorified our nature. The prophetic word teaches, then, that impiety and the error of idolatry will be extinguished and that the division of the kingdoms will come to an end; and coming under one leadership and shepherded by one shepherd, they will acknowledge their own God and Master. "And they shall walk in my ordinances, and keep my judgments and do them. (25) And they shall dwell on [their?] land [?]…"
[Notes:] "all of them": A has "all." "he calls" (λέγει): B has "he names" (καλεῖ). [?] "nor." "and": A has "that."

…the land which I gave to my servant Jacob, in which their fathers dwelt; and they shall dwell on it, they and their sons and their sons' sons, for ever; and David my servant shall be their ruler for ever." Let the Jews say who this everlasting king of theirs is, the one called David. They would agree themselves that such titles do not fit Zerubbabel at all. First, he never reigned as king but remained a leader of the people. Second, even that leadership of his ended with his death. But if they take this everlasting David to mean the line of David, let them show us David's line reigning. And if, quite apart from the kingship, even David's line itself is now lost to view, then for the present one of two things must follow: either we suppose the prophecy false, or we worship the kingdom of Christ the Master, who is from David according to the flesh. They would themselves admit that the prophecy does not lie. And if it does not lie, as indeed it does not, then consider the facts. We see no other kingdom of the Jews. David's line itself is not plain or known. Yet he who is from David according to the flesh, but Son of God according to his divinity, now rules and holds everlasting dominion. So their stupidity and unbelief are plain and evident, and so is our knowledge of God. For what follows confirms what has been said:

"And I will make with them," he says [?], "a covenant of peace; it shall be an everlasting covenant with them." Let them, then, show us either the covenant of peace or the everlasting one. But they cannot: they have been deprived of both, while the Master has given us both. He both promised us good things and granted us reconciliation with himself. "For he is our peace," as the divine Apostle says. And again: "There is one mediator, God [?] the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all." And what comes after this again fits those who have been reconciled [?]…

"And I will establish them," he says, "and multiply them, and I will set my holy things in their midst for ever. (27) And my dwelling shall be among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people." And yet the temple is desolate. So [where are?] the [holy things?] in their midst for ever, and his dwelling among them [?]? We do not see these things fulfilled as the Jews understand them, and we know the truth of the spiritual words. Therefore we shall understand these too in keeping with what we have already interpreted, and we also have the evidence of the facts agreeing with us. For not only the holy houses of God

but also the divine altars have been given to all people. They were given not only to those from the Gentiles but also to those from the Jews who have believed, and one and the same God is called the God of both. "For the same Lord," he says, "is Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him." Fittingly he went on: (28) "And the nations shall know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them, when my holy things are in their midst for ever." For in truth the nations too received the light of the knowledge of God through those from the Jews who believed. The divine apostles were from the Jews, and so were the first disciples of the apostles. And the nations learned about Christ our Saviour from the prophetic books kept among the Jews, and so believed the divine preaching. For this reason the divine Apostle said that those from the Gentiles who believe are grafted into the godly root of the Jews, while those from the Jews who disbelieve are broken off and cut away from this root. Since salvation, then, he says, is given first to the Jews, the nations will know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them. For Christ the Master is from the Jews according to the flesh. The cross, the tomb and the resurrection took place among the Jews, and the apostles and the first heralds came from the Jews. Fittingly, then, the nations enjoy salvation through them.

CHAPTER XXXVIII. (1, 2) "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against Gog and the land of Magog, ruler of Rosh, Meshech and Tubal." Gog and Magog are Scythian nations. Meshech, they say, means the Cappadocians, and Tubal the Iberians. In the Hebrew language "Rosh" means "head," and Aquila too rendered "Rosh" as "head" of Meshech. (3, 4) "And say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: [?] ruler of Rosh, Meshech and Tubal. And I will [?] you round about, and I will put a bridle in your jaws, and I will gather you and all your force, horses and horsemen, all clothed in breastplates [?], a great host, all of them with light shields and [?], helmets and swords and shields." He has taught us through these words [?] of the divine working [?]. No such thing happens without the divine will. Either God arranges it for good, or he permits painful things to happen because of earlier

sins. So when he says, "I will put a bridle in your jaws, and gather you," we do not take this as a physical bridle put into the mouth. We understand that Gog and Magog, and all who were with him, were led by the divine nod. He lists their peoples: (5) "For Persians," he says, "and Ethiopians and Lydians and Libyans, and Put with them." Put too was one of the sons of Ham, and he became the forefather of the western Libyans. "All with helmets and light shields": all these had shields, helmets and light shields. (6) "Gomer, and all those around him": this is what he calls the Galatians. "The house of Togarmah": he says these are the Phrygians. "From the far north, and all his supports, and many nations with him." By "supports" he means his subjects, who uphold and sustain the kingdom. (7, 8) "Be prepared, prepare yourself, you and all your host that is gathered to you, and you shall be my guard. After many days you shall be prepared, and at the end of the years you shall come to the land that has been brought back from the sword, gathered from many peoples, to the land of Israel, which had been wholly desolate." The teachers of the Church who have arisen in their times say that these nations made war on Judea after the return from Babylon, and this interpretation agrees with the prophecy. For it says, "You shall come to the land that has been brought back from the sword," that is, rid of its enemies and freed from captivity. And it adds: "gathered from many peoples, to the land of Israel, which had been wholly desolate." They say that these nations were destroyed while Zerubbabel was in command, and that the divine temple was built from the spoils. Poor men and captives would not have had plenty of money. It is also likely that their neighbours, envying the good fortune of the Jews, hired these nations against them. The book of Ezra testifies that these neighbours hindered the building, deceiving now the governors, now the kings of the Persians. To this he adds: "And they have come out from the nations, and all of them dwell in peace." This too makes it clear that the attack of these nations came immediately after the return. For he says, "And they have come out from the nations and dwell in peace." (9) "And you shall come up like

rain, and you shall come like a storm and like a cloud to cover the land; and you shall fall, you and all those around you, and many nations with you." You expect one thing, he says, and will suffer another; you hope for victory and will be handed over to destruction. Then he describes Gog's reasonings too. (10–12) "Thoughts shall come up," he says, "into your heart, and you shall devise evil schemes, and say: I will go up against a land that has been cast off. I will come upon peaceful peoples living quietly in the land, where there is no wall, nor gates, nor bars, to take spoil and seize their plunder, to turn my hand against the desolate land that has been resettled, against a nation gathered from many nations, who have acquired possessions and property, who dwell at the navel of the earth." All this teaches us that it happened after the captivity, when, as the prophecy says, the cities of Judea had neither walls nor gates nor bars. That is why the nations mentioned dared to campaign against them. After the return the Israelite people had become famous, since they had obtained their return through divine power. Just as the exodus from Egypt had given them great renown, so the return from Babylon made them illustrious and admired, and that is why these nations dared to campaign against them. Let no one think the prophecy implausible because of the great distance between the Scythian nations and Judea. Let him consider that in our own times too this nation overran the whole East and went away having enslaved a vast multitude. He says that the Phrygians and Galatians, Iberians and Persians and Ethiopians campaigned with Gog, not as his subjects but as mixed in with him in various ways. Some had deserted and joined the campaign willingly, while others had been taken captive and forced to fight alongside him. To this the divine word also adds a speech in the person of the other nations: (13) "For Sheba," he says, "and Dedan, the merchants of Tarshish, and all their villages shall say to you: Have you come for plunder, to take plunder and seize spoil? Have you assembled your people to take silver and gold, to carry off possessions and property, to take great spoil?" Sheba, as has already been said, is an Ethiopian and Indian nation. Dedan lies near Idumea, though there is also another Dedan in Ethiopia. Tarshish is Carthage. These things, he says…

(14–16) "Therefore prophesy, son of man, and say to Gog: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Is it not on that day, when my people Israel are settled in peace, that you will know and be roused? And you shall come from your place in the far north, you and many nations with you, all of them riding horses, a great host and a mighty force. And you shall come up against my people Israel like a cloud to cover the land." "It shall be in the last days": that is, after the return of Israel. He said this above as well: "When my people are settled in peace, you will know and be roused." The blessed Moses said something similar: "I will show them what will happen in the last of days, for it is a perverse generation." By "the last of days" he means not the end of the world but the time when their dispersion took place. "And I will bring you up against my land, so that all the nations may know me, when I am sanctified in you before them, O Gog." The nations do not now need Gog to teach them about the God of all, for they received this knowledge through Christ the Master. But long ago, before the Lord became man, they needed such wonders [?]. When [?] lost those many thousands in Judea, the nations recognized the God of all through the wonder. That is why the blessed David cries out: "God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel." And when these nations were destroyed in Judea, all people learned the power of the God of all and moved their tongues to sing hymns. That is why he says: "so that all the nations may know me, when I am sanctified in you," that is, when I am glorified, once my power has become evident. (17) "Thus says Adonai the Lord to Gog: You are the one of whom I spoke in former days by the hand of my servants the prophets of Israel, who prophesied in those days and years, that I would bring you up against [?]…" [?] other prophets foretold things about these nations. For Hosea says: "And I will make a covenant for them on that day with the beasts of the field, and with the birds of the sky, and with the creeping things of the earth; and I will break bow and sword and war from the land, and I will make you dwell in hope." And Joel says: "Behold, I, in those days and at that

time, when I turn back the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, I will gather all the nations and bring them down into the Valley of Jehoshaphat, and there I will enter into judgment with them on behalf of my people and my inheritance Israel." Micah speaks thus: "Be in labour and be strong, daughter of Zion, like a woman giving birth. For now you shall go out of the city and camp in the open field, and you shall come as far as Babylon; from there the Lord your God will rescue you from the hand of your enemies. And now many nations have gathered against you, saying: We shall gloat, and our eyes shall look upon Zion. But they did not know the thought of the Lord, nor understand his counsel, that he has gathered them like sheaves on the threshing floor. Arise and thresh them, daughter of Zion, for I will make your horns iron and your hooves bronze. You shall beat down nations among them and crush many peoples, and you shall dedicate their multitude to the Lord, and their strength to the Lord of all the earth." And Zechariah says: "This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel: Not by great might, nor by strength, but by my Spirit, says the Lord Almighty. Who are you, O great mountain, before Zerubbabel, that you should prosper [?]?" From these passages it is clear that these nations made war after the return and were destroyed by the divine hand. (18, 19) "And it shall be on that day, on whatever day Gog comes against the land of Israel, says Adonai the Lord, that my wrath shall rise up in my anger, and my jealousy in the fire of my anger. I have spoken: on that day there shall be a great earthquake upon the land of Israel." He calls the greatness of the event an earthquake. For just as we all feel an earthquake with fear, so too we receive the knowledge of great wonders. Yet it is not unlikely that an actual earthquake also took place when the punishment was brought on the ungodly and savage invaders. We shall understand the wrath, the anger, the jealousy and the fire of anger in a way that befits God. He has used these human terms to point to the punishment.
