He says that from fear of what happens not only people will be shaken, but also the fish and the birds [?] … will be broken apart [?], the ravines will be filled in, and the walls torn down. From this it is clear that he truly meant an earthquake when he spoke of an earthquake. For an earthquake brings fear not only on rational beings but also on irrational ones. It splits mountains apart, so that the ravines are blocked up by the pieces broken off. It tears down walls, buries cities, and [?]… (21) "And I will summon against him the fear of the sword [?] on all my mountains, says Adonai the Lord." When the earthquake has come first, he says, [I will bring?] cowardice upon them [?]… [Joel 3:1, 2. Micah 4:10, 13. Zech. [?]]

and fear of their enemies, so that, taking to flight, they will [fail to recognize one another?] and be killed by [one another?]. He made this clear by saying: "[?] each man's sword shall be against his brother. (22) And I will judge him with death and blood." Not only will they be destroyed by one another, he says, but I too will fight against them from above. "With torrential rain and hailstones, and fire and brimstone, I will rain upon him and upon all who are with him. And I will be magnified and glorified and sanctified, and I will make myself known before many nations, and they shall know that I am the Lord." For when these have been handed over to destruction, those who until then did not know me will recognize my power and will worship my [?]…

Then he again commands the prophet to prophesy against Gog and against the nations with him: they will come from the far north by God's permission, to pay a penalty worthy of their savagery. He also describes the weakness that will come upon them. (3, 4) "For I will knock your bow out of your left hand," he says, "and your arrows out of your right hand. And I will cast you down on the mountains of Israel, and you shall fall, you and all those around you, and the many nations with you." I will break your strength, he says, so that the weapons you carry fall from your hands. To this he adds that they will be given as food to the birds of the sky and to the flesh-eating beasts. And the words (6) "I will send fire upon Gog, and the islands shall be inhabited in peace, and they shall know that my name is the Lord" show that, once Gog has suffered that total destruction, not only the people of the mainland but also the islanders will take courage, for they had been afraid when they heard of that army's campaign. (7) "And my holy name," he says, "shall be known in the midst of Israel, and my holy name shall no longer be profaned." And he gives the reason: "And the nations shall know that I am the Lord, the Holy One in the midst of Israel." For once the nations have learned the power of my providence and how I defend the people who bear my name, they will no longer accuse me of weakness, nor think that my people's earlier captivity happened because I was powerless. Then he [confirms] the certainty of what has been said:

(8) "Behold, it has come, and you shall know that it will be, says Adonai the Lord." Consider these things already done, he says, and hold an unquestioning faith in them as in things that have happened, for what I have foretold will certainly come to pass. "This is the day of which I spoke." I have often spoken beforehand of this day, he says. By "day" he means the time of Gog's punishment. Then he teaches that all Israel will use the enemy's weapons instead of firewood: spears and bows and arrows, large shields and light shields, and staves. They will not need to cut wood, for these weapons will be enough for their needs for seven years. In this way too he points to the size of the enemy host. He also foretells the tomb that Gog will have. (11) "For it shall be on that day," he says, "that I will give Gog a famous place, a tomb in Israel, the mass grave of those who came from the east of the sea." Where they buried those who came against them from the eastern regions, he says, there they will bury him too. By this he reminds them of the slaughter of the Assyrians under Sennacherib: they enjoyed his help then, and they would receive his providential care afterwards as well. Because of the great number of the dead, he says, "they shall wall up the mouth of the ravine and bury there Gog and all his multitude, and it shall be called the Valley of the Mass Grave of Gog." For the number of the slain, he says, will be so great that no man-made pit could hold them. The deepest ravine will become their tomb, walled in on both sides and heaped over from above. Seven months, he says, will be spent on this burial, and they will make the day of Gog's total destruction a day to be remembered. "For it shall be a name for them, the day on which I am glorified, says Adonai the Lord." Moreover, he says, they will set men apart to go round the land and bury those who met their death while fleeing. (15) "And they shall search, everyone who passes through the land and travels about; and whoever sees a human bone shall set up a marker beside it, until the buriers bury it in the Valley of the Mass Grave of Gog." For a long time, he says, they will go round giving burial to the unburied. And if travellers find a bone anywhere, they will heap up stones over it and so point it out to those charged with the burying, so that these remains too may be gathered and given the customary rites. (16) "And the name of the place shall be called

[Notes on variant readings:] "for a name … I am glorified": Aquila reads "famous, on the day on which he was glorified." "They shall search": Theodotion [?] reads "they shall pass through." "And … shall be called": A [?] reads "For indeed the name of the city."

…a downfall and a common burial ground, and the land shall be cleansed.” Having foretold these things, he summons the birds and the beasts to come as if to a banquet and a feast, since many bodies, indeed countless ones, have been cast out. He does not give this command to them as rational beings. He does it to convince the rational that these things too happen with his permission. The words “You shall eat the flesh of calves, and rams, and lambs, and goats, and bulls, all of them fattened” he spoke figuratively. By calves, rams, goats and bulls he named their kings, rulers and champions, and by lambs he meant their subjects. He has called their destruction, which came about by his decision, his sacrifice. (20) “And you shall be filled,” he says, “at my table,” that is, with the food I have set before you. And to show what this food is, he added: “horse and rider, and giant, and every man of war, says the Lord Adonai.” With these words he explained the rams, the bulls and the goats. (21) “And I will set my glory among you, and all the nations shall see my judgment which I have carried out, and my hand which I have brought upon them.” When the slaughter has taken place, he says, and such a feast has been set before you, all the nations will see both the power of my providence and the justice of my judgment. And the house of Israel too, he says, will learn from these very events that I am their Lord and Master. The phrase “from this day and onward” accuses them of their former ignorance. (23, 24) “And all the nations shall know that the house of Israel was taken captive because of their sins, because they rebelled against me. So I turned my face away from them and handed them over into the hands of their nations [?], and they all fell by the sword. I dealt with them according to their uncleannesses and according to their transgressions, and I turned my face away from them.” When the nations see the destruction brought upon Gog, he says, they will know that I could have inflicted this same punishment on the Babylonians too. But I was making Israel pay the penalty for its impiety and lawlessness, so I allowed them to be enslaved and granted them no help. This also teaches us clearly that the uprising of these nations took place immediately after the return. (“For all the nations,” he says, “shall know that the whole house of Israel was taken captive because of their sins.”) Everyone who sees the wholesale destruction of those peoples and reasons soundly will understand that the Israelites endured that captivity as the penalty for their sins. What follows also bears witness to this:

(25–27) “Therefore thus says the Lord Adonai: Now I will turn back the captivity of Jacob and have mercy on the house of Israel, and I will be jealous for my holy name. And they shall bear their dishonor and all the wrongs they committed against me, when they dwell on their own land in peace with no one to make them afraid, when I bring them back from the nations and lead them out of their lands.” The words “They shall bear their lawlessness and all the wrongs they committed against me” mean this: through the miseries they endured they will come to understand that they brought these things on themselves, and that their wrongdoing was the cause of their dishonor. They will reason in this way, he says, once they have returned to their own land and been freed from these harsh enemies. For then “I shall be sanctified among them before the nations.” That is: once my power has become manifest, I shall receive worship from all, because of the [?] I have shown toward these people.

(28) “And they shall know that I am the Lord their God, when I appear to them among the nations.” For through my providence they will be freed from the domination of the Babylonians, and they will see the destruction of the Scythian nations. “And I will gather them into their own land, and I will no longer leave any of them there.” This too came to pass, as far as divine care was concerned. But those who were used to resisting the divine laws did not want to return, and the majority preferred a foreign land to the land of their fathers. (29) “And I will no longer turn my face away from them, because I have poured out my wrath on the house of Israel, says the Lord Adonai.” This too depends on human will. For it is up to us to bring good promises to fulfillment. In the same way the Master has promised us the kingdom of heaven, but we shall not attain it if we live unworthily. If we are diligent and keep the divine laws with all eagerness, we shall certainly enjoy the promised blessings. So too he promised the Jews that he would not turn his face away from them, provided, clearly, that they obeyed him, believed, and kept the divine laws. History bears witness that this is so. When he led the people out of Egypt, he promised to bring them into the promised land. But since they kept resisting the divine decrees and went on living in impiety, he handed them all over to death in the desert. Of all those who had received the promises, he fulfilled them for only two. Here too, then, those who have believed and received the saving proclamation hold the promise securely, for he has not turned

his face away from them. But those who act against the divine will are somewhere far from God's watchful care and enjoy no providence. Instead, as the prophet Isaiah says, they are “walking in the light of their fire and in the flame they have kindled,” and, as the divine David says, they will walk “in their own devices.” This is how divine Scripture has taught us to understand these things. But I am amazed at the folly not only of the Jews but also of some who bear the Christian name and yet listen to Jewish fables. They say that the uprising of Gog and Magog has not yet happened and expect it in the future. They ought to have seen, first, that this prophecy is joined to the recall from Babylon, and second, that he said the nations would learn the power of God through these events. Let them tell us: what teaching do the nations need now in order to recognize the divine power? They have been taught to believe in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, they have learned to glorify and worship the divine nature, and they have been freed from the error of idols. And what teaching could the destruction of Gog have offered to compare with what the preaching of the holy apostles contains? That preaching teaches all people about the Trinity and the unity, and that in the one nature we contemplate three properties. It teaches besides the resurrection of the dead, the judgment, the repayment of good and of its opposite, the kingdom of heaven, the punishment in Gehenna, the lessons of virtue, the precepts of the philosophic life, and everything else that the divine Gospel and the sacred writings of the apostles contain. The destruction of Gog, however, taught the nations only that the God of the Jews has very great power, and that the Jews fell under the Babylonians because of their own lawlessness, not because of any weakness of his. So if the events concerning Gog have not yet happened but will happen in the last days, and if through him the nations will learn to worship the God of all, then the events concerning Gog are greater than the saving cross, greater than the death that destroyed death, and greater than the divine apostles, who lit up the world with the light of the knowledge of God. On that view, all these things could not teach the nations about the God of all, and the destruction of Gog alone will make him known to everyone! So plainly do those who tell these fables Judaize. We, however, have followed divine Scripture in giving the interpretation set out above, and we teach that Gog has come and that the events concerning him have reached their end. At that time the nations learned that the Jews endured captivity because of their own lawlessness, not because of any divine weakness. But at present, through the Master’s death and resurrection, the [?] of the knowledge of God

(1) “And it came to pass in the twenty-fifth year of our captivity, in the first month, on the tenth day of the month, in the fourteenth year after the city was taken.” From this it is clear that the prophet shared the captivity of King Jeconiah. After him Zedekiah reigned for eleven years less a few months, and the city was taken in the eleventh year of Zedekiah’s reign. So he rightly said that the fourteenth year after the capture of the city was the twenty-fifth year of their captivity. “On that very day the hand of the Lord came upon me. (2) And he brought me there in a vision of God. He brought me into the land of Israel and set me on a very high mountain, and on it, opposite, was something like the structure of a city.” The God of all had foretold to them their return from captivity and had shown his power through the resurrection of those dry bones. Now he also foretells the rebuilding of the city and the temple. He does not use words alone; he also shows the prophet a vision of this kind, having lit up the eye of his mind by the working of the divine Spirit. We do not want to weary the readers of this book with a long discussion by interpreting each detail, so we shall give a summary paraphrase of what was shown in the Spirit to the inspired prophet. He says, then, that “in a vision of God,” that is, in a spiritual and not a bodily sight, his mind was carried off to the land of Israel. On a high mountain he saw a building and someone standing there. This figure had human form, but its colour was that of the most brilliant and beautiful bronze. It carried a reed and a builder’s line, and it urged me both to look at what was being shown

and to listen to what was being said. For he said that he had come for this very purpose, to show and to teach: “So that you too,” he says, “may convey these things to the house of Israel.” Then, measuring with the reed, he showed me all the measurements of the building. First came the measurements of the gates, and of what are called the thresholds and lintels, and the doorposts. He calls the doorpost ail in the singular and ailamoth in the plural. Again, he calls the threshold and the lintel thee, and theeim is the plural of the same. This is how I found these words interpreted in the Syriac. He says that he saw not only the outer gates but also the inner ones, as well as the courts between them and those further in. Some were set apart for the priests, while others were open to all Israelites. The divine temple had a single enclosure all around it, very large and very high. Inside it the open space was divided by further walls. Some areas were assigned to all the people, while the inner ones next to the temple itself were consecrated to the priests alone. He says, then, that in the inner court he saw chambers and thirty colonnades. The Syriac called the chambers “exedras.” These too were set apart for the priests, as the prophet himself teaches. God says to the inspired Isaiah: “Go into the chamber to Shebna the scribe.” He says that a width of a hundred cubits was assigned to the outer courts, to the one facing north, to the one facing south, and likewise to the one facing the rising sun. Each of the inner courts was twenty-five cubits long and fifty cubits wide. He also says that the gates resembled one another in every respect, both in their measurements and in their carvings of palm trees. He calls the cornices or mouldings on either side of the door aileu, and he said the images of palm trees were carved on them. He says he also saw tables set on either side of the gates. On these the priests laid the victims and slaughtered them, both the whole burnt offerings and those offered for sin and for ignorance. Nearby, he said, there was a channel that received the blood of the sacrifices and no doubt carried it away to some remote spot. The tables, he says, also had roofs covering them from above, which kept off the rain and the sun. After this he relates that he saw two exedras, one facing north and the other south, both built in the inner courts. The one facing south, he said, was assigned to the priests who keep the divine temple, and the one facing north to those who keep the outer altar. He said that both groups traced their descent from Zadok, for long ago the God of all had put an end to the priesthood of

Abiathar’s line, in accordance with the sentence pronounced against Eli the high priest. He says that the inner court, which faced the rising sun, measured a hundred cubits from the porch of the divine temple to the gate, and was the same in width. The altar stood opposite the temple. The porch of the temple was twenty cubits long and fourteen wide. Its door was likewise fourteen cubits wide, and the jambs or pilasters on either side of it, up to the corner, were three cubits each. This makes up the measure of twenty cubits: the door takes fourteen, and the jambs on either side (he called these “shoulders”) take the other six, three on this side and three on that. The door of the temple itself, he said, was ten cubits wide, and the jambs on either side were five cubits each, so that once again the total is twenty cubits. He also measured the temple itself, he says, and showed me that it was forty cubits long and twenty wide, the same width as the porch. “I also saw,” he says, “another, inner door, six cubits wide, with jambs of seven cubits on either side.” So fourteen cubits added to six again make twenty. He says that he also saw the doors that separate the Holy of Holies from the Holy Place. Their width was equal to that of the temple, that is, twenty cubits, and their height was forty cubits. But when I looked up the measurements in both the Syriac and the Hebrew, I found the height equal to the width. Both the Syriac and the Hebrew agreed in giving twenty cubits for the width and the height alike. He says he also saw a double structure around the temple, with further walls built outside the roof [?], and a walkway and passage running around between the two walls. He also gives the reason for this construction: “So that no one,” he says, “may come near the walls of the temple.” This narrow circuit, he said, was divided into lower and upper storeys. It had windows that were narrow on the outside and wider on the inside, the kind we usually call slanted. “And I saw,” he says, “two more exedras on either side of the divine temple, one facing north and the other south.” He called this “prayer,” because the Jews who live north of Jerusalem customarily face south when they pray, in keeping with where the city lies. He says that five cubits separated the divine temple from the so-called exedra, and that from the western wall to the exedra itself was seventy cubits, with a width of ninety. In the middle, he says, stood the divine temple, entirely covered with boards: not only the walls but also the floor and the ceiling. It also had latticed windows,

that is, pierced through like a net. The carvings on the [?] … on the walls and on the doorposts bore likenesses of cherubim and palm trees. Each cherub had two faces, one of a lion and one of a man, and one face looked toward this palm tree, the other toward that one. He saw two faces carved instead of four because it was not possible to carve four faces precisely on boards. He says he also saw the altar in front of the [holy place?]. It was three cubits high, two cubits long and the same in width, that is, a square with equal sides. “I was taught by the one who was showing me these things that this was the table that stands before the Lord.” It should be noted that he called the table that holds the loaves of presentation an altar, whereas the great Moses called it only a table. In this way the prophecy opens a door in advance for our own usage. And the door of the holy place, he says, was not two-leaved [?] but four-leaved, so that when opened the leaves folded back on themselves, and they had the same carvings. He says he also saw other exedras in the outer court, with a walkway in front of them ten cubits wide and a hundred long. By “the light of the walkway” he means what we call a skylight. He said that these rooms too were set apart for the priests, for eating the consecrated food. The one who showed him these things gave instructions that no one should share with the priests the right to enter them. Nor should the priests themselves go out into the outer court while wearing the priestly vestment and performing the divine liturgy. For none of the people may lawfully touch them while they wear the priestly vestment. They must therefore take off the clothing reserved for the services in those rooms, put on other clothes, and only then go out to the people. “He also showed me the circuit,” he says, “using the measure. By measuring it he taught me that each of the four sides, east, west, south and north, was five hundred cubits, so that the circuit, five hundred taken four times, comes to two thousand cubits.”

CHAPTER 43. (1, 2) “And he led me,” he says, “to the gate that faces east, and he brought me out. And behold, the glory of the God of Israel was coming by the way of the east, and the sound of the camp was like the sound of many redoubling their cry [?].” In the Hebrew and in the Syriac I found “like the sound of many waters.” “And the earth shone like a radiance from his glory all around.”

(3) “And the vision that I saw was like the vision I saw when I went in to anoint the city.” Here again I found in both the Syriac and the Hebrew: “when I came to destroy the city.” He is referring to the second vision. In it he saw those who carried axes and struck down the city, and the one who scattered the coals over the whole city, and he also saw the mark placed on those who groaned over the transgressions of the people. The Seventy probably paid attention to the sense and so called the marking of the foreheads “anointing.” Those who were marked were spared the punishment carried out by the slayers. “And the vision of the chariot was like the vision I saw by the river Chobar.” At once

“I fell,” he says. (4) “And the glory of the Lord entered the house by the way of the gate that faces east.” He did not say that the Lord entered, for the divine nature cannot be contained in any place. He said that the glory of the Lord entered, that is, the vision that was seen. (5, 6) “And the Spirit took me up and brought me into the inner court, and behold, the house of the Lord was full of glory. And I stood, and behold, there was a voice from the house of one speaking to me.” When blessed Moses set up the tabernacle, the glory of the Lord filled it. When Solomon had finished building the temple and celebrated the feast of its dedication, the glory of the Lord likewise filled the house. So now that this building too has been shown, the Master must appear and fill the house with his own glory. In this way he shows that it will not only be built but also filled with divine power. “And the man was standing beside me.” This showed that it was an angel who had measured the building and shown it to him. It was probably the holy Michael, since the care of the people had been entrusted to him. (7) “And he said to me” (not the angel, but the Master): “Son of man, you have seen the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet.” In the same way blessed David calls the divine temple God’s footstool: “Worship at the footstool of his feet,” he says, “for he is holy.” He called it the place of his throne because he rests upon it. Then he adds: “In which my name shall dwell in the midst of the house of Israel forever.” He did not say “dwelt” but “shall dwell.” And it shall dwell forever in the midst of the saints and of those who are truly Israel

…who are so named and are able to see him, as far as it is possible for a human being to see: not in the type, but in the truth. That was the place of the heavenly things. “For see,” he says, “that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.” The promise, then, is not false; for Christ the Master also confirmed it when he said to the holy apostles: “In my Father's house there are many dwelling places; if it were not so, I would have told you, for I go to prepare a place for you. And I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you may be also.” So in the type God neither dwelt nor will he dwell for ever; for he passed sentence on them, saying: “Behold, your house is left to you desolate.” It is right, then, to rise from the types to the truth and to await that dwelling of God. And what follows agrees with the interpretation already given. “And the house of Israel shall no longer profane my holy name,” he says, “they and their leaders, by their fornication and by the transgressions of their leaders in their midst.” If anyone takes this simply as referring to Israel, he will find it false; for Ezra accuses them of great impiety even after the return, and so does the history of the Maccabees, and not only of the other Israelites but also of the priests and high priests. And what excess of impiety does their frenzy against the Master leave out? So these words too do not apply simply to Israel, but to those who keep the eye of the mind pure, who are able to see God, and who embrace spiritual worship. 8. “When they set my threshold by their thresholds,” he says, “and my [?] next to their doorposts, and made my wall as though joined both to me and to them, they profaned my holy name by the lawless deeds that they did.” Throughout he teaches that not even to them was the divine temple regarded as holy, so that they did in it everything they did in their own houses. That is why he says: “And I consumed them in my wrath and in slaughter.” I exacted punishment from them, he says, for their lawlessness, and handed them over to slaughter. Then he urges them to leave their former way and to be rid of impiety, both they and their leaders; and he promises that, if this is done, he will dwell in their midst for ever. And they would have obtained the promises if they had received the Master when he came to them. But since, on seeing him, they said to one another, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours,” those, for their part, out of the [?]

vineyard he cast out and scattered throughout the world, and he leased the vineyard to other tenants, with whom he dwells for ever, receiving the fruits from them in their season. Then he commands the prophet to show the people the building of the temple, so that, put to shame by the greatness of the benefit and by the hope of being recalled, they might stop sinning and acting impiously. And he was ordered not only to sketch and draw out the building for the people, but also to show them its ordinances and statutes, so that by keeping these they might serve the Master. He says that he also saw the altar of incense, two cubits high, a cubit long, and of equal breadth. He says too that he saw two mercy seats, not of the same size, but one smaller and the other larger. We must ask why, when blessed Moses made one mercy seat according to the divine command, the prophet sees two here. I think the small one is a type of the larger; for the Old Testament is a type of the New, and that mercy seat a type of our mercy seat. And Christ is our mercy seat, as the divine Apostle says: “whom God put forward as a mercy seat in his own blood, to show his righteousness.” He also says that between the two mercy seats there were four cubits, equal in number to the divine Gospels; for between the law and the good things hoped for, the grace of the Gospels was given to humankind. 16. “And the Ariel,” he says, “twelve cubits long, and the breadth equal.” In the Hebrew language Ariel means “mountain of God,” or, by another interpretation, “light of God”; and by this name, I think, he calls the base of the mercy seat. This number of cubits also corresponds to the holy apostles, who became the bases and steps of divine grace, and the foundation and groundwork of the Church. “For you are Peter,” said the Lord, “and on this rock I will build my Church.” And again: “You are the light of the world.” The mercy seat itself he says is two cubits greater than the Ariel, both in length and in breadth; for not only in his divinity but also in the humanity he assumed, the Master is greater than his servants by an infinite measure. Then the God of all commands the prophet to teach the priests the laws about the sacrifices: how they must bring the calf for sin and sacrifice it, and where it should be disposed of, and how they must sprinkle the horns of the altar and the corners of the mercy seat; then that they should bring the goats for sin, free from every blemish, and again in the same way sprinkle the altar with the blood. And so, he says,

when these things are done and the atonement for sin has been completed, they shall offer a calf and a ram, these too free from blemish, and complete the sacrifice with salt. Salt is a token of reason, discernment and a devout mind; for they will not do these things carelessly or as slaves to habit, but with a reason and with a purpose that has chosen piety. They shall make such sacrifices, he says, for seven days; and from the eighth day onward, such sacrifices, so that not each

Chapter 44. He also showed me the gate facing east, shut, and charged that it should remain shut continually and be reserved for the Master of all himself. This was not because he who is present everywhere and stands by all things needed a door when he wished to enter. For how could he have entered while it was shut, if it were his nature to enter through doors? Rather, he lays these things out in this way, coming down to the level of weaker hearers. And it is likely that by these words we are also given a hint of the virgin womb, through which no one has entered or come out except the Master alone. He also commanded that the leader, that is, the high priest, should eat his food by the gate, and should pass through the porch both going out and coming in; for this is what he called the ailam. When these things had been both spoken and shown, he again sees the glory of God at the north gate, and is ordered to tell the embittering people (or “the contentious and quarrelsome,” for so the other translators rendered it) to be content with their former lawlessness, which they persisted in daring, bringing foreigners and uncircumcised people into the divine temple. And the greatest of the charges was that not only did they have the flesh uncircumcised, but, before the flesh, the mind. So it is clear that circumcision of the heart is the attainment of righteousness, while circumcision of the flesh is a sign and seal of the circumcision of the mind. The God of all therefore charges that those uncircumcised in soul, and those foreign and alien in body, should stay far from the divine precincts; and that the Levites who shared in the people's lawlessness and embraced the worship of idols should be removed from their proper rank, and should neither keep the gates nor slaughter the whole burnt offering and the sacrifice for sin, nor approach the holy things, but should reap dishonor as the fruit of their own impiety; and that only the line of Zadok, which had remained in the piety of their fathers, should minister, keep guard, and fulfil all the other duties. It is fitting for them, he says, never to use woven woollen garments, but to wear only linen clothing at the time of their ministry; and let each put a turban on his head, and let undergarments be worn underneath.

When they go out to the people, let them take off their liturgical vestments and go out through the gates wearing other clothes; for it is not right for anyone outside the priesthood to come near the priestly vestments. Nor shall they shave their heads, for it was the custom of the priests of idols to do this. “And they shall not make their hair bare.” The Hebrew and the Syriac said, “they shall not let it grow.” For it is not fitting for them, he says, either to be shaved or to let their hair grow long, but to keep to a moderate cut; this is what he meant when he said, “Covering they shall cover their heads.” At the time of their ministry they must abstain from drinking wine. And when they wish to marry, they must take neither a widow nor a divorced woman, but a virgin. But if a woman who had been a priest's wife were widowed and someone wished to marry her, not even such a marriage is unlawful; for the priestly line remains untouched, since a woman who was joined to a priest is again joined to a priest. They must also teach the people the difference between the common and the holy. They themselves shall judge cases of bloodshed and settle other disputes, honoring justice everywhere. And let them keep the feasts according to the law, and honor the Sabbaths with rest and in other ways. “And they shall not go near a human soul so as to be defiled,” that is, near a dead body; for so the Hebrew and the Syriac said; “but only,” he says, “for father and mother, son and daughter, brother, and a sister not yet married.” Then he directs how the unclean person must be purified and so approach the ministry. This was not because it was truly abominable to look at the dead; for if it really defiled, the sight of a dead father or mother or brother would also have done harm. Rather, by these means he wished the priest to be held in greater reverence among the Jews, who had learned to make much of small things. Then he orders the priest, when he is about to enter the holy place, to offer the sacrifice for himself, and not to take a portion with the sons of Israel in the division of the land. “For I,” he says, “am their inheritance and their possession.” For the firstborn that are offered to me, and the firstfruits, I give them to enjoy, and the portions set apart from the sacrifices I have in turn assigned to them. For I have need of nothing.

Chapter 45. He also orders some land to be set apart as an estate for the priests: from the rising sun toward the west, ten thousand cubits, and from north to south, twenty-five thousand; so that, he says, having the tithes, the firstfruits, the firstborn, the set-apart portions of the sacrifices, and the support from the land, they may be content with what is just and not covet more, nor wrong the people, since they enjoy a sufficiency. Therefore

9. “Let it suffice you, rulers of Israel: cast away injustice and misery, and do judgment and righteousness, and remove oppression from my people, says the Lord Adonai.” Then he lays down laws about balances, weights and measures, and says that these too must be respected with fairness and justice, and he commands that there be one measure for receiving and for paying out. And he teaches us that the kor holds ten gomor, and each gomor ten choenixes, so that the kor is a hundred choenixes. And he says that the oiphi is equal to the choenix. He commands that the mina have fifty shekels, and each shekel twenty obols; and he calls the ten kotylai of oil a gomor, which he said was a tenth of the kor. He orders that the firstfruits offered from wheat and barley be a sixth of the gomor, which among us is called a half-medimnus; for since the kor is thirty medimni, and the gomor has been called a tenth of the kor, the gomor must be three medimni, and a sixth of three medimni is a half-medimnus. He also commanded that one kotyle out of ten be offered, and likewise the tithes of the sheep. All these, he says, the people shall give to the leader for the needs of the sacrifices, so that at the feasts, the new moons and the Sabbaths the sacred rites may be performed by him and God may be propitiated for the people. Then he teaches what should be done at the new moon of the tenth month, and what on the fourteenth, and again in the seventh month. He calls the offering of fine flour a sacrifice: “For you shall make a sacrifice,” he says, “a cake for the calf and a cake for the ram, and a hin of oil for the cake.” The hin I found rendered in the Syriac as a hemina.

Chapter 46. He orders that the gate facing east be shut on the six days of the week, but on the Sabbath be open all day long. While the priests offer the sacrifices on behalf of the high priest, he says, he himself shall stand at this gate, and while the sacrifice is being offered he shall stand at the threshold and worship, and then go out; and all the people shall offer worship to God before this door on the Sabbaths and at the new moons; and the high priest shall offer the whole burnt offering of the Sabbaths. He calls him the leader. He also states the number of the [?]; and likewise he teaches what must be offered at the new moons. He calls the offering of fine flour manaa; for so the Syriac too [?] … and those who enter the [?] court [?] the worship of God [?] … if they entered by the north gate, to go out by the one facing south; and if from there [?]

they made their entrance, to make their exit through the other, so that, entering and leaving in order, they might offer worship to God without any disturbance; and let the high priest be present while this is done, so that the worship may take place with greater reverence. He commanded that the door facing east be opened for all the people on the Sabbaths and on the other feasts; and if the high priest wishes to offer God a freewill sacrifice out of his abundance, on whatever day he wishes to perform the sacrifice, let him be allowed, he says, to open the door. For let the sacrifice he offers, he says, be like the sacrifice of the Sabbaths. If he wishes to give one of his sons some of the land set apart for him, the one who receives it, he says, shall hold ownership of it permanently; but if it is given to a servant, let the servant hold ownership until the year of release, and in the so-called seventh year he shall return the inheritance to the high priest; for this allotment has been set apart for the priestly line alone. For it is not right that, with the sons deprived and stripped of their ancestral inheritance, the injustice should pass to the people, with other land again being set apart for the priests to make up for it. So let the line be heir to the land set apart for the priests. He also showed me, he says, another place lying to the west, next to the northern chambers, and said that it was set apart for the priests for boiling, so that they might boil there the offerings for ignorance and sin, and bake the manaa there. For it is not right, he says, to make common what has once been set apart and sanctified by carrying it outside. I also saw other courts smaller than that one, set around the greatest court; each was thirty cubits long and forty wide; and beside them were built [?] houses, which he called chambers, in which he directed that the people's sacrifices be boiled.

Chapter 47. 1. “From there he took me again and brought me to the doorway of the house, and behold, water was coming out from under the court of the house toward the east, for the front of the house faced east; and the water was going down from the right side of the house, from the south, to the altar.” Having been taught in this way about the sacrifices, and having learned how the offerings for sins must be offered as types, he is taught the true cleansing of souls, which comes about through water and the Spirit. He sees this water coming out from the doors of the house, passing through the altar, and moving through the more northern parts toward the east. For salvation came to the nations from the Jews, and Christ, who according to the flesh was from David, appearing from the virgin womb as from a kind of divine doorway, has bestowed on the world rebirth through water and the Spirit. Blessed Isaiah also foretells this, saying: “It shall be in that day like a glorious river

flowing in a thirsty land.” And blessed Zechariah, having foretold the saving passion and the darkness that came upon it — “For it is not day,” he says, “and not night, and that day is known to the Lord” (for it was neither full day, he says, nor full night, since darkness came at midday) — went on: “In that day living water shall go out from Jerusalem, half of it to the last sea, and half of it to the first sea.” By these he indicates the east and the west, by which the whole world is meant. He also states the time when it will gush forth: “In summer and in spring it shall be so.” The Lord too says this to the Samaritan woman: “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again, but the water that I will give him will become a spring of water welling up to eternal life.” And elsewhere: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” This is the water that the inspired Ezekiel saw issuing from the doorway of the house — for our good things were foretold through the law and the prophets — and coming through the altar; for it merely passed through the Jews on its way. But since in their unbelief they refused to yield the fruits of faith, it went over to the nations, and it waters the greatest and most beautiful paradise of the churches. Then he says that he saw someone measure a thousand with the measure and pass through it up to the ankles; then measure the same amount again and pass through up to the knees; and apply the measure a third time and pass through up to the waist; but when he completed the fourth count, it became, he says, a very great torrent, which could not be crossed, because the water was surging like the rush of a torrent that no one will cross. By these things he has taught us that at first the preaching of the gospel would bring few to salvation; then it would double and triple them; and after this it would fill the world, according to the prophecy that says: “The whole earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant water covers the seas.” It should be noted that he measured four times, and applied a measure equal in number to the divine Gospels. I think the fourth measure points to the Gospel of the inspired John, which contains a theology impassable and insurmountable for human beings. For what mind could go beyond “In the beginning”? And who could get past “was”? That is why he said that the water came out surging like the rush of a torrent that no one will cross. At once, he says, and immediately he showed me, along the bank of the water, trees laden with fruits of every kind. These trees were on both banks; for not

…this water has made people bring forth not only faith in God but also action in keeping with God. "And he said to me," he says, "This water of the river, which goes out into Galilee toward the east, and goes down into the uninhabited land, and comes as far as the sea, to the water of the sea's outlet." These things too can be found exactly in history. For the saving preaching first ran into Galilee; from there it went into the uninhabited land of the nations, empty of piety. It reached also the surging sea, the races of the barbarians [?]. He adds that it will also sanctify the waters: for it will make the Greek and mythical teachings serve the divine preaching, and those diseased waters, sanctified through these waters, will become givers of health. 9. "And it shall be that every living soul of the creatures that swarm, upon everything to which the river comes there, shall live." For everyone, he says, who enjoys the saving waters will obtain salvation. He says also that this water will become full of fish and will have many fishermen; for many are those caught for salvation through these waters, and many also those entrusted with this hunt. The phrase "from Engaddi to Enaglim" signifies the joy that comes after temptations and afflictions. For Engaddi means "testing of the eyes", and Enaglim "the eye of a calf" offered in sacrifice and loosing sin, or drawn under the yoke and entrusted with farming. And "drying-place of nets" signifies not only the number of the fishermen but also their diligence. For they will not give up fishing, he says, but will rest there; he called their rest "the drying of nets", since fishermen, when they stop fishing, usually spread out their nets and dry them. "It will be by itself," he says; that is, the soul being saved will be separated from impiety. He says also that the multitude of fish is like not a river but the greatest sea. For the new people is not equal in number to the former people, but is likened to the sea of the nations and fills the world. To this he adds: 11. "And at its outlet, and at its turning, and at its overflow, its marshes shall not be healed; they are given over to salt." And we see this has happened at the present time: for once we had grown into a multitude, we ran aground on sloth. The Master too foretold the same: "For when lawlessness is multiplied," he says, "the love of many will grow cold." So the superficial, who merely wear the preaching like a cloak, as most of us do, he calls marshes; for marshes too

are not deep, but have their water on the surface. So he says that those in this condition do not obtain healing. Yet even so, he says, they are not useless to the rest; for when they are chastised they will become an occasion of benefit to others. That is why he said, "They will be given over to salt." For not only the teaching word but also the punishment inflicted for sin knows somehow how to season us and fill us with benefit. Having thus foretold what concerns the slothful, he again describes the fruits of the earnest and the saints, and says that nothing among them is fruitless, but everything is good to eat. And besides the fruit:

12. "And its leaf shall not fall off, nor shall it grow old upon it, nor shall its fruit fail; from its newness it will bear first fruits for its months, because their waters flow out from the holy places; and their fruit shall be for food, and their growth for health." All these trees, he says, will bear this edible fruit continually. For not once a year, but every month; for the saints are not pious only at festivals, but continually fulfil the keeping of the divine laws. And the leaves too, he says, shall not fall from them. For delight follows on them in the practice of virtue. "And their fruit is all for food." For we are accustomed to admire the athletes of virtue. "And their growth for health." For when we reckon how great a good is the life that accords with God, we reap the benefit of it and obtain the health that accords with God. Next the prophet is taught what the borders of Israel are. On the north, he says, is the road of Hamath, between the borders of Damascus. Hamath some call Epiphania, and others Emesa. For the divine Scripture knows two places of the same name; it says: "To Hamath the great." On the east he says the border is the Jordan and the palm grove toward the east; on the south, as far as the waters of contradiction, for that is how the Syrian translated "Marimoth"; and on the west the border is the sea. He commanded that this land be divided not only among those who trace their descent from Israel but also among the proselytes who sojourn in their midst, "who," he says, "have begotten sons among you." "And the proselytes who live with each tribe," he says, "shall receive their inheritance with that same tribe."

CHAPTER 48. Then he commands that the tribe of Dan receive the first portion, starting from the north; Asher the second, Naphtali the third, Manasseh the fourth, Ephraim the fifth, Reuben the sixth, Judah the seventh; then the portion set apart for the priests, twenty-five thousand in breadth and ten thousand in length; and he commands that this allotment be placed around the

city. "For my sanctuary shall be in their midst, for the priests who are sanctified, the sons of Zadok, who keep the charge of the house." Then again he marks off the five hundred cubits of the temple in the middle of the city. And while the city is being built, he says, let the produce of this land be set apart for those working on the building. Then after this he commands Benjamin to take his allotment, after him Simeon, then Issachar, and Zebulun after him, and Gad last. He says also that the city will have twelve gates, three on each side; and the whole circuit, he said, is eighteen thousand cubits. 35. "And the name of the city, from whatever day it comes to be, shall be its name." It did not take another name after it was built; for it was called Jerusalem even after Zerubbabel. Rather, by these words he hinted that it would again become illustrious. For Scripture often uses "name" to mean glory, just as the same prophet said to Jerusalem in the person of God: "And you gained a name." This rebuilding of the city after the return from Babylon was first undertaken by Zerubbabel, who took a long time to build the temple because of the war with the neighbouring peoples; Nehemiah restored the walls, eighty years having passed in between after the building of the temple was finished. Under the Maccabees too it again enjoyed great prosperity and renovation, and after them Herod in turn made it more splendid. But Apollinaris, who delights in myths and differs in no way from old women telling fables, promises us another building of Jerusalem, and worship according to the law of the Jews, and in addition to the keeping of the law [?] … "I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me; another comes in his own name, and him you will receive." And concerning the temple he says, first, that "there shall not be left here one stone upon another that shall not be thrown down." Then: "Behold, your house is left to you desolate." And Isaiah too cries out: "The city of the ungodly shall never be built." And:

"The house of Israel has fallen; it shall rise no more." Nor, it seems, has he heard the teaching of Paul, which he set before the Galatians, saying: "You who are justified by the law have fallen from grace." And again: "For by works of the law no flesh shall be justified, but through faith in Jesus Christ." And: "For the law brings about wrath; for where there is no law, there is no transgression either." And again: "For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the just requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit." And elsewhere: "Therefore, being justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." And to Peter, who had made a show of keeping the law because of the weakness of the disciples, he said in front of everyone: "If you, being a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, why do you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?" Then he adds: "We who are Jews by nature, and not Gentile sinners, knowing that a person is not justified by works of the law but through the hearing of faith, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, in order to be justified by faith." So he calls the Galatians foolish for submitting to circumcision after coming to faith. And writing to the Philippians, accusing those who teach these things, he calls them dogs, saying: "Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of the mutilation; for we are the circumcision, who worship God in the Spirit and put no confidence in the flesh." And so that no one might suppose that he relied on spiritual things because he had no share in fleshly ones, he fittingly added: "Though I myself have grounds for confidence even in the flesh. If anyone else thinks he has confidence in the flesh, I have more." And he recounts the marks of Jewish distinction: "Circumcised on the eighth day." I received circumcision according to the law, he says. And since it happened that the sons of proselytes were also circumcised after this number of days, he necessarily added: "Of the stock of Israel." And he is not content with the name of the patriarch, but also gives the name of the tribe, to show its distinction: "of the tribe of Benjamin." For I trace my descent, he says, from Rachel, the beloved. Not only am I not one of the half-slaves, but even compared with the free I have a distinction,

since I sprang from the one who was betrothed first and greatly loved. From there he goes up to the more ancient root: "a Hebrew of Hebrews." For the Hebrews were named after Eber. And I also belonged, he says, to the finest sect: "as to the law, a Pharisee." I did not have merely the name of piety, but chose also to be adorned with the reality: "as to zeal," he says, "a persecutor of the church." Having thus recounted everything that seemed honourable, he added: "But whatever was gain to me, these things I have counted as loss for Christ's sake, and I count all things as refuse, that I may gain Christ." Yet the very things that blessed Paul called loss and refuse when he set them beside spiritual things, these the most wise Apollinaris said will be proclaimed to the Jews by Elijah and confirmed by Christ the Master himself. Let him tell us, then: why ever will he give the Jews the way of life according to the law? Because faith cannot give salvation? And in that case, why would he not grant this to all of us Gentiles as well, so as to give them complete salvation? But if he put an end to the observance of the law because faith suffices both to save and to procure the kingdom of heaven, why will he again impose on the Jews the law that cannot save? For that most of it provides no righteousness to those who keep it, God himself has taught us through this prophet: "For I gave them," he says, "statutes that were not good, and ordinances by which they shall not live." How then will he again impose on the Jews what is not good and cannot give life, if he wishes to save them and not to destroy them? And from another angle it is easy to see the folly of anyone who expects these things. For if the things of the Jews are a type of ours—and he agrees with this and does not dispute it—what need is there of the yearly lamb after the sacrifice of the spotless Lamb, who took away the sin of the world? What benefit is there in unleavened bread after the heavenly bread, or in a Passover of types after the one celebrated spiritually [?]? But he neither hears the divine Apostle saying: "Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. For Christ our Passover was sacrificed for us"; nor the Lord teaching his disciples and saying: "This is my body, which is broken for you; do this in remembrance of me." And: "This is my blood, which is shed for you for the forgiveness of sins; do this in remembrance of me." And elsewhere, having said to the Jews, "Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died," he added: "This is

the bread of life, so that one may eat of it and not die." And to pass over the other points, which are countless: there are now in Jerusalem the church of the Cross, and the church of the Resurrection, and that of the Ascension, and the church on Zion, and holy Bethlehem, and countless other houses of prayer besides. When the Jewish temple has been rebuilt, then, will these be destroyed, or will they too remain in honour? And if they keep their former honour, will they be honoured by the Jews or dishonoured? If the Jews dishonour them, they will remain in their former madness and will gain no benefit from the preaching of the great Elijah. But if they honour them, which house of prayer will they honour more? That of the Cross, or that of the Resurrection, or the one that is to be built? If they honour that one more, they will do so because they lack perfect knowledge; if they prefer these, the building of that one is superfluous; and if they give equal honour to these and to that one, they will offer their sacrifices there and partake of the sacred mysteries here. And how can they partake of the divine mysteries together with those who have come to faith from among the Gentiles, when the law forbids mixing with the Gentiles? It remains, then, that in the temple itself both the rites of the gospel and those of the law be performed at the same time; and then there must again be fighting and strife, with us living by our own way of life and them choosing worship according to the law. And how then is Paul telling the truth when he says: "Christ is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the dividing wall of the partition, abolishing in his flesh the enmity, the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, so that he might create the two"—that is, the Gentile and the Jew—"into one new man, and reconcile both in one Spirit to the Father"? And again: "There is neither Jew nor Greek." And elsewhere: "Where there is neither Jew nor Greek, circumcision nor uncircumcision, but Christ is all and in all." "Yes," says the most wise one, "even in the time of the apostles the Jews in Jerusalem who had believed the preaching kept up the worship according to the law, while the other churches lived outside the law." And he does not understand that the holy apostles, condescending to their weakness, allowed this to happen at that time, while they themselves broke the law without fear—which they would never have dared to break if they had known that keeping the law was necessary. But they themselves, knowing that life according to the law was superfluous, pursued the life of the gospel, while to those who were weak they conceded the keeping of the law, little by little

guiding them toward what is more perfect. Thus blessed Paul circumcised Timothy and appointed him a teacher of the gospel way of life. But perhaps we too have taken on a share of Apollinaris' drivel by trying to refute his mythology, which is not only false but tedious as well; to him blessed Paul might fittingly say: "I wish those who unsettle you would even cut themselves off!" Here, then, we bring our discourse to a close, and we ask those who read this book, if they find anything in our interpretation worthy of their eagerness, to praise the Master of all, who for the common good has granted the revelation of hidden things; but if the gain is less than they hoped and the fruit not equal to the labour, to grant pardon to the weakness of our nature, yet still to accept our eagerness, and to repay our labours with prayers, asking forgiveness of sins for us from the Saviour of all; with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the endless ages of ages. Amen.
